subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Drugs used in Disorders of Ear, Nose, Throat and Eye
question: Classify the drugs used in disorders of the eye. Describe the method of instilling eye drops and the nurse's responsibilities. Name two antibiotics used in eye infections.

diagram.caption: Instillation of eye drops into the lower conjunctival sac
labels: lower lid pulled down to form a pocket
dropper held 1–2 cm above without touching
finger pressing the inner canthus (nasolacrimal occlusion)

answer_html:
Introduction The eye is treated mostly by topical drugs – drops, ointments and gels – because they reach the cornea and conjunctiva in high concentration with little effect on the rest of the body. A few eye diseases (glaucoma attacks, severe infections, uveitis) need oral or injectable drugs as well. Every ward and OPD nurse instils eye medicines, so correct technique and knowledge of each group are essential.

1. Classification of ocular drugs | Group | Examples (usual strength) | Main use | |---|---|---| | Antibacterial | Chloramphenicol 0.5%, gentamicin 0.3%, tobramycin 0.3%, ciprofloxacin 0.3%, ofloxacin, moxifloxacin 0.5%, sulfacetamide 10–20% | Bacterial conjunctivitis, corneal ulcer, stye, post-operative prophylaxis | | Antiviral | Acyclovir 3% eye ointment, ganciclovir 0.15% gel | Herpes simplex keratitis (dendritic ulcer), herpes zoster ophthalmicus | | Antifungal | Natamycin 5% suspension, voriconazole 1%, fluconazole 0.3% | Fungal keratitis (very common in Indian farmers after vegetable-matter injury) | | Corticosteroids | Prednisolone acetate 1%, dexamethasone 0.1%, fluorometholone, loteprednol | Uveitis, allergic eye disease, after cataract surgery | | NSAIDs | Ketorolac 0.5%, nepafenac, flurbiprofen | Post-operative inflammation, cystoid macular oedema prevention | | Anti-allergic | Olopatadine 0.1%, ketotifen, sodium cromoglycate 2% | Allergic and vernal conjunctivitis | | Mydriatics and cycloplegics | Atropine 1%, homatropine 2%, cyclopentolate 1%, tropicamide 1%, phenylephrine 2.5–10% | Fundus examination, refraction, uveitis | | Miotics | Pilocarpine 1–4% | Angle-closure glaucoma | | Anti-glaucoma drugs | Latanoprost, timolol, brimonidine, dorzolamide; oral acetazolamide; IV mannitol | Glaucoma | | Local anaesthetics | Proparacaine 0.5%, lignocaine 4% | Tonometry, foreign body removal, minor procedures | | Tear substitutes (lubricants) | Carboxymethylcellulose 0.5%, hydroxypropyl methylcellulose, polyethylene glycol gels | Dry eye, exposure keratopathy, unconscious patients | | Diagnostic agents | Fluorescein 2%, rose bengal | Staining corneal abrasions and ulcers | | Antiseptic | Povidone-iodine 5% | Pre-operative preparation of conjunctival sac |

Two antibiotics used in eye infections: chloramphenicol 0.5% eye drops and moxifloxacin 0.5% eye drops (others – ciprofloxacin, gentamicin, tobramycin).

2. Dosage forms and their features

  • Eye drops (solutions/suspensions) – easy to use, quick action, but washed away by tears in 5–10 minutes; suspensions must be shaken well.
  • Eye ointments – longer contact time, used at night; blur vision, so usually given at bedtime.
  • Gels – in-between action, fewer instillations.
  • Periocular and intravitreal injections – given by ophthalmologists for endophthalmitis or macular disease.
  • Systemic drugs – oral acetazolamide, IV mannitol, oral antivirals and steroids when topical therapy is not enough.

3. Method of instilling eye drops

  1. Check the order – right patient, right drug, right eye (RE/LE/BE), right strength, right time; check the expiry date and the date of opening.
  2. Wash hands; explain the procedure; make the patient sit or lie with the head tilted back and looking up.
  3. Clean any discharge from the lid margin from the inner to the outer canthus with sterile moist cotton, using a separate swab for each eye.
  4. Gently pull the lower lid down to form a pocket (lower conjunctival sac).
  5. Hold the dropper 1–2 cm above the eye without touching the lashes or cornea; instil one drop into the lower fornix, not directly on the cornea.
  6. Ask the patient to close the eye gently (not squeeze) and press the inner canthus (nasolacrimal duct) for 1–2 minutes – this keeps the drug in the eye and reduces systemic absorption (important for timolol and atropine, especially in children).
  7. If more than one drop is ordered, keep a gap of 5 minutes between drops; drops before ointment.
  8. Ointment – apply a 1 cm ribbon along the lower fornix from inner to outer canthus.
  9. Wipe excess fluid, replace the cap, wash hands and document drug, eye and time.

4. Nurse's responsibilities

  1. Separate bottle for each patient (and often each eye after surgery) to prevent cross-infection; never use another patient's drops.
  2. Discard opened bottles after 4 weeks (or as labelled); write the opening date on the bottle; store some drops (e.g. chloramphenicol, latanoprost before opening) in the refrigerator as directed.
  3. Steroid drops – never used without an eye specialist's advice: they can worsen herpes and fungal ulcers and cause cataract and glaucoma with long use; taper, do not stop suddenly in uveitis.
  4. Local anaesthetic drops – only for examination; never given to the patient to take home, because repeated use delays healing and damages the cornea; protect the numb eye from dust and rubbing.
  5. Observe for allergy (redness, itching, lid swelling), stinging and blurred vision; warn the patient not to drive until vision clears.
  6. Contact lenses must be removed before instilling drops and reinserted after about 15 minutes.
  7. In corneal ulcer, drops may be needed hourly day and night in the first 48 hours – plan care so that no dose is missed; fortified antibiotic drops from the pharmacy must be kept cold.
  8. Patient teaching – hand washing, technique, timing, completing the course, not sharing drops, and attending follow-up.

Nursing importance

  • Most eye infections and post-operative complications can be prevented or cured by correctly timed and correctly instilled drops.
  • Wrong drug in the wrong eye, contaminated bottles or misuse of steroid and anaesthetic drops can cause blindness, so double-checking is part of safe practice.

Conclusion Ocular drugs include anti-infectives, anti-inflammatories, anti-allergics, pupil-acting drugs, anti-glaucoma agents, lubricants and diagnostic dyes. The nurse makes them effective by correct choice of bottle, aseptic technique, nasolacrimal occlusion and good patient teaching.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Drugs used in Disorders of Ear, Nose, Throat and Eye
question: Classify the drugs used in glaucoma. Describe their mechanism of action, adverse effects and the nurse's responsibilities.

diagram.caption: Aqueous humour flow and sites of action of anti-glaucoma drugs
labels: ciliary body producing aqueous (blocked by timolol
trabecular meshwork and Schlemm's canal (increased by pilocarpine)

answer_html:
Introduction Glaucoma is a group of eye diseases in which raised intraocular pressure (IOP) damages the optic nerve and causes progressive, irreversible loss of the visual field – often called the "silent thief of sight". Normal IOP is 10–21 mmHg. Anti-glaucoma drugs lower IOP either by reducing the production of aqueous humour by the ciliary body or by increasing its outflow through the trabecular meshwork or uveoscleral route.

1. Classification | Group | Drugs | How IOP falls | |---|---|---| | Prostaglandin (PGF2α) analogues | Latanoprost 0.005%, bimatoprost, travoprost | ↑ uveoscleral outflow | | β-blockers | Timolol 0.25–0.5%, betaxolol | ↓ aqueous production | | α2-agonists | Brimonidine 0.2%, apraclonidine | ↓ production and ↑ uveoscleral outflow | | Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (CAIs) | Topical dorzolamide 2%, brinzolamide 1%; oral/IV acetazolamide | ↓ production | | Miotics (cholinergic agonists) | Pilocarpine 1–4% | ↑ trabecular outflow; pulls the iris away from the angle | | Hyperosmotic agents | Mannitol 20% IV, oral glycerol 50% | Draw water out of the vitreous – rapid fall in IOP | | Fixed combinations | Timolol + dorzolamide, timolol + brimonidine, latanoprost + timolol | Two actions in one bottle – better adherence |

2. Prostaglandin analogues – first-line drugs for open-angle glaucoma

  • Latanoprost 0.005%, one drop once daily at night (more frequent use is less effective).
  • Adverse effects: conjunctival redness, stinging, brown darkening of the iris (permanent, more in hazel eyes), longer and darker eyelashes, darkening of eyelid skin, rarely macular oedema and flare of uveitis or herpes.
  • Unopened bottles are stored in the refrigerator.

3. β-blockers – timolol

  • One drop twice daily; lowers IOP by 20–25%.
  • Systemic absorption through the nasolacrimal duct can cause bradycardia, heart block, hypotension, bronchospasm (dangerous in asthma and COPD), masking of hypoglycaemia, fatigue and depression.
  • Contraindicated in asthma, COPD, sinus bradycardia, second/third-degree heart block and uncontrolled heart failure; betaxolol (β1-selective) is safer in mild lung disease.

4. α2-agonists – brimonidine

  • Used three times daily, also as add-on therapy; apraclonidine prevents IOP spikes after laser.
  • Adverse effects: allergic follicular conjunctivitis, dry mouth, drowsiness and fatigue.
  • Contraindicated in infants and young children (CNS depression, apnoea) and with MAO inhibitors.

5. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors

  • Topical dorzolamide/brinzolamide – stinging, bitter taste, corneal oedema in damaged corneas.
  • Oral acetazolamide 250 mg four times daily (or 500 mg SR twice daily); IV 500 mg in an acute attack.
  • Adverse effects of acetazolamide: tingling of fingers and toes (paraesthesia), frequent urination, hypokalaemia, metabolic acidosis, kidney stones, loss of appetite, depression; avoid in sulfonamide allergy, severe liver or kidney disease.

6. Miotics – pilocarpine

  • Contracts the ciliary muscle and sphincter pupillae → opens the trabecular meshwork and the angle.
  • Used mainly in acute angle-closure glaucoma (after the IOP has been reduced) and before laser iridotomy.
  • Adverse effects: brow ache and headache, small pupil with dim vision in poor light and night-driving difficulty, induced myopia, rarely retinal detachment; systemic – sweating, salivation, diarrhoea, bradycardia.

7. Hyperosmotic agents

  • Mannitol 20% 1–2 g/kg IV over 30–45 minutes – rapid fall in IOP in acute attacks and before surgery.
  • Oral glycerol 50% (1–1.5 g/kg, with lemon juice) – avoid in diabetics.
  • Adverse effects: headache, nausea, fluid overload and pulmonary oedema (care in heart and kidney disease), dehydration, urinary retention in elderly men.

8. Emergency drug regimen in acute angle-closure glaucoma

  1. IV acetazolamide 500 mg, then oral 250 mg 6-hourly.
  2. Topical timolol, brimonidine and prednisolone drops.
  3. Pilocarpine 2% every 15 minutes for two doses once IOP starts falling (both eyes – the other eye is at risk).
  4. IV mannitol if IOP remains very high; analgesics and antiemetics.
  5. Definitive treatment – laser peripheral iridotomy in both eyes.

9. Nurse's responsibilities

  1. Teach correct instillation with nasolacrimal occlusion for 1–2 minutes and a 5-minute gap between different drops.
  2. Check pulse and ask about asthma/breathlessness before starting timolol; report pulse below 60/min.
  3. Explain that glaucoma treatment is lifelong – drugs control but do not cure, and vision already lost does not return; poor adherence is the main reason for blindness in treated patients.
  4. Warn patients on pilocarpine about dim vision at night; advise good lighting at home to prevent falls in the elderly.
  5. During acetazolamide therapy – encourage fluids, monitor potassium, give potassium-rich foods or supplements as ordered.
  6. During mannitol infusion – use an in-line filter, warm the bottle if crystals are seen, monitor urine output, breath sounds and BP; insert a catheter if needed in elderly men.
  7. Avoid drugs that dilate the pupil (atropine, antihistamines, some antidepressants) in patients with narrow angles or angle-closure glaucoma; check the drug chart for such orders.
  8. Advise regular IOP and visual-field check-ups and screening of first-degree relatives above 40 years.

Nursing importance

  • Glaucoma is a leading cause of irreversible blindness in India; most patients have no symptoms, so the nurse's teaching on adherence and follow-up decides the outcome.
  • Recognising an acute attack (severe eye pain, headache, vomiting, haloes, red eye, sudden blurred vision) and starting the emergency regimen quickly can save the eye.

Conclusion Glaucoma drugs reduce aqueous production (β-blockers, α2-agonists, CAIs) or increase outflow (prostaglandin analogues, miotics), while hyperosmotic agents give rapid relief in emergencies. Safe, lifelong use with correct technique and monitoring preserves the patient's remaining vision.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Drugs used in Disorders of Ear, Nose, Throat and Eye
question: Write a note on chloramphenicol eye drops – composition, action, dose, indications, contraindications, adverse effects and nursing implications.
answer_html:
Introduction Chloramphenicol is a broad-spectrum antibiotic that is rarely given by mouth now because of serious blood toxicity, but it remains one of the most widely used topical eye antibiotics because it penetrates the eye well and is cheap.

1. Composition and preparations

  • Chloramphenicol eye drops 0.5% w/v (5 mg/mL), often with a preservative; eye ointment 1%.
  • Combinations: chloramphenicol with dexamethasone or polymyxin B (used only on prescription).
  • Unopened bottles are usually stored in the refrigerator (2–8°C); once opened, discard after 28 days.

2. Mechanism of action

  • Binds to the 50S ribosomal subunit of bacteria and inhibits protein synthesis – mainly bacteriostatic.
  • Active against many Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms – Staphylococci, Streptococci, H. influenzae, Neisseria, Chlamydia; poor against Pseudomonas.

3. Dose

  • 1–2 drops every 2 hours for the first 48 hours, then every 4 hours, continued for 48 hours after the eye looks normal (usual course 5–7 days).
  • Ointment – applied at bedtime, or 3–4 times a day if drops are not used.

4. Indications

  • Acute bacterial conjunctivitis (sticky red eye).
  • Blepharitis, stye (hordeolum) with conjunctivitis.
  • Prophylaxis after removal of corneal foreign bodies, minor injuries and eye surgery.
  • Superficial corneal infections (along with specialist care for ulcers).

5. Contraindications and precautions

  • Hypersensitivity to chloramphenicol.
  • Personal or family history of bone-marrow aplasia or blood disorders (very rare aplastic anaemia has been reported even after eye use).
  • Caution in pregnancy, breastfeeding and neonates (systemic chloramphenicol causes "grey baby syndrome"); avoid prolonged or repeated courses.
  • Not a substitute for specialist care in corneal ulcer, painful red eye with reduced vision, or neonatal conjunctivitis.

6. Adverse effects

  • Transient stinging or burning, blurred vision for a few minutes.
  • Allergic reactions – itching, lid swelling, contact dermatitis.
  • Superinfection with resistant bacteria or fungi on long use.
  • Rarely – bone-marrow depression (aplastic anaemia).

7. Nursing implications

  1. Check the eye, strength and expiry/opening date; keep a separate bottle for each patient.
  2. Clean discharge first; instil into the lower fornix; press the inner canthus for a minute.
  3. Teach the patient to remove contact lenses during treatment and not to wear them until the infection clears.
  4. Stress completing the course; review if no improvement in 48 hours or if pain, photophobia or reduced vision develops.
  5. Advise hand washing, separate towels and avoiding rubbing the eyes – conjunctivitis spreads easily in schools and hostels.
  6. Ask about previous blood disorders and report any unusual bruising, fever or sore throat on long courses.

Nursing importance Chloramphenicol drops are among the most common prescriptions in eye OPDs and casualty after foreign-body removal. Correct use cures infection and prevents corneal ulcer; misuse encourages resistance.

Conclusion Chloramphenicol 0.5% eye drops are an effective, low-cost, broad-spectrum eye antibiotic. Frequent correct instillation, a full course and attention to rare blood toxicity make their use safe.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Drugs used in Disorders of Ear, Nose, Throat and Eye
question: Explain the mydriatics and cycloplegics with their uses, adverse effects and nursing implications.
answer_html:
Definition Mydriatics are drugs that dilate the pupil. Cycloplegics are drugs that paralyse the ciliary muscle, abolishing accommodation. Antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) drops are both mydriatic and cycloplegic, whereas sympathomimetic drops such as phenylephrine dilate the pupil without cycloplegia.

1. Classification | Drug | Type | Duration of action | Main use | |---|---|---|---| | Atropine 1% drops/ointment | Antimuscarinic | 7–10 days (up to 2 weeks) | Refraction in young children, uveitis | | Homatropine 2% | Antimuscarinic | 1–3 days | Uveitis (iridocyclitis) | | Cyclopentolate 1% | Antimuscarinic | About 24 hours | Refraction in older children and adults | | Tropicamide 0.5–1% | Antimuscarinic | 4–6 hours | Fundus examination, routine dilatation | | Phenylephrine 2.5–10% | α1-agonist (sympathomimetic) | 3–5 hours | Dilatation with tropicamide before cataract surgery or fundus exam |

2. Mechanism of action

  • Antimuscarinics block acetylcholine at the sphincter pupillae (→ mydriasis) and the ciliary muscle (→ cycloplegia).
  • Phenylephrine stimulates α1 receptors of the dilator pupillae (→ mydriasis only).

3. Uses

  1. Fundus examination (diabetic and hypertensive retinopathy, retinal detachment) – tropicamide ± phenylephrine.
  2. Refraction (cycloplegic refraction) in children, because their strong accommodation hides refractive errors – atropine or cyclopentolate.
  3. Uveitis (iritis) – atropine/homatropine relieve pain from ciliary spasm, rest the eye and prevent posterior synechiae (adhesion of iris to lens).
  4. Before and after cataract and retinal surgery.
  5. Low-dose atropine 0.01% – used by specialists to slow the progression of myopia in children.
  6. To break recent synechiae (mydriatic combinations).

4. Adverse effects

  • Local: stinging, photophobia and glare, blurred near vision, allergic contact dermatitis (atropine).
  • Precipitation of acute angle-closure glaucoma in people with narrow angles (especially elderly hypermetropes).
  • Systemic atropine toxicity, especially in infants and young children – dry mouth, flushing, fever, rapid pulse, restlessness, delirium and convulsions ("hot as a hare, dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter").
  • Phenylephrine 10% – rise in BP and tachycardia; avoid in infants, hypertension and heart disease.

5. Nursing implications

  1. Ask about glaucoma or previous eye pain with haloes before dilating; report severe eye pain or headache after dilatation.
  2. Use nasolacrimal occlusion and the lowest strength in children; keep atropine bottles out of reach of children.
  3. Tell patients that vision will be blurred for several hours (tropicamide) or days (atropine) – no driving; give dark glasses for glare.
  4. In outpatient fundus clinics, record the time of instillation and check pupil dilatation after 20–30 minutes.
  5. Watch infants for flushing, fever and irritability; wipe excess drops from the cheek.

Nursing importance Mydriatics are used every day in eye OPDs, diabetic screening camps and before cataract surgery. Screening for narrow angles and warning about blurred vision prevent avoidable glaucoma attacks and road accidents.

Conclusion Antimuscarinic drops dilate the pupil and paralyse accommodation, while phenylephrine only dilates the pupil. Their choice depends on the duration needed, and their safe use depends on careful patient selection and teaching.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Drugs used in Disorders of Ear, Nose, Throat and Eye
question: Explain the drugs used in disorders of the ear, including soda glycerine and boric spirit ear drops, with the method of instillation.
answer_html:
Introduction Ear disorders such as impacted wax, otitis externa, fungal infection (otomycosis) and otitis media are treated with topical ear drops, sometimes with oral antibiotics and analgesics. The most important rule in ear pharmacology is to know whether the ear drum (tympanic membrane) is intact, because many drops damage the middle and inner ear if they pass through a perforation.

1. Ceruminolytics (wax softeners)

  • Soda glycerine ear drops – sodium bicarbonate (about 5%) in glycerine and water; alkaline solution that softens and loosens wax.
    • Dose: 3–5 drops, 3–4 times a day for 3–5 days before syringing or suction.
    • Avoid in perforated ear drum, active infection and grommets.
  • Others: liquid paraffin, olive oil, docusate sodium, hydrogen peroxide solution.

2. Antiseptic and drying drops – boric spirit

  • Boric acid (2–4%) dissolved in rectified spirit (alcohol).
  • Actions: mild antiseptic and antifungal, acidifies the ear canal, dries a moist canal.
  • Uses: otomycosis, mild otitis externa, prevention of "swimmer's ear", drying a wet canal after aural toilet.
  • Precautions: causes burning pain if the drum is perforated or the canal is raw; not used in infants (boric acid toxicity) or on large raw areas.

3. Antibiotic and antibiotic–steroid drops

  • Ciprofloxacin 0.3%, ofloxacin 0.3% – preferred in chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM) with perforation because quinolones are not ototoxic.
  • Gentamicin, neomycin, framycetin, polymyxin B – effective, but ototoxic; avoid when the drum is perforated.
  • Combinations with steroids (betamethasone, dexamethasone) – reduce swelling and itching in otitis externa.

4. Antifungal ear drops

  • Clotrimazole 1% (often with lignocaine), miconazole, nystatin; combinations with chloramphenicol and beclomethasone.
  • Used for otomycosis (Aspergillus niger – black spores, Candida) after careful cleaning of the canal.

5. Others

  • Analgesic drops (lignocaine, benzocaine combinations) – for pain of acute otitis media with intact drum.
  • Oral drugs – analgesics (paracetamol, ibuprofen), antibiotics (amoxicillin in acute otitis media), antihistamines/decongestants, and betahistine or vestibular sedatives for vertigo.

6. Method of instilling ear drops

  1. Check the order (right/left/both ears); warm the bottle in the hand – cold drops cause giddiness.
  2. Patient lies on the side with the affected ear up.
  3. Straighten the canal – adults: pull the pinna up and back; children under 3 years: pull down and back.
  4. Instil the prescribed drops along the canal wall without touching the ear; press the tragus gently a few times.
  5. Keep the patient in the same position for 2–5 minutes; place a loose cotton plug only if ordered.

Nursing implications

  • Do aural toilet (dry mopping or suction) before drops – drops cannot act through pus or debris.
  • Never use ototoxic drops or soda glycerine in a perforated or discharging ear; report dizziness, ringing or reduced hearing.
  • Teach patients not to use oil, cotton buds or sharp objects in the ear and to keep the ear dry during treatment.

Conclusion Ear drugs include wax softeners, antiseptic drying agents, antibiotic, antifungal and steroid drops. Knowing the state of the ear drum and using the correct technique make them safe and effective.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Drugs used in Disorders of Ear, Nose, Throat and Eye
question: Explain the drugs used for the nose and buccal cavity, with special reference to chlorhexidine mouthwash.
answer_html:
Introduction The nose and mouth are lined by mucous membranes that are easily infected, inflamed or ulcerated. Local drugs used here clean the surface, kill germs, relieve pain and shrink swelling. Nurses use these preparations daily in oral care of sick, unconscious and ventilated patients, in cancer wards and in ENT OPDs.

1. Drugs used for the nose

  • Saline nasal drops/spray (0.65%) – thin and clear mucus; safe for infants with blocked nose before feeds.
  • Nasal decongestants (oxymetazoline, xylometazoline) – short-term use only (not more than 5–7 days) to avoid rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa).
  • Intranasal corticosteroids – fluticasone, mometasone, budesonide; first choice for allergic rhinitis and nasal polyps; act after several days of regular use.
  • Antihistamine spray – azelastine for allergic rhinitis.
  • Mupirocin 2% nasal ointment – to clear nasal carriage of MRSA in hospital staff and patients.
  • Topical vasoconstrictor + local anaesthetic packs – used by ENT surgeons in epistaxis and before nasal procedures.

2. Drugs used for the buccal cavity (mouth and throat) A. Chlorhexidine mouthwash

  • Composition: chlorhexidine gluconate 0.12–0.2% solution.
  • Action: broad-spectrum antiseptic – damages bacterial cell membranes; binds to teeth and mucosa and keeps acting for hours (substantivity); reduces plaque and gum inflammation.
  • Dose: 10–15 mL rinsed in the mouth for 30–60 seconds, twice daily, then spat out (not swallowed).
  • Uses: gingivitis and plaque control, oral care of ventilated, unconscious and post-operative patients, after dental extraction and oral surgery, aphthous and denture-related stomatitis, prevention of oral infection in chemotherapy patients.
  • Adverse effects: brown staining of teeth and tongue, altered taste, burning sensation, dry mouth, rarely parotid swelling or allergy.
  • Precautions: use 30 minutes after brushing with toothpaste (some toothpaste ingredients inactivate it); avoid eating and drinking for 30 minutes after rinsing; do not use for long periods without advice.

B. Other mouth preparations

  • Povidone-iodine 1% gargle – sore throat, oral antisepsis (avoid in thyroid disease and iodine allergy).
  • Antifungals for oral thrush – nystatin suspension (1 lakh units/mL, 1 mL four times daily, swish and swallow), clotrimazole 10 mg troches five times daily, miconazole oral gel.
  • Topical analgesic and anti-inflammatory gels – lignocaine 2% viscous gel, choline salicylate gels, benzydamine mouthwash for mucositis after radiotherapy or chemotherapy.
  • Triamcinolone oral paste – recurrent aphthous ulcers.
  • Saline or soda bicarbonate mouthwash – simple cleansing in stomatitis and mucositis.

3. Nursing implications

  1. Give regular oral care – brushing, rinsing and moisturising lips – in all dependent patients; it prevents aspiration pneumonia.
  2. In ventilated patients, use the chlorhexidine oral care protocol of the unit along with tooth brushing and suction.
  3. Teach patients not to swallow antiseptic mouthwashes; supervise children.
  4. Remove dentures before applying antifungal drugs; soak dentures in antifungal or antiseptic solution overnight.
  5. Watch for stains, taste change and allergy; reassure that stains can be removed by dental cleaning.

Conclusion Saline, steroid and decongestant preparations treat nasal problems, while chlorhexidine, povidone-iodine, antifungals and protective gels keep the mouth healthy. Correct use of chlorhexidine mouthwash is a simple, powerful tool for preventing hospital infections.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Drugs used in Disorders of Ear, Nose, Throat and Eye
question: Explain the use of antihistamines in ear, nose, throat and eye disorders, with nursing implications.
answer_html:
Introduction Antihistamines (H1-receptor blockers) block the action of histamine released from mast cells during allergic reactions. Histamine causes sneezing, itching, watery discharge, swelling and redness of the nose and eyes. Antihistamines are therefore among the most commonly prescribed drugs in ENT and eye clinics.

1. Mechanism of action

  • Competitively block H1 receptors on blood vessels, nerve endings and smooth muscle → reduce itching, sneezing, rhinorrhoea, lacrimation and oedema.
  • Older (first-generation) drugs also block muscarinic receptors and enter the brain – causing sedation but also helping in vertigo and motion sickness.

2. Uses in ENT and eye disorders | Condition | Antihistamines used | |---|---| | Allergic rhinitis (seasonal and perennial) | Oral cetirizine 10 mg, levocetirizine 5 mg, fexofenadine 120–180 mg, loratadine 10 mg once daily; azelastine nasal spray; often with intranasal steroid | | Allergic and vernal conjunctivitis | Olopatadine 0.1% eye drops twice daily, ketotifen, azelastine eye drops (also mast-cell stabilising) | | Common cold (symptomatic) | Chlorpheniramine in combination with decongestants – limited benefit | | Acute urticaria and angioedema of lips/face | Oral or injectable chlorpheniramine; adrenaline first if airway is involved | | Motion sickness | Promethazine, dimenhydrinate, cinnarizine – taken 30–60 minutes before travel | | Vertigo, Ménière's disease, labyrinthitis | Cinnarizine, promethazine, dimenhydrinate (vestibular sedatives); betahistine (a histamine analogue, not a blocker) | | Pre-operative sedation and antiemetic use | Promethazine |

3. Adverse effects

  • First-generation: drowsiness, impaired driving and work performance, dizziness, dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation, paradoxical excitement in children, confusion in the elderly; may worsen glaucoma.
  • Second-generation: much less sedation; occasionally headache, dry mouth; cetirizine can cause mild drowsiness.
  • Topical eye drops: stinging, headache, bitter taste (azelastine).
  • Cinnarizine in the elderly: weight gain, parkinsonism-like symptoms with long use.

4. Nursing implications

  1. Warn patients on first-generation drugs not to drive, operate machines or drink alcohol.
  2. Prefer non-sedating drugs for students and working adults; give sedating ones at bedtime.
  3. Avoid first-generation drugs in elderly men with prostate enlargement and in narrow-angle glaucoma; watch for confusion and falls in the elderly.
  4. Avoid in infants (risk of sedation and breathing problems) unless prescribed.
  5. Teach allergen avoidance – dust, pollen, pets, smoke – and correct use of nasal sprays (head slightly forward, spray away from the septum).
  6. Remember that antihistamines do not replace adrenaline in anaphylaxis with airway swelling.

Conclusion Antihistamines relieve the allergic symptoms of the nose and eyes and control vertigo and motion sickness. Choosing the right generation, warning about sedation and teaching allergen avoidance make treatment both safe and effective.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Drugs used in Disorders of Ear, Nose, Throat and Eye
question: Name the antifungal ear drops and write their contraindications.
answer_html:
Antifungal ear drops (used in otomycosis)

  • Clotrimazole 1% ear drops (alone or with lignocaine for pain).
  • Miconazole 2%, nystatin, econazole.
  • Combinations – clotrimazole + beclomethasone + chloramphenicol + lignocaine; boric spirit is also mildly antifungal.

Contraindications

  1. Hypersensitivity to the azole or any ingredient.
  2. Perforated tympanic membrane / grommets – especially combination drops containing chloramphenicol, steroid or lignocaine (risk of middle-ear irritation and ototoxicity).
  3. Steroid-containing combinations – not in viral (herpes) or tuberculous infections of the ear.
  4. Use with caution in pregnancy and young infants.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)

question: Write the uses and adverse effects of chlorhexidine mouthwash.
answer_html:
Chlorhexidine gluconate 0.12–0.2% mouthwash is a broad-spectrum antiseptic that binds to teeth and mucosa and acts for several hours.

Uses

  1. Control of dental plaque and gingivitis.
  2. Oral care of ventilated, unconscious and post-operative patients (part of VAP prevention bundles).
  3. After dental extraction and oral surgery; denture stomatitis.
  4. Prevention of oral infection in patients on chemotherapy.

Adverse effects

  1. Brown staining of teeth, tongue and fillings.
  2. Altered taste and burning sensation.
  3. Dry mouth, mucosal irritation; rarely allergy or parotid swelling.

question: Write the uses of fluorescein dye in eye care.
answer_html:
Fluorescein sodium is an orange dye that glows green under cobalt-blue light; it stains areas where the corneal epithelium is lost.

Uses

  1. Detecting corneal abrasions, ulcers and foreign bodies – damaged areas stain bright green.
  2. Applanation tonometry – with a local anaesthetic, to measure intraocular pressure.
  3. Seidel test – to detect aqueous leak after injury or surgery.
  4. Fluorescein angiography (IV injection) – to study retinal blood vessels in diabetic retinopathy.
  5. Assessing tear film break-up time in dry eye and fitting contact lenses.

Use single-use strips to avoid contamination; IV use can cause nausea and rare allergy.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Classify diuretics. Describe the mechanism of action, uses, adverse effects and nursing responsibilities of furosemide, thiazides, spironolactone and mannitol.

diagram.caption: Sites of action of diuretics in the nephron
labels: thick ascending limb of loop of Henle (furosemide)

answer_html:
Definition Diuretics are drugs that increase the output of urine and sodium (natriuresis) by acting on the kidney tubules. They reduce the volume of extracellular fluid and are used in oedema, heart failure, hypertension, raised intracranial pressure and glaucoma.

1. Classification (according to efficacy and site of action) | Group | Site | Examples | |---|---|---| | High-ceiling (loop) diuretics | Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle – Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter | Furosemide, torsemide, bumetanide | | Medium-efficacy (thiazide and thiazide-like) | Early distal convoluted tubule – Na⁺–Cl⁻ symporter | Hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, indapamide, metolazone | | Weak – potassium-sparing | Late distal tubule and collecting duct | Spironolactone, eplerenone (aldosterone antagonists); amiloride, triamterene (Na⁺ channel blockers) | | Weak – carbonic anhydrase inhibitors | Proximal tubule | Acetazolamide | | Osmotic diuretics | Proximal tubule and loop (whole nephron) | Mannitol, glycerol, isosorbide |

2. Furosemide (loop diuretic)

  • Mechanism: blocks the Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter in the thick ascending limb, where about 25% of filtered sodium is reabsorbed → powerful diuresis even when the GFR is low; also dilates veins (relief of pulmonary congestion before diuresis starts).
  • Dose: 20–80 mg orally or 20–40 mg IV (higher doses in kidney failure); IV onset in 5 minutes, oral in 30–60 minutes; action lasts about 6 hours.
  • Uses: acute pulmonary oedema (left ventricular failure), congestive heart failure, oedema of nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis and kidney failure, hypertension with kidney failure, hypercalcaemia and hyperkalaemia (with saline), forced diuresis.
  • Adverse effects: hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypovolaemia and postural hypotension, metabolic alkalosis, hyperuricaemia (gout), hyperglycaemia, ototoxicity (rapid IV injection, high doses, with aminoglycosides), rash (sulfonamide allergy).

3. Thiazides (hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, indapamide)

  • Mechanism: block the Na⁺–Cl⁻ symporter in the distal tubule; moderate diuresis; ineffective when GFR falls below about 30 mL/min (except metolazone).
  • Dose: hydrochlorothiazide 12.5–25 mg, chlorthalidone 12.5–25 mg, indapamide 1.5 mg SR once daily (morning).
  • Uses: hypertension (first-line, especially in the elderly), mild oedema, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (paradoxical reduction of urine volume), recurrent calcium stones (they reduce urinary calcium).
  • Adverse effects: hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia (elderly women), hyperuricaemia, hyperglycaemia, raised lipids, hypercalcaemia, erectile dysfunction, photosensitivity.

4. Spironolactone (potassium-sparing aldosterone antagonist)

  • Mechanism: competitively blocks aldosterone receptors in the collecting duct → less Na⁺ reabsorption and less K⁺ excretion.
  • Dose: 25–100 mg/day (up to 400 mg in ascites).
  • Uses: ascites of cirrhosis (drug of choice), heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (improves survival), primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome), resistant hypertension, with loop/thiazide diuretics to prevent hypokalaemia, hirsutism in PCOS.
  • Adverse effects: hyperkalaemia (dangerous with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium supplements, kidney failure), gynaecomastia, breast tenderness, menstrual irregularities, impotence; eplerenone causes less gynaecomastia.

5. Mannitol (osmotic diuretic)

  • Mechanism: a sugar alcohol that is filtered but not reabsorbed; it holds water in the tubules by osmosis and also draws water out of tissues (brain, eye) into the blood.
  • Dose: 20% solution, 0.25–1 g/kg IV over 20–30 minutes, repeated 6–8 hourly as ordered.
  • Uses: raised intracranial pressure / cerebral oedema (head injury, brain tumour), acute angle-closure glaucoma and before eye surgery, forced diuresis in some poisonings and to protect the kidney in specific situations.
  • Adverse effects: circulatory overload and pulmonary oedema (initial expansion of blood volume), headache, nausea, dehydration, hypernatraemia or hyponatraemia, rebound rise of ICP, thrombophlebitis and tissue damage if it leaks.
  • Contraindications: anuria, congestive heart failure / pulmonary oedema, severe dehydration, active intracranial bleeding (relative).

6. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Baseline and daily monitoring – weight (same time, same scale), intake–output chart, BP lying and standing, pulse, oedema, breath sounds, serum K⁺, Na⁺, Mg²⁺, creatinine, urea, glucose and uric acid.
  2. Give oral diuretics in the morning (and a second dose before 4 pm) to avoid nocturia and disturbed sleep; keep a urinal or commode near elderly patients.
  3. Furosemide IV – inject slowly (not faster than about 4 mg/min for large doses) to prevent ototoxicity; check for tinnitus and hearing loss.
  4. Hypokalaemia (weakness, leg cramps, arrhythmia) – report K⁺ below 3.5 mEq/L; encourage potassium-rich foods (banana, coconut water, orange, tomato, green leafy vegetables) with loop and thiazide diuretics; remember that hypokalaemia increases digoxin toxicity.
  5. Hyperkalaemia with spironolactone – avoid potassium supplements and salt substitutes; monitor K⁺ especially with ACE inhibitors and in kidney disease.
  6. Mannitol – use an in-line filter, dissolve crystals by warming the bottle, give through a large vein; monitor urine output hourly (catheter), CVP or signs of fluid overload, serum osmolality and neurological status.
  7. Prevent falls – rise slowly; watch elderly patients closely in the first days of therapy.
  8. Diabetic patients on thiazides – monitor blood sugar; gout patients – watch for acute attacks.
  9. Teach – purpose of the drug, daily weight at home, reporting rapid weight gain or loss, cramps, dizziness; not to stop drugs suddenly in heart failure; limit salt intake.

Nursing importance

  • Diuretics are used in almost every medical ward and ICU; electrolyte disorders, dehydration and falls caused by them are common, preventable adverse events.
  • The nurse's intake–output chart and daily weight are the simplest and best guides to diuretic dose.

Conclusion Loop diuretics are the most powerful, thiazides are best for hypertension, potassium-sparing drugs balance potassium loss and help in cirrhosis and heart failure, and mannitol reduces brain and eye pressure. Careful monitoring of fluid, electrolytes and kidney function makes diuretic therapy safe.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Explain the renin–angiotensin system and the drugs acting on it, with nursing implications.

diagram.caption: Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and drug sites
labels: angiotensinogen (liver) to angiotensin I by renin (blocked by aliskiren)
to angiotensin II by ACE in lungs (blocked by ACE inhibitors)
AT1 receptor (blocked by ARBs) causing vasoconstriction and aldosterone release (blocked by spironolactone)

answer_html:
Introduction The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) is a hormone system through which the kidney controls blood pressure, sodium and water balance. Overactivity of this system raises BP and damages the heart and kidneys, so drugs that block it are among the most important medicines for hypertension, heart failure and chronic kidney disease.

1. Steps of the renin–angiotensin system

  1. Renin is released from the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney when renal perfusion falls, sodium reaching the macula densa falls, or sympathetic (β1) stimulation increases.
  2. Renin converts angiotensinogen (from the liver) into angiotensin I.
  3. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), mainly in the lungs, converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II; ACE also breaks down bradykinin.
  4. Angiotensin II acts on AT1 receptors → vasoconstriction, release of aldosterone (Na⁺ and water retention, K⁺ loss), ADH release and thirst, sympathetic stimulation, and growth/remodelling of heart and blood vessels.
  5. In the kidney, angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole, keeping the GFR up when perfusion is low.

2. Drugs acting on the system | Group | Examples | Key point | |---|---|---| | Direct renin inhibitor | Aliskiren | Rarely used; never combined with ACEI/ARB | | ACE inhibitors ("-pril") | Enalapril, ramipril, lisinopril, perindopril, captopril | Block formation of angiotensin II; ↑ bradykinin → cough | | Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) ("-sartan") | Telmisartan, losartan, olmesartan, valsartan | Block AT1 receptors; no cough | | ARNI | Sacubitril + valsartan | Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction | | Aldosterone antagonists | Spironolactone, eplerenone, finerenone | Heart failure, cirrhosis, diabetic kidney disease | | β-blockers | Metoprolol, atenolol | Reduce renin release |

3. Uses

  • Hypertension, especially with diabetes, proteinuria, heart failure or after MI.
  • Heart failure – reduce symptoms, hospital admission and death.
  • Diabetic nephropathy and proteinuric CKD – slow progression by reducing intraglomerular pressure.
  • After myocardial infarction – prevent remodelling.

4. Adverse effects

  • First-dose hypotension, dizziness.
  • Dry cough (ACEI) – switch to ARB.
  • Angioedema of lips, tongue and larynx – emergency.
  • Hyperkalaemia, rise in creatinine – especially in dehydration, bilateral renal artery stenosis, or with NSAIDs and diuretics ("triple whammy" for the kidney).
  • Contraindicated in pregnancy – cause foetal kidney damage, oligohydramnios and skull defects.

5. Nursing implications

  1. Check BP before each dose; give the first dose at bedtime with the patient lying down.
  2. Monitor serum K⁺ and creatinine at baseline and 1–2 weeks after starting or increasing the dose.
  3. Teach patients to stop the drug and seek help for swelling of face or lips; report persistent cough.
  4. Avoid potassium supplements, salt substitutes and NSAIDs unless prescribed; teach "sick-day rules" – hold the drug during vomiting, diarrhoea or dehydration and contact the doctor.
  5. Women of reproductive age need contraception counselling; stop the drug as soon as pregnancy is confirmed.

Conclusion The RAAS raises BP through vasoconstriction and salt retention. Renin inhibitors, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, ARNI and aldosterone antagonists block it at different steps, protecting the heart and kidneys when monitored carefully.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Explain urinary acidifiers and alkalinisers with their uses and nursing implications.
answer_html:
Introduction Normal urine pH is about 6 (range 4.5–8). Changing the urine pH helps in treating urinary infections, preventing certain kidney stones, relieving burning micturition and removing some poisons. Drugs that lower urine pH are urinary acidifiers; drugs that raise it are urinary alkalinisers.

1. Urinary acidifiers

  • Ammonium chloride – converted in the liver to urea and hydrochloric acid → acid urine; also used in metabolic alkalosis.
  • Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) in large doses (0.5–2 g/day in divided doses).
  • L-methionine, sodium acid phosphate; cranberry products (mainly prevent bacterial adhesion, little acidifying effect).

Uses

  1. To make methenamine (hexamine) effective – it releases formaldehyde only in acid urine (pH below 5.5–6).
  2. To prevent phosphate (struvite) and calcium phosphate stones, which form in alkaline urine, and to dissolve phosphate encrustation on catheters.
  3. Adjunct in some recurrent UTIs with urea-splitting organisms (Proteus).
  4. Ammonium chloride – correction of metabolic alkalosis.

Contraindications: kidney failure, liver failure (ammonium chloride may cause hyperammonaemia), metabolic acidosis, uric acid and cystine stones, and use with sulfonamides (crystals form in acid urine).

Adverse effects: gastric irritation, nausea, metabolic acidosis, rarely hepatic encephalopathy (ammonium chloride).

2. Urinary alkalinisers

  • Potassium citrate, sodium citrate, disodium hydrogen citrate syrups/granules (common in Indian OPDs), sodium bicarbonate; acetazolamide also alkalinises urine.

Uses

  1. Symptomatic relief of burning micturition (dysuria) in cystitis.
  2. Prevention and dissolution of uric acid and cystine stones; potassium citrate prevents calcium oxalate stones in patients with low urinary citrate.
  3. Enhancing excretion of weak acid poisons – salicylate (aspirin) and phenobarbitone poisoning (urinary alkalinisation).
  4. Preventing crystal formation with sulfonamides and high-dose methotrexate; preventing uric acid nephropathy in tumour lysis.
  5. Correcting metabolic acidosis in kidney disease (sodium bicarbonate).

Contraindications: kidney failure and hyperkalaemia (potassium salts), heart failure, hypertension and oedema (sodium salts), phosphate stones, infections with urea-splitting organisms; reduce the effect of nitrofurantoin and methenamine.

Adverse effects: abdominal discomfort, diarrhoea, hyperkalaemia (potassium citrate), sodium overload (sodium salts), metabolic alkalosis.

3. Nursing implications

  1. Check urine pH with dipstick to see whether the target is reached (e.g. 6.5–7 for uric acid stones).
  2. Dilute syrups/granules in a full glass of water and give after meals to reduce gastric upset.
  3. Encourage 2.5–3 litres of fluid per day in stone formers and UTI patients unless restricted.
  4. Monitor serum potassium, sodium, bicarbonate and creatinine; watch for oedema and BP rise with sodium salts.
  5. Check drug combinations – do not give acidifiers with sulfonamides, or alkalinisers with methenamine/nitrofurantoin.

Conclusion Acidifiers help methenamine act and prevent phosphate stones; alkalinisers relieve dysuria, prevent uric acid and cystine stones and remove acid poisons. Monitoring urine pH and electrolytes guides their safe use.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Explain the urinary antiseptics and the drug treatment of urinary tract infection, with nursing responsibilities.
answer_html:
Introduction Urinary antiseptics are drugs that are concentrated in the urine and kill or inhibit bacteria in the urinary tract without reaching useful levels in the blood. Together with selected systemic antibiotics, they are used to treat and prevent urinary tract infection (UTI) – one of the most common infections in women, catheterised patients and the elderly.

1. Urinary antiseptics | Drug | Key features | |---|---| | Nitrofurantoin | 100 mg twice daily (modified release) for 5 days in uncomplicated cystitis; 50–100 mg at bedtime for prophylaxis; urine turns brown-yellow; give with food; avoid in significant kidney impairment, at term pregnancy and in G6PD deficiency (haemolysis); can cause peripheral neuropathy and lung reactions on long use | | Fosfomycin trometamol | Single 3 g sachet dissolved in water, taken at bedtime after emptying the bladder; useful in ESBL organisms; safe in pregnancy | | Methenamine (hexamine) hippurate | 1 g twice daily for prevention of recurrent UTI; releases formaldehyde in acid urine; not for acute infection; do not combine with sulfonamides or alkalinisers | | Nalidixic acid | Older quinolone, now rarely used because of resistance |

2. Systemic antibiotics commonly used in UTI

  • Cotrimoxazole (if local resistance is low), cephalexin, cefuroxime, amoxicillin–clavulanate.
  • Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) – kept for complicated infections because of rising resistance.
  • Pyelonephritis and sepsis – IV ceftriaxone, aminoglycosides (amikacin), piperacillin–tazobactam or carbapenems for resistant organisms, chosen by culture.

3. Urinary analgesic

  • Phenazopyridine 200 mg three times daily for 2 days – relieves burning; turns urine orange-red and may stain contact lenses and clothes; avoid in kidney failure and G6PD deficiency.

4. Principles of drug treatment of UTI

  1. Send a clean-catch midstream urine (or catheter port sample) for culture before the first dose in complicated, recurrent, male, pregnant or hospital-acquired UTI.
  2. Start empirical therapy according to local antibiogram and national guidelines; change according to culture report.
  3. Short courses for simple cystitis (3–5 days); 7–14 days for pyelonephritis.
  4. Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria, except in pregnancy and before urological procedures.
  5. Remove or change urinary catheters; treat obstruction and stones.

5. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Collect samples correctly and send immediately (or refrigerate up to 4 hours).
  2. Encourage 2–3 litres of fluid daily, frequent voiding, voiding after intercourse, front-to-back cleaning and cotton undergarments.
  3. Give drugs at regular intervals, with food where advised; complete the course.
  4. Monitor temperature, urine output, flank pain and confusion in elderly patients (sign of urosepsis).
  5. Follow CAUTI bundle – insert catheters only when needed, aseptic insertion, closed drainage, bag below bladder level, daily review for removal.
  6. Explain harmless urine colour changes (nitrofurantoin, phenazopyridine) to prevent anxiety.

Conclusion Nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin and methenamine act mainly in the urine, while systemic antibiotics treat deeper infections. Culture-guided treatment, short appropriate courses and good nursing hygiene measures cure UTI and limit antibiotic resistance.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: What are nephrotoxic drugs? Explain the drugs toxic to the kidney and the measures to prevent drug-induced kidney damage.
answer_html:
Definition Nephrotoxic drugs are drugs that can damage the structure or function of the kidney. Because the kidney receives about 25% of the cardiac output and concentrates many drugs in its tubules, it is very vulnerable. Drug-induced kidney injury accounts for a significant share of acute kidney injury (AKI) in hospitals.

1. Mechanisms of kidney damage

  • Reduced renal blood flow (pre-renal injury).
  • Direct tubular cell injury (acute tubular necrosis).
  • Allergic inflammation of the interstitium (acute interstitial nephritis).
  • Crystal deposition in tubules.
  • Glomerular damage and chronic scarring.

2. Common nephrotoxic drugs | Drug group | How it damages the kidney | |---|---| | Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, amikacin) | Proximal tubular necrosis – non-oliguric AKI; risk ↑ with long courses, elderly, dehydration | | Amphotericin B | Constriction of renal vessels and tubular damage – hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, AKI | | Vancomycin (especially with piperacillin–tazobactam), polymyxins/colistin | Tubular injury | | NSAIDs (diclofenac, ibuprofen) | Block prostaglandins that keep the afferent arteriole open → pre-renal AKI; interstitial nephritis; analgesic nephropathy (papillary necrosis) | | ACE inhibitors / ARBs | Remove efferent constriction → fall in GFR in dehydration or renal artery stenosis | | Iodinated contrast media | Contrast-associated AKI within 48–72 hours | | Cisplatin, ifosfamide, high-dose methotrexate | Tubular damage, magnesium loss, crystal nephropathy | | Acyclovir IV, sulfonamides, indinavir | Crystals in tubules | | Cyclosporine, tacrolimus | Renal vasoconstriction; chronic scarring | | Lithium | Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, chronic kidney disease | | Penicillins, PPIs, rifampicin, allopurinol | Acute interstitial nephritis (fever, rash, eosinophilia) | | Tenofovir | Proximal tubular damage (Fanconi-like syndrome) |

3. Patients at high risk

  • Elderly, pre-existing CKD, diabetes, heart failure, cirrhosis, dehydration, sepsis, multiple nephrotoxic drugs together.
  • The "triple whammy" – ACE inhibitor/ARB + diuretic + NSAID – is a well-known cause of AKI.

4. Measures to prevent drug-induced kidney damage

  1. Check serum creatinine and eGFR before starting; adjust doses to kidney function.
  2. Avoid combinations of nephrotoxic drugs; choose safer alternatives (e.g. paracetamol instead of NSAIDs in CKD).
  3. Hydration – IV normal saline before and after contrast studies and cisplatin; adequate fluids with acyclovir and methotrexate.
  4. Therapeutic drug monitoring – trough levels of gentamicin, amikacin and vancomycin; once-daily aminoglycoside dosing; shortest effective course.
  5. Use liposomal amphotericin, saline loading and potassium/magnesium replacement.
  6. Sick-day rules – temporarily stop metformin, ACEI/ARB, diuretics and NSAIDs during vomiting, diarrhoea or fever with poor intake.
  7. Stop the suspected drug at the first rise in creatinine.

5. Nurse's role

  • Maintain an accurate intake–output chart; report urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours.
  • Monitor creatinine, urea, electrolytes and drug levels as ordered; check timing of trough samples.
  • Ask about over-the-counter painkillers and herbal products; educate CKD patients to avoid self-medication.

Conclusion Many common drugs can injure the kidney. Identifying high-risk patients, adjusting doses, avoiding harmful combinations, hydrating and monitoring urine output and creatinine prevent most drug-induced kidney damage.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Explain the antidiuretics – vasopressin and desmopressin – with their uses, adverse effects and nursing implications.
answer_html:
Introduction Antidiuretics are drugs that reduce urine volume by increasing water reabsorption in the kidney. The natural antidiuretic is antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) from the posterior pituitary. Its lack causes diabetes insipidus (DI) – passage of large volumes of dilute urine with intense thirst.

1. Mechanism of action

  • ADH acts on V2 receptors in the collecting duct, inserting aquaporin-2 water channels → water is reabsorbed and urine becomes concentrated.
  • On V1 receptors it causes vasoconstriction (blood vessels, gut, coronary arteries).
  • Desmopressin (DDAVP) is a synthetic analogue that is highly selective for V2 receptors and longer acting, with little vasoconstrictor effect.

2. Preparations and uses A. Vasopressin (aqueous injection)

  • Central diabetes insipidus (acute, e.g. after head injury or pituitary surgery).
  • Vasodilatory (septic) shock – low-dose infusion (about 0.03 units/min) added to noradrenaline.
  • Bleeding oesophageal varices – now largely replaced by terlipressin.

B. Desmopressin

  • Central diabetes insipidus – intranasal spray 10–40 µg/day, oral tablets 0.1–0.2 mg two to three times daily, or injection.
  • Primary nocturnal enuresis in children above 5–6 years – oral dose at bedtime.
  • Mild haemophilia A and von Willebrand disease (type 1) – IV/intranasal desmopressin releases factor VIII and von Willebrand factor before minor surgery or dental extraction.
  • Nocturia in adults (carefully, because of hyponatraemia risk).

C. Other drugs that reduce urine volume

  • Thiazide diuretics – paradoxically reduce urine volume in nephrogenic DI.
  • Carbamazepine, chlorpropamide – increase ADH action (rarely used).
  • Indomethacin – used with thiazides in nephrogenic DI.

3. Adverse effects

  • Water retention and hyponatraemia (water intoxication) – headache, nausea, vomiting, confusion, convulsions; risk is highest in children, the elderly and when fluid intake is not limited.
  • Vasopressin: pallor, abdominal cramps, coronary vasoconstriction (angina, MI), hypertension, gangrene with extravasation.
  • Intranasal desmopressin: nasal irritation, nosebleed; absorption falls with a cold.

4. Nursing implications

  1. Daily weight, intake–output chart, urine specific gravity/osmolality and serum sodium.
  2. Teach fluid restriction – for enuresis, limit fluids from 1 hour before to 8 hours after the bedtime dose.
  3. Watch for headache, drowsiness or confusion – early signs of hyponatraemia; withhold and report.
  4. Teach correct use of the nasal spray and storage (some preparations need refrigeration).
  5. With vasopressin infusion – monitor ECG, BP, peripheral circulation and the IV site; use a central line where possible.
  6. Patients with DI should carry an identification card and never be deprived of water if they are unable to take their drug.

Conclusion Vasopressin and desmopressin concentrate urine through V2 receptors and are life-saving in diabetes insipidus, while desmopressin also helps enuresis and mild bleeding disorders. Strict monitoring of fluids and sodium prevents water intoxication.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Name two osmotic diuretics and state their uses.
answer_html:
Osmotic diuretics are pharmacologically inert substances that are filtered but not reabsorbed, so they hold water in the tubules and draw water out of tissues.

Examples: Mannitol (20% IV), glycerol (oral 50%); also isosorbide and urea.

Uses

  1. Raised intracranial pressure – cerebral oedema in head injury, brain tumour.
  2. Acute angle-closure glaucoma and before eye surgery – to lower intraocular pressure.
  3. Forced diuresis in selected poisonings and to maintain urine flow in specific situations.

Caution: contraindicated in anuria and heart failure (risk of pulmonary oedema).

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Write the uses and precautions of nitrofurantoin.
answer_html:
Nitrofurantoin is a urinary antiseptic that reaches high concentrations only in urine.

Uses

  1. Uncomplicated cystitis (lower UTI) – 100 mg twice daily (modified release) for 5 days.
  2. Prophylaxis of recurrent UTI – 50–100 mg at bedtime.
  3. Cystitis due to many ESBL-producing E. coli.

Precautions

  1. Give with food or milk to reduce nausea.
  2. Avoid in significant kidney impairment (ineffective and toxic), at term pregnancy and in newborns, and in G6PD deficiency (haemolysis).
  3. Warn that urine turns brown-yellow.
  4. Report tingling, cough or breathlessness – signs of neuropathy or lung reaction on long use.
  5. Not useful in pyelonephritis (no tissue levels).

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: What are potassium-sparing diuretics? Give examples and their main danger.
answer_html:
Potassium-sparing diuretics are weak diuretics acting on the late distal tubule and collecting duct that increase sodium excretion while reducing potassium loss.

Examples

  1. Aldosterone antagonists – spironolactone, eplerenone.
  2. Epithelial sodium-channel blockers – amiloride, triamterene.

Uses: with loop/thiazide diuretics to prevent hypokalaemia, cirrhotic ascites, heart failure, hyperaldosteronism.

Main danger: hyperkalaemia (arrhythmia, cardiac arrest), especially with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium supplements and kidney failure – monitor serum potassium. Spironolactone also causes gynaecomastia.

Nursing tip: avoid salt substitutes (they contain potassium) and check serum potassium within the first week of starting the drug.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Classify non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Explain their mechanism of action, uses and adverse effects, with special reference to aspirin and the nurse's responsibilities. Illustrate the WHO analgesic ladder.

diagram.caption: WHO three-step analgesic ladder
labels: NSAID) ± adjuvant; step 2 moderate pain – weak opioid (codeine
tramadol) + non-opioid ± adjuvant; step 3 severe pain – strong opioid (morphine
fentanyl) ± non-opioid ± adjuvant; arrow of increasing pain

answer_html:
Introduction NSAIDs are drugs that relieve pain (analgesic), fever (antipyretic) and inflammation (anti-inflammatory) without being steroids or opioids. They are the most widely used medicines in India – from a headache tablet bought over the counter to injections in casualty – and are also the commonest cause of drug-induced gastric bleeding and kidney injury.

(a) Classification (4 marks) | Group | Examples | |---|---| | A. Non-selective COX inhibitors | | | Salicylates | Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) | | Propionic acid derivatives | Ibuprofen, naproxen, ketoprofen, flurbiprofen | | Acetic acid derivatives | Diclofenac, aceclofenac, indomethacin, ketorolac | | Fenamates (anthranilic acids) | Mefenamic acid | | Oxicams (enolic acids) | Piroxicam, tenoxicam | | Pyrazolones | Metamizole (restricted use), phenylbutazone (obsolete) | | B. Preferential COX-2 inhibitors | Nimesulide (not for children below 12 years in India), meloxicam, etodolac | | C. Selective COX-2 inhibitors (coxibs) | Celecoxib, etoricoxib, parecoxib (injection) | | D. Analgesic–antipyretics with poor anti-inflammatory action | Paracetamol (acetaminophen), nefopam |

(b) Mechanism of action

  1. Tissue injury releases arachidonic acid from cell membranes.
  2. The enzyme cyclooxygenase (COX) converts it into prostaglandins (PGs), prostacyclin and thromboxane A2.
  3. COX-1 is "housekeeping" – protects the stomach lining, maintains kidney blood flow and helps platelet aggregation; COX-2 is induced at sites of inflammation and in the brain during fever.
  4. NSAIDs inhibit COX → fewer prostaglandins → less sensitisation of pain receptors (analgesia), resetting of the hypothalamic thermostat (antipyresis) and less vasodilation and swelling (anti-inflammatory).
  5. Aspirin acetylates COX irreversibly; in platelets (which cannot make new enzyme) this blocks thromboxane A2 for the whole 7–10-day life of the platelet → antiplatelet effect.

(c) Uses of NSAIDs

  • Pain – headache, toothache, dysmenorrhoea (mefenamic acid), musculoskeletal pain, post-operative pain (ketorolac, diclofenac), renal and biliary colic (diclofenac).
  • Fever – paracetamol is preferred.
  • Inflammatory disorders – rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gout (indomethacin, naproxen).
  • Low-dose aspirin – prevention of MI and stroke, unstable angina, after stenting, prevention of pre-eclampsia in high-risk pregnancy.
  • Patent ductus arteriosus closure in preterm babies (indomethacin, ibuprofen).

(d) Adverse effects of NSAIDs

  • Gastrointestinal – dyspepsia, gastric erosions, peptic ulcer, haematemesis and melaena (less with coxibs).
  • Kidney – sodium and water retention, oedema, raised BP, hyperkalaemia, acute kidney injury, analgesic nephropathy.
  • Cardiovascular – increased risk of MI and stroke with coxibs and high-dose diclofenac; worsening of heart failure.
  • Bleeding – antiplatelet effect (aspirin, most non-selective NSAIDs).
  • Respiratory – aspirin/NSAID-exacerbated asthma (bronchospasm, nasal polyps).
  • Hypersensitivity – urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis, Stevens–Johnson syndrome.
  • Liver – raised enzymes (diclofenac, nimesulide); paracetamol overdose causes liver failure.
  • Pregnancy – avoid in the third trimester (premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, prolonged labour, oligohydramnios).

(e) Aspirin – drug profile

  • Doses: analgesic/antipyretic 325–650 mg every 4–6 hours (maximum about 4 g/day); antiplatelet 75–150 mg once daily; acute MI 150–325 mg chewed immediately.
  • Contraindications: children and adolescents with viral fever (risk of Reye's syndrome – liver failure and encephalopathy), dengue and other bleeding disorders, active peptic ulcer, haemophilia, aspirin-sensitive asthma, G6PD deficiency, late pregnancy, 7 days before elective surgery.
  • Salicylism (chronic high dose): tinnitus, deafness, vertigo, headache, mental confusion, hyperventilation.
  • Acute poisoning: vomiting, hyperthermia, respiratory alkalosis followed by metabolic acidosis, hypoglycaemia, coma – treated with activated charcoal, IV fluids, urinary alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate and haemodialysis in severe cases.

(f) Nurse's responsibilities

  1. Give NSAIDs after food or with milk; use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time; add a PPI (pantoprazole) in elderly and high-risk patients as ordered.
  2. Ask about peptic ulcer, asthma, kidney disease, bleeding disorders, pregnancy and anticoagulant use before giving.
  3. Never give aspirin or other NSAIDs for fever during the monsoon "dengue season" until dengue is excluded – use paracetamol.
  4. Watch for black stools, vomiting of blood, epigastric pain, reduced urine output, oedema and rising BP; monitor creatinine in the elderly.
  5. Low-dose aspirin – teach to take daily, not to stop on their own after stenting, to report bruising, and to inform dentists and surgeons.
  6. Enteric-coated tablets should not be crushed; chewable aspirin is used in suspected MI.
  7. Discourage self-medication and repeated injections of diclofenac for minor pain, a common practice in rural clinics.

(g) WHO analgesic ladder (pain relief in cancer and chronic pain) | Step | Pain severity (0–10 scale) | Drugs | |---|---|---| | Step 1 | Mild (1–3) | Non-opioid – paracetamol, NSAIDs ± adjuvant | | Step 2 | Moderate (4–6) | Weak opioid – codeine, tramadol + non-opioid ± adjuvant | | Step 3 | Severe (7–10) | Strong opioid – morphine, fentanyl, oxycodone ± non-opioid ± adjuvant |

  • Adjuvants – amitriptyline, gabapentin/pregabalin (nerve pain), dexamethasone, bisphosphonates (bone pain), antispasmodics.
  • Principles: "by the mouth, by the clock, by the ladder, for the individual, with attention to detail" – regular doses rather than "as needed", step up if pain is not controlled, step down when pain settles.
  • In severe pain the patient may start directly at step 3.

Nursing importance

  • Nurses assess pain, give analgesics on time and detect complications early; NSAID-related bleeding and kidney injury are among the most preventable drug harms in wards.
  • Using the WHO ladder ensures that cancer and chronic-pain patients receive adequate, stepwise and regular pain relief.

Conclusion NSAIDs relieve pain, fever and inflammation by blocking cyclooxygenase, and low-dose aspirin protects against heart attack and stroke. Careful patient selection, gastric and kidney protection, and stepwise analgesia according to the WHO ladder make their use safe and effective.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Classify opioid analgesics. Describe the pharmacology of morphine – actions, uses, adverse effects, contraindications and nursing implications. Name the opioid antagonists.

diagram.caption: Actions of morphine on body systems
labels: vomiting centre; eye – pinpoint pupil; gut – constipation; bladder – retention; skin – itching from histamine release

answer_html:
Introduction Opioid analgesics are drugs that act like the body's own endorphins and enkephalins on opioid receptors (μ, κ, δ) in the brain, spinal cord and gut. They are the most powerful pain relievers available. Morphine, the main alkaloid of opium (from the poppy Papaver somniferum), is the standard against which other opioids are compared.

1. Classification | Group | Examples | |---|---| | Natural opium alkaloids | Morphine, codeine | | Semi-synthetic | Diacetylmorphine (heroin – not used medically in India), oxycodone, hydromorphone | | Synthetic | Pethidine (meperidine), fentanyl, methadone, tramadol, tapentadol | | Partial agonist | Buprenorphine | | Mixed agonist–antagonists | Pentazocine, butorphanol, nalbuphine | | Pure antagonists | Naloxone, naltrexone, nalmefene | | Antitussive opioids | Codeine, pholcodine (dextromethorphan acts centrally but is non-addictive) |

2. Mechanism of action of morphine

  • Acts mainly on μ (mu) receptors → opens K⁺ channels and closes Ca²⁺ channels in neurons → reduces release of pain transmitters (substance P, glutamate) in the dorsal horn and changes the brain's perception of pain.
  • Relieves both the sensation and the emotional distress of pain.

3. Pharmacological actions of morphine

  1. CNS: strong analgesia, sedation, euphoria (basis of addiction), mental clouding.
  2. Respiration: respiratory depression – reduces the response of the respiratory centre to CO₂; the commonest cause of death in overdose.
  3. Cough centre: depressed (antitussive).
  4. Eye: miosis – pinpoint pupils (an important sign of poisoning).
  5. Vomiting: stimulates the chemoreceptor trigger zone → nausea and vomiting.
  6. Gut: ↓ peristalsis, ↑ sphincter tone → constipation (no tolerance develops); biliary spasm.
  7. Urinary tract: ↑ sphincter tone → urinary retention.
  8. Cardiovascular: vasodilation and postural hypotension, bradycardia; reduces preload (relief in acute left ventricular failure).
  9. Histamine release: itching, flushing, sweating, bronchospasm.
  10. Raised intracranial pressure – secondary to CO₂ retention.
  11. Endocrine: ↑ ADH, ↓ sex hormones with long use.

4. Dose and routes

  • Injection: 10 mg IM/SC 4-hourly (adults); IV 2–5 mg slowly, titrated to effect.
  • Oral immediate-release morphine 5–10 mg every 4 hours in cancer pain; sustained-release tablets every 12 hours; dose titrated upward without a fixed ceiling.
  • Also epidural/intrathecal, PCA pumps.

5. Uses

  1. Severe acute pain – myocardial infarction, fractures and trauma (not head injury), burns, post-operative pain, renal and biliary colic (with an antispasmodic).
  2. Cancer and palliative care pain (step 3 of WHO ladder); breathlessness in terminal illness.
  3. Acute left ventricular failure (carefully; less used now).
  4. Pre-anaesthetic medication and during balanced anaesthesia (fentanyl more often).
  5. Severe diarrhoea and cough (codeine, loperamide – not morphine itself).

6. Adverse effects

  • Respiratory depression, apnoea (especially in infants, the elderly and with sedatives/alcohol).
  • Nausea, vomiting, constipation, urinary retention, itching, sweating.
  • Sedation, confusion, dizziness, postural hypotension, falls.
  • Tolerance, physical dependence and addiction; withdrawal syndrome – yawning, lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, sweating, dilated pupils, gooseflesh, abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, restlessness.
  • Acute poisoning – triad of coma, pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression.

7. Contraindications and cautions

  • Head injury (masks pupils and consciousness; raises ICP), respiratory depression, acute severe asthma, COPD with CO₂ retention.
  • Infants and the elderly (reduced dose), hypothyroidism, liver failure.
  • Acute abdomen before diagnosis (masks signs), biliary colic (use with antispasmodic).
  • During labour – neonatal respiratory depression (pethidine or fentanyl preferred; naloxone kept ready).
  • MAO inhibitors (with pethidine – dangerous reaction).

8. Nursing implications

  1. Assess pain with a pain score before and after each dose; give regular doses in cancer pain ("by the clock").
  2. Check respiratory rate, sedation level and SpO₂ before giving; withhold and report if RR is below 10–12/min or the patient is difficult to rouse.
  3. Give IV doses slowly; keep naloxone, bag-valve-mask and oxygen at hand.
  4. Start a laxative (lactulose, senna) along with regular opioids; encourage fluids and fibre.
  5. Watch for urinary retention after surgery; give antiemetics as ordered.
  6. Fall precautions – side rails, assist with ambulation.
  7. Legal responsibilities – morphine is an essential narcotic drug under the NDPS Act; store under double lock, record every dose in the narcotic register with two signatures, return empty ampoules, report discrepancies.
  8. Reassure patients and families that properly used morphine for cancer pain rarely causes addiction; explain that tolerance needs dose adjustment, not refusal of pain relief.
  9. Taper after prolonged use to avoid withdrawal.

9. Opioid antagonists

  • Naloxone – pure antagonist, given IV/IM/SC/intranasally; 0.4–2 mg IV, repeated every 2–3 minutes in overdose (0.04–0.1 mg titrated for post-operative depression so that pain relief is not fully lost); acts for 30–90 minutes – shorter than morphine, so watch for re-narcotisation.
  • Naltrexone – oral, long acting (50 mg/day); used in de-addiction (opioid and alcohol dependence).
  • Nalmefene – longer-acting antagonist; used in alcohol dependence.

Nursing importance

  • Opioids are high-alert medicines; most serious harms – respiratory arrest, falls, constipation – are prevented by nursing monitoring.
  • Fear of morphine ("opiophobia") among staff and families is a major cause of untreated cancer pain in India; the nurse plays a key role in correcting it.

Conclusion Opioids such as morphine give unmatched relief from severe pain by acting on μ receptors, but depress respiration, slow the gut and can cause dependence. Careful dosing, monitoring, prevention of side effects, legal record keeping and ready availability of naloxone make morphine both safe and compassionate.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Classify general anaesthetics. Describe the pharmacology of commonly used inhalational and intravenous anaesthetics and the nurse's responsibilities.

diagram.caption: Components of balanced general anaesthesia

answer_html:
Introduction General anaesthetics (GA) are drugs that produce a reversible loss of consciousness and sensation, so that surgery can be done without pain or memory. Modern anaesthesia is "balanced anaesthesia" – a combination of drugs for unconsciousness, analgesia, muscle relaxation, amnesia and suppression of harmful reflexes, each in smaller, safer doses.

1. Classification A. Inhalational anaesthetics

  • Gas: nitrous oxide (N₂O).
  • Volatile liquids: isoflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane; halothane (rarely used now); ether (obsolete, inflammable).

B. Intravenous anaesthetics

  • Fast-acting inducing agents: propofol, thiopentone sodium, etomidate.
  • Dissociative anaesthetic: ketamine.
  • Slower-acting drugs: benzodiazepines (midazolam, diazepam); opioid analgesics (fentanyl, morphine) used in high doses; dexmedetomidine (sedation).

2. Inhalational anaesthetics a) Nitrous oxide ("laughing gas")

  • Colourless, sweet-smelling, non-irritant gas, supplied in blue cylinders.
  • Good analgesic but weak anaesthetic – used as a carrier gas with oxygen and volatile agents; Entonox (50% N₂O + 50% O₂) for labour pain, dressing changes and ambulance analgesia.
  • Diffusion hypoxia at the end of anaesthesia (N₂O rushes into the alveoli and dilutes oxygen) → give 100% oxygen for 5–10 minutes after stopping.
  • Expands closed gas spaces – avoid in pneumothorax, bowel obstruction and middle-ear surgery; prolonged use inactivates vitamin B12 (megaloblastic anaemia, neuropathy).

b) Isoflurane

  • Pungent, used mainly for maintenance; stable heart rhythm; dilates blood vessels → hypotension; relaxes muscles.

c) Sevoflurane

  • Sweet, non-pungent, non-irritant – the agent of choice for inhalational induction in children and adults with difficult IV access; rapid induction and recovery; bronchodilator.
  • Emergence agitation in children.

d) Desflurane

  • Very rapid recovery (useful in day-care and obese patients); pungent, so not used for induction; needs a special heated vaporiser.

e) Halothane – potent, sweet; can cause halothane hepatitis and arrhythmias with adrenaline; now largely replaced.

3. Intravenous anaesthetics a) Propofol

  • Most widely used inducing agent – milky lipid emulsion; dose 1.5–2.5 mg/kg IV; unconsciousness in 30–40 seconds; smooth, clear-headed recovery with less nausea (antiemetic).
  • Also used by infusion for total intravenous anaesthesia (TIVA) and ICU sedation.
  • Adverse effects: pain on injection (lignocaine added), hypotension, apnoea, bacterial contamination of opened vials, propofol infusion syndrome with long high-dose infusions.

b) Thiopentone sodium

  • Ultra-short-acting barbiturate; 3–5 mg/kg IV of a 2.5% solution; rapid smooth induction; reduces brain pressure (used in neurosurgery and refractory status epilepticus).
  • Adverse effects: hypotension, laryngospasm; extravasation causes tissue necrosis; accidental intra-arterial injection causes severe pain and gangrene; contraindicated in porphyria.

c) Ketamine

  • Produces "dissociative anaesthesia" – patient appears awake with eyes open but feels no pain; profound analgesia, amnesia.
  • IV 1–2 mg/kg or IM 5–10 mg/kg; raises BP and heart rate and keeps airway reflexes – useful in shock, asthma, children, burns dressings and field/disaster surgery.
  • Adverse effects: emergence reactions – vivid dreams, hallucinations, delirium (reduced by midazolam and a quiet recovery room), excess salivation, raised intracranial and intraocular pressure.

d) Etomidate – minimal effect on heart and BP (useful in cardiac patients); causes involuntary movements and adrenal suppression.

e) Midazolam – benzodiazepine used for sedation, amnesia and co-induction; reversed by flumazenil.

f) Fentanyl – potent short-acting opioid used for analgesia during induction and surgery; chest-wall rigidity with large fast doses.

4. Ideal sequence (balanced anaesthesia) Pre-medication (anxiolytic, antiemetic, antacid) → pre-oxygenation → IV induction (propofol) + opioid (fentanyl) → muscle relaxant (succinylcholine/rocuronium) → intubation → maintenance with O₂ + air/N₂O + volatile agent (sevoflurane/isoflurane) + additional relaxant and analgesic → reversal (neostigmine + glycopyrrolate or sugammadex) → recovery.

5. Common complications related to anaesthetic drugs

  • Hypotension, arrhythmias, respiratory depression, airway obstruction and aspiration.
  • Post-operative nausea and vomiting (PONV), shivering and hypothermia, sore throat.
  • Malignant hyperthermia – rare genetic reaction to volatile agents and succinylcholine (rapid rise of temperature, rigidity, high CO₂); treated with IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg, cooling and stopping the trigger.
  • Awareness under anaesthesia, delayed recovery, allergic reactions.

6. Nurse's responsibilities

  1. Pre-operative: confirm informed consent, fasting (about 6 hours for solids, 2 hours for clear fluids or as per protocol), allergy history, removal of dentures, jewellery and nail polish, and administration of pre-medication on time.
