  • Tubal disease and severe male factor need surgery or ART (IUI, IVF, ICSI) rather than drugs alone.

3. Adverse effects

  • Clomiphene: hot flushes, abdominal discomfort, visual disturbances (stop the drug), thin endometrium, multiple pregnancy (about 5–10%).
  • Gonadotropins: ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) – abdominal distension, pain, nausea, ascites, reduced urine output, thrombosis; multiple pregnancy; injection-site reactions.
  • Cabergoline/bromocriptine: nausea, dizziness, postural hypotension.

4. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Explain the treatment cycle, timing of tablets and injections, and follicular monitoring by ultrasound.
  2. Teach subcutaneous self-injection, storage of gonadotropins in the refrigerator and safe disposal of needles.
  3. Advise timed intercourse or IUI around ovulation as instructed.
  4. Teach the warning signs of OHSS – rapid weight gain, abdominal swelling, breathlessness, reduced urine – and arrange urgent review; monitor weight, girth and intake–output in admitted patients.
  5. Provide emotional support – infertility causes stress, stigma and family pressure in Indian society; involve the male partner in evaluation.
  6. Counsel about costs, success rates and multiple pregnancy; refer to registered ART clinics under the ART (Regulation) Act, 2021.

Conclusion Clomiphene, letrozole and gonadotropins induce ovulation, while cabergoline, metformin, thyroxine and progesterone correct specific causes. Careful monitoring for OHSS and multiple pregnancy and compassionate counselling are key nursing roles.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Drugs used for Hormonal Disorders and Supplementation, Contraception and Medical Termination of Pregnancy
question: Explain the drugs used for medical termination of pregnancy, with nursing responsibilities.
answer_html:
Introduction Medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) is the ending of a pregnancy by a registered medical practitioner under the conditions of the MTP Act, 1971 (amended 2021). Medical methods of abortion (MMA) use drugs instead of surgery and are safe and effective in early pregnancy.

1. Legal framework (MTP Amendment Act, 2021) – in brief

  • Up to 20 weeks – on the opinion of one registered medical practitioner.
  • 20–24 weeks – for special categories (survivors of sexual assault or incest, minors, women with disability, change of marital status, foetal malformation, humanitarian settings) – opinion of two practitioners.
  • Beyond 24 weeks – only for substantial foetal abnormalities on the decision of a Medical Board.
  • Confidentiality of the woman is mandatory; consent of the woman alone is needed if she is an adult.

2. Drugs used A. Mifepristone (RU 486)

  • Antiprogestin – blocks progesterone receptors → decidual breakdown, detachment of the pregnancy, softening of the cervix and increased sensitivity of the uterus to prostaglandins.
  • Dose: 200 mg orally (single dose).

B. Misoprostol

  • Prostaglandin E1 analogue – causes uterine contractions and cervical ripening.
  • Dose: 800 µg (four 200 µg tablets) buccal, sublingual or vaginal, 24–48 hours after mifepristone.

Standard regimen (up to 9 weeks/63 days, as approved in India):

  1. Day 1: mifepristone 200 mg orally at the facility.
  2. Day 2–3: misoprostol 800 µg; bleeding and cramps usually begin within a few hours and the pregnancy is expelled.
  3. Day 15: follow-up visit – clinical/ultrasound confirmation of complete abortion. - For later gestations, repeated doses of misoprostol are used in hospital under supervision.

C. Other drugs

  • Methotrexate (50 mg/m² IM) – for selected unruptured ectopic pregnancy.
  • Oxytocin infusion – for second-trimester termination in some protocols.
  • Anti-D immunoglobulin – for Rh-negative women after abortion.
  • Analgesics (ibuprofen, paracetamol), antiemetics, and prophylactic antibiotics where indicated.

3. Contraindications to medical method

  • Suspected or confirmed ectopic pregnancy, IUD in place (remove first), chronic adrenal failure, long-term steroid therapy, bleeding disorders or anticoagulants, severe anaemia, inherited porphyria, allergy to the drugs, no access to emergency care.

4. Adverse effects

  • Bleeding (heavier than a period, may last 1–2 weeks), cramping pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, fever and chills (misoprostol).
  • Incomplete abortion (needs repeat misoprostol or vacuum aspiration), continuing pregnancy (risk of malformation – misoprostol is teratogenic), rarely infection or haemorrhage.

5. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Confirm gestational age, exclude ectopic pregnancy (ultrasound if needed), check Hb and blood group; ensure written consent and maintain confidentiality of records.
  2. Explain what to expect – timing of bleeding and cramps, use of pads, pain relief; give written instructions.
  3. Teach danger signs – soaking more than two pads an hour for two hours, fever lasting more than 24 hours, foul discharge, severe abdominal pain, fainting – and give a contact number.
  4. Ensure follow-up on day 15; give anti-D when indicated.
  5. Provide post-abortion contraception counselling – most methods can be started immediately (pills, injectable, implant; IUD after confirmed complete abortion).
  6. Offer non-judgemental emotional support.

Conclusion Mifepristone followed by misoprostol is a safe, effective, non-surgical method of abortion in early pregnancy under the MTP Act. Careful selection, clear information, follow-up and post-abortion contraception are essential parts of nursing care.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Drugs used for Hormonal Disorders and Supplementation, Contraception and Medical Termination of Pregnancy
question: Classify uterine relaxants (tocolytics). Explain their use in preterm labour with the nurse's responsibilities.
answer_html:
Definition Tocolytics are drugs that relax the uterine muscle and suppress uterine contractions. Their main use is to delay preterm labour for 24–48 hours so that antenatal corticosteroids can mature the baby's lungs and the mother can be shifted to a centre with a neonatal intensive care unit.

1. Classification | Group | Examples | Notes | |---|---|---| | Calcium channel blockers | Nifedipine | Oral; widely used first-line; e.g. 10–20 mg loading, then 10–20 mg every 6–8 hours as per protocol | | β2-adrenergic agonists | Terbutaline (0.25 mg SC), ritodrine, isoxsuprine | Rapid action; more maternal side effects | | Oxytocin receptor antagonist | Atosiban (IV infusion) | Fewest side effects; expensive | | Prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors (NSAIDs) | Indomethacin | Below 32 weeks, for not more than 48 hours | | Magnesium sulphate | IV | Now used mainly for foetal neuroprotection below 32 weeks, not as a tocolytic | | Nitric oxide donors | Glyceryl trinitrate patch | Rarely used | | Progesterone | Vaginal micronised progesterone, 17-OHPC | Prevention of preterm birth in high-risk women, not for active labour |

2. Uses

  1. Threatened preterm labour (24–34 weeks) – to gain time for corticosteroids (dexamethasone 6 mg IM 12-hourly × 4 doses or betamethasone 12 mg IM 24 hours apart × 2) and in-utero transfer.
  2. Uterine hyperstimulation during oxytocin infusion or with foetal distress – acute tocolysis (terbutaline SC) as intrauterine resuscitation.
  3. During external cephalic version and cervical cerclage.

3. Contraindications

  • Intrauterine foetal death, lethal foetal anomaly, chorioamnionitis, severe pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, antepartum haemorrhage with instability, foetal distress, advanced labour; maternal heart disease (β-agonists), hypotension (nifedipine).

4. Adverse effects

  • β2-agonists: maternal tachycardia, palpitations, tremor, hyperglycaemia, hypokalaemia, pulmonary oedema, chest pain; foetal tachycardia.
  • Nifedipine: headache, flushing, hypotension, reflex tachycardia.
  • Indomethacin: gastric upset; in the foetus – premature closure of ductus arteriosus, oligohydramnios.
  • Atosiban: nausea, injection-site reactions.

5. Nurse's responsibilities

  1. Confirm gestational age, assess contractions, cervical changes (by doctor) and foetal heart rate; position the mother in left lateral; ensure bed rest during acute treatment.
  2. Monitor maternal pulse, BP, respiration and breath sounds – withhold β-agonist if pulse exceeds about 120/min and report; watch for breathlessness (pulmonary oedema); restrict IV fluids as ordered.
  3. Monitor blood sugar (especially with steroids and β-agonists) and potassium.
  4. Give corticosteroids on time and document; arrange transfer with records.
  5. Keep calcium gluconate ready when magnesium sulphate is used.
  6. Support the anxious mother and family; explain the plan and NICU care.

Conclusion Tocolytics such as nifedipine, β2-agonists and atosiban delay preterm labour for a short time so that steroids and transfer can improve newborn survival. Careful monitoring of mother and foetus is essential because these drugs have significant side effects.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Drugs used for Hormonal Disorders and Supplementation, Contraception and Medical Termination of Pregnancy
question: Give two examples and two uses of tocolytics.
answer_html:
Tocolytics are drugs that relax the uterus and suppress contractions.

Examples

  1. Nifedipine (calcium channel blocker).
  2. Terbutaline / isoxsuprine (β2-agonists); also atosiban (oxytocin antagonist) and indomethacin.

Uses

  1. Threatened preterm labour – delay delivery 24–48 hours to give antenatal corticosteroids and transfer the mother to a centre with NICU.
  2. Uterine hyperstimulation or foetal distress during labour (acute tocolysis), and during external cephalic version.

Nursing point: during tocolysis, monitor maternal pulse and BP, breath sounds (pulmonary oedema with β-agonists), blood sugar and foetal heart rate; give antenatal corticosteroids on time.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Drugs used for Hormonal Disorders and Supplementation, Contraception and Medical Termination of Pregnancy
question: Write the drugs, dose and timing of emergency contraception.
answer_html:
Emergency contraception prevents pregnancy after unprotected intercourse, contraceptive failure (condom burst, missed pills) or sexual assault.

  1. Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg single tablet ("E-pill") – as soon as possible, within 72 hours (some effect up to 120 hours); available free under the national programme and over the counter.
  2. Ulipristal acetate 30 mg – single dose within 120 hours (5 days).
  3. Copper IUD – inserted within 5 days; most effective method and gives long-term contraception.

They mainly delay ovulation and do not cause abortion of an established pregnancy. They are not for regular use; counsel about a regular method and STI protection.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Drugs used for Hormonal Disorders and Supplementation, Contraception and Medical Termination of Pregnancy
question: What is centchroman (Chhaya)? Write its dose schedule.
answer_html:
Centchroman (ormeloxifene) is a non-steroidal, non-hormonal oral contraceptive developed by the Central Drug Research Institute, Lucknow, and supplied free as "Chhaya" in the national family planning programme. It is a selective oestrogen receptor modulator that makes the endometrium unreceptive to implantation and speeds tubal transport.

Dose schedule: 30 mg tablet twice a week for the first 3 months, then once a week (on the same day every week) for as long as contraception is needed; started on the first day of the period.

Advantages: once-weekly, no hormonal side effects, safe during breastfeeding. Side effect: delayed (prolonged) menstrual cycles in some women. Avoid in PCOS, liver disease and cervical hyperplasia.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Drugs used for Pregnant Women during Antenatal Period, Labour and Postnatal Period
question: Describe the pharmacology of oxytocin – actions, preparations, uses, adverse effects, contraindications and the nurse's responsibilities during oxytocin infusion.
tags: active management of third stage of labour

diagram.caption: Monitoring a mother on oxytocin infusion
labels: uterine contractions 3–4 in 10 minutes lasting 40–60 seconds
stop if hyperstimulation or abnormal FHR

answer_html:
Introduction Oxytocin is a peptide hormone (nine amino acids) made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. It causes rhythmic contractions of the uterus and milk ejection. Synthetic oxytocin is one of the most important – and most dangerous – drugs in labour rooms, listed as a high-alert medicine.

1. Actions

  • Uterus: increases the force and frequency of contractions – rhythmic, with relaxation in between at low doses; sustained (tetanic) contraction at high doses. Sensitivity rises sharply towards term because oxytocin receptors increase.
  • Breast: contracts myoepithelial cells around alveoli → milk ejection (let-down reflex).
  • Kidney: weak ADH-like antidiuretic effect in high doses → water retention.
  • Blood vessels: rapid IV bolus causes vasodilation, hypotension and reflex tachycardia.

2. Preparations

  • Injection 5 IU/mL and 10 IU/mL for IM or IV use; store in the refrigerator (2–8°C) – part of the labour-room cold chain.
  • Carbetocin – long-acting analogue; a heat-stable formulation is an alternative for PPH prevention where cold storage is difficult.

3. Uses

  1. Induction of labour – post-term pregnancy, pre-labour rupture of membranes, pre-eclampsia, diabetes, intrauterine death – usually after cervical ripening.
    • Typical regimen: 5 IU in 500 mL Ringer's lactate or normal saline, starting at 2–4 mU/min (about 4–8 drops/min), increased by 2–4 mU/min every 30 minutes until there are 3–4 good contractions in 10 minutes, each lasting 40–60 seconds; maximum as per hospital protocol.
  2. Augmentation of labour in slow progress due to inadequate contractions (with intact pelvis and normal presentation).
  3. Active management of third stage of labour (AMTSL) – 10 IU IM within one minute of the baby's birth (after excluding another baby), with controlled cord traction and uterine massage – prevents postpartum haemorrhage (PPH).
  4. Treatment of PPH due to uterine atony – 10 IU IM/slow IV, followed by 20–40 IU in 1 litre of fluid at 40–60 drops/min.
  5. Caesarean section – 3–5 IU slow IV after delivery of the baby, followed by infusion.
  6. After evacuation for incomplete abortion or molar pregnancy – to contract the uterus.
  7. Oxytocin challenge (contraction stress) test – rarely used now.

4. Adverse effects

  • Uterine hyperstimulation (tachysystole) – more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes or prolonged contractions → foetal hypoxia, foetal distress, abruption.
  • Uterine rupture – especially in grand multipara, previous caesarean scar, obstructed labour.
  • Water intoxication – hyponatraemia, headache, vomiting, convulsions – with large doses given in large volumes of electrolyte-free fluid over long periods.
  • Hypotension, tachycardia and arrhythmia with rapid IV bolus.
  • Postpartum atonic haemorrhage after prolonged infusion (receptor desensitisation), neonatal jaundice, nausea; rarely anaphylaxis.

5. Contraindications

  • Cephalopelvic disproportion, obstructed labour, malpresentation (transverse lie, brow).
  • Foetal distress, placenta praevia, vasa praevia, cord presentation or prolapse.
  • Previous classical caesarean or major uterine surgery.
  • Hypertonic uterine contractions; relative – grand multiparity, overdistended uterus (twins, polyhydramnios).

6. Nurse's responsibilities during oxytocin infusion

  1. Ensure a written order with dilution, starting rate, increments and maximum; prepare and label the infusion clearly; use an infusion pump (or careful drop counting with a dedicated IV line).
  2. Before starting – record maternal pulse, BP, temperature, foetal heart rate (FHR), contractions and cervical findings; ensure the bladder is empty.
  3. Never leave the woman alone; record contractions (frequency, duration, strength) and FHR every 15–30 minutes (continuous CTG if available) on the partograph.
  4. Increase the rate only as ordered and only if contractions are inadequate.
  5. Stop the infusion immediately if there is hyperstimulation (more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes or contractions lasting more than 90 seconds), abnormal FHR (below 110 or above 160/min, decelerations), or signs of rupture (sudden pain, bleeding, loss of contractions) – then turn to left lateral, give oxygen, run IV fluids, inform the doctor; acute tocolysis (terbutaline) may be ordered.
  6. Maintain intake–output, avoid prolonged infusion in dextrose alone; watch for headache, vomiting or confusion (water intoxication).
  7. Third stage: give 10 IU IM promptly after delivery of the baby; monitor uterine tone and bleeding for at least 2 hours; massage the uterus as needed.
  8. Store oxytocin in the refrigerator, check the expiry, and never use heat-exposed or discoloured ampoules.
  9. Explain the procedure and support the mother throughout labour.

Nursing importance

  • Oxytocin saves lives by preventing and treating PPH, the leading cause of maternal death in India, yet its misuse in labour causes foetal distress and uterine rupture.
  • Continuous one-to-one nursing observation is the most important safety measure during oxytocin infusion.

Conclusion Oxytocin stimulates rhythmic uterine contractions and milk ejection and is used for induction, augmentation and prevention and treatment of PPH. Correct dilution, controlled infusion, close monitoring of contractions and FHR, and prompt action on warning signs make it safe.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Drugs used for Pregnant Women during Antenatal Period, Labour and Postnatal Period
question: Explain the use of ergometrine, methylergometrine and carboprost (15-methyl prostaglandin F2α) in obstetrics.
answer_html:
Introduction Uterotonics are drugs that make the uterus contract. After oxytocin, ergot alkaloids and prostaglandins are the main uterotonics used to prevent and control postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) due to uterine atony.

1. Ergometrine and methylergometrine (ergot alkaloids)

  • Action: produce a sustained (tonic) contraction of the uterus, compressing blood vessels in the placental bed; also constrict blood vessels.
  • Dose: 0.2 mg IM or slow IV (over 1 minute); may be repeated every 2–4 hours (maximum about 1 mg/5 doses). Onset – IV within 1 minute, IM about 5–7 minutes.
  • Uses:
    1. Treatment of atonic PPH (along with oxytocin).
    2. Prevention of PPH (as part of AMTSL where oxytocin is not available, or with oxytocin – syntometrine = oxytocin 5 IU + ergometrine 0.5 mg).
    3. Bleeding after abortion and evacuation; subinvolution of uterus.
  • Contraindications: hypertension, pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, heart disease, peripheral vascular disease, severe liver/kidney disease, sepsis; before delivery of the baby (first and second stage) and before delivery of a second twin; HIV patients on protease inhibitors.
  • Adverse effects: nausea, vomiting, sudden rise in BP, headache, chest pain (coronary spasm), peripheral vasoconstriction, retained placenta (if given before placental delivery in some regimens).
  • Storage: refrigerate (2–8°C) and protect from light – ergometrine loses potency quickly in heat.

2. Carboprost (15-methyl PGF2α)

  • Action: synthetic prostaglandin that causes strong uterine contractions.
  • Dose: 250 µg deep IM (or intramyometrial by the obstetrician), repeated every 15–90 minutes up to a maximum of 2 mg (8 doses).
  • Uses: refractory atonic PPH not responding to oxytocin and ergometrine; also second-trimester termination in some protocols.
  • Contraindications: bronchial asthma (causes bronchospasm), active cardiac, lung, kidney or liver disease.
  • Adverse effects: diarrhoea, vomiting, fever, flushing, bronchospasm, hypertension, shivering.
  • Storage: refrigerated.

3. Comparison | Feature | Ergometrine | Carboprost | |---|---|---| | Type of contraction | Sustained/tonic | Strong rhythmic and tonic | | Main danger | Hypertension | Bronchospasm | | Avoid in | Pre-eclampsia, heart disease | Asthma |

4. Nursing implications

  1. Check BP before giving ergometrine – do not give if BP is raised or the woman has pre-eclampsia; ask about asthma before carboprost.
  2. Confirm delivery of all babies before giving ergometrine.
  3. Monitor uterine tone, vaginal bleeding (pad count), pulse, BP and respiration; keep the bladder empty; continue uterine massage.
  4. Maintain the cold chain; check potency (colour, expiry).
  5. Be ready with IV fluids, blood, misoprostol, tranexamic acid and the PPH kit; follow the PPH protocol.

Conclusion Ergometrine gives sustained uterine contraction but is dangerous in hypertension, while carboprost is powerful in refractory PPH but must be avoided in asthma. Careful selection, correct storage and close monitoring make them life-saving second-line uterotonics.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Drugs used for Pregnant Women during Antenatal Period, Labour and Postnatal Period
question: Explain the use of magnesium sulphate in pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, with the monitoring required and the nurse's responsibilities.
answer_html:
Introduction Magnesium sulphate (MgSO₄) is the drug of choice for preventing and treating convulsions in severe pre-eclampsia and eclampsia – it is more effective and safer than diazepam or phenytoin. It is available as 50% injection (for IM and diluted IV use); a 20% solution is used for IV loading.

1. Mechanism of action

  • Acts as a calcium antagonist – reduces acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, dilates cerebral vessels and reduces cerebral irritability → prevents seizures.

2. Regimens A. Pritchard (IM) regimen – widely used in India

  • Loading dose: 4 g IV (20 mL of 20% solution) slowly over 10–15 minutes plus 10 g IM – 5 g (10 mL of 50%) deep IM in each buttock (with 1 mL of 2% lignocaine).
  • Maintenance: 5 g of 50% deep IM every 4 hours in alternate buttocks.
  • Continue for 24 hours after delivery or after the last convulsion, whichever is later.
  • At first-referral and PHC levels, the loading dose is given before referral.

B. Zuspan (IV) regimen

  • Loading 4 g IV over 10–15 minutes, then 1 g/hour by infusion pump.

Recurrent convulsion: a further 2 g IV (20%) over 5 minutes.

3. Other uses

  • Foetal neuroprotection when birth is expected before 32 weeks (reduces cerebral palsy).
  • Severe acute asthma, torsades de pointes, hypomagnesaemia, tetanus spasms.

4. Monitoring before each dose (and hourly with infusion) | Parameter | Safe to continue if | |---|---| | Patellar (knee) reflex | Present | | Respiratory rate | At least 16 breaths per minute | | Urine output | At least 30 mL/hour (100 mL in 4 hours) | - Withhold or delay the dose and inform the doctor if any is abnormal. - Therapeutic serum level is about 4–7 mEq/L; loss of knee jerk occurs around 10 mEq/L, respiratory depression around 12–15 mEq/L and cardiac arrest at higher levels.

5. Signs of magnesium toxicity

  • Flushing, warmth, nausea, loss of patellar reflex, muscle weakness, slow shallow breathing, drowsiness, slurred speech, hypotension, bradycardia, cardiac arrest.

6. Antidote

  • Calcium gluconate 10% – 10 mL (1 g) IV slowly over 10 minutes; support ventilation; stop MgSO₄.

7. Nurse's responsibilities

  1. Keep calcium gluconate, oxygen, suction and a bag-valve-mask at the bedside.
  2. Give IM injections deep in the upper outer quadrant, using a long needle, with strict asepsis (abscess risk).
  3. Insert a Foley catheter and maintain hourly urine output; restrict IV fluids as ordered (risk of pulmonary oedema).
  4. Record BP, pulse, RR, reflexes, SpO₂ and FHR as per protocol on the eclampsia chart.
  5. Nurse in left lateral position, in a quiet, dim room with padded side rails; never leave the patient alone.
  6. Continue antihypertensives (labetalol, nifedipine) and plan delivery as ordered.
  7. Watch the newborn for hypotonia and respiratory depression.

Conclusion Magnesium sulphate given by the Pritchard or Zuspan regimen prevents eclamptic convulsions and saves mothers' lives. Checking knee reflex, respiration and urine output before every dose and having calcium gluconate ready are essential nursing safeguards.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Drugs used for Pregnant Women during Antenatal Period, Labour and Postnatal Period
question: Explain the uses of misoprostol in obstetrics, with adverse effects and nursing responsibilities.
answer_html:
Introduction Misoprostol is a synthetic prostaglandin E1 analogue available as 200 µg tablets (and 25 µg tablets for induction). It causes uterine contractions and cervical ripening. Because it is cheap, heat-stable and can be taken by mouth, it is very useful in low-resource and home-birth settings.

1. Obstetric uses and doses | Use | Usual dose (as per national/WHO guidance) | |---|---| | Prevention of PPH where oxytocin is not available, including home deliveries (community distribution through ASHAs) | 600 µg orally immediately after birth of the baby, after confirming no second baby | | Treatment of PPH (adjunct to oxytocin) | 800 µg sublingually | | Induction of labour / cervical ripening at term | 25 µg vaginally every 4–6 hours or 25 µg orally every 2 hours (maximum as per protocol) | | Medical abortion (with mifepristone) up to 9 weeks | 800 µg buccal/sublingual/vaginal 24–48 hours after mifepristone | | Incomplete abortion | 400–600 µg | | Missed abortion / intrauterine death | Doses according to gestational age | | Cervical priming before surgical evacuation or hysteroscopy | 400 µg about 3 hours before |

2. Advantages

  • Does not need refrigeration, low cost, oral/sublingual route, long shelf life.

3. Adverse effects

  • Shivering and fever (common, usually short-lived), nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps.
  • Uterine hyperstimulation and foetal distress during induction.
  • Uterine rupture – especially in women with a previous caesarean scar (avoid for third-trimester induction in scarred uterus).
  • Teratogenic – Möbius syndrome and limb defects if pregnancy continues after a failed abortion.

4. Contraindications

  • Previous caesarean/uterine scar (for induction at term), suspected ectopic pregnancy (for medical abortion), allergy to prostaglandins; caution in asthma and severe cardiovascular disease.

5. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Rule out a second twin before giving the PPH-prevention dose.
  2. Explain that shivering and fever are expected; give paracetamol and warm blankets; continue observation of bleeding and uterine tone.
  3. During induction – monitor contractions and FHR as for oxytocin; do not start oxytocin within 4 hours of the last misoprostol dose.
  4. After medical abortion – teach about bleeding, pain relief and warning signs; ensure follow-up and contraception.
  5. Educate ASHAs and families on correct timing and dose in home deliveries and on prompt referral if bleeding continues.

Conclusion Misoprostol is a versatile, heat-stable prostaglandin used to prevent and treat PPH, induce labour and complete abortion. Correct dosing, exclusion of a second baby or uterine scar, and close monitoring prevent its serious complications.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Drugs used for Pregnant Women during Antenatal Period, Labour and Postnatal Period
question: Explain the drug supplementation given to pregnant women during the antenatal and postnatal period – iron, folic acid, calcium, deworming, tetanus prophylaxis and vitamin K1 for the newborn.
answer_html:
Introduction Pregnancy increases the need for iron, folic acid and calcium, and exposes mother and baby to infections such as tetanus. Under the National Health Mission and Anaemia Mukt Bharat, routine drug supplements are given free during antenatal care (ANC) and the postnatal period. Nurses and ANMs are the main providers of these supplements.

1. Folic acid

  • 400 µg (0.4 mg) daily from before conception (at least 1 month) up to 12 weeks of pregnancy to prevent neural tube defects (spina bifida, anencephaly).
  • Higher dose (4–5 mg/day) for women with a previous NTD-affected baby, epilepsy on antiepileptics, diabetes or obesity.

2. Iron and folic acid (IFA)

  • Prophylaxis: one IFA tablet daily (60 mg elemental iron + 500 µg folic acid) from the second trimester (after 12–14 weeks) for at least 180 days in pregnancy and 180 days after delivery (earlier programmes used 100 mg iron).
  • Treatment of anaemia: therapeutic doses (two tablets daily) for mild anaemia; IV iron (iron sucrose or ferric carboxymaltose) for moderate anaemia or poor tolerance; blood transfusion for severe anaemia near term.
  • Side effects: nausea, epigastric discomfort, black stools, constipation.
  • Advice: take after meals or at bedtime, with vitamin C-rich foods (lemon, amla, guava); avoid tea, coffee and calcium tablets within 1–2 hours.

3. Calcium

  • 1 g elemental calcium daily (500 mg twice a day, with vitamin D) from 14 weeks of pregnancy until 6 months after delivery.
  • Reduces the risk of pre-eclampsia and supports foetal bone growth; take separately from iron tablets.

4. Deworming

  • Albendazole 400 mg single dose in the second trimester – reduces hookworm-related anaemia (not in the first trimester).

5. Tetanus prophylaxis

  • Td (tetanus–diphtheria) vaccine 0.5 mL IM: Td-1 early in pregnancy and Td-2 four weeks later; a single booster if the woman received two doses in a pregnancy within the last 3 years.
  • Protects the mother and prevents neonatal tetanus (India achieved maternal and neonatal tetanus elimination in 2015).

6. Vitamin K1 for the newborn

  • Vitamin K1 (phytomenadione) 1 mg IM (0.5 mg for babies below 1000 g) in the anterolateral thigh soon after birth – prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding (haemorrhagic disease of the newborn).

7. Other drugs

  • Antenatal corticosteroids (dexamethasone) in threatened preterm labour; anti-D for Rh-negative mothers as indicated; low-dose aspirin (75–150 mg) for women at high risk of pre-eclampsia, as prescribed.

8. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Check Hb at every ANC visit, distribute IFA and calcium tablets and count/verify compliance; record in the MCP card.
  2. Explain side effects of iron and how to reduce them; dispel the myth that iron makes the baby too big.
  3. Give Td injections as scheduled and record; ensure vitamin K to every newborn before discharge.
  4. Counsel on diet – green leafy vegetables, pulses, jaggery, millets, milk and eggs.
  5. Identify and refer women with severe anaemia for IV iron or transfusion.

Conclusion Routine folic acid, IFA, calcium, deworming, Td vaccination and newborn vitamin K are simple, low-cost measures that prevent maternal anaemia, pre-eclampsia, neural tube defects, neonatal tetanus and newborn bleeding. Good nursing counselling ensures that the tablets are actually taken.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Drugs used for Pregnant Women during Antenatal Period, Labour and Postnatal Period
question: Write the uses of calcium gluconate in obstetrics.
answer_html:
Calcium gluconate 10% injection (1 g in 10 mL) is used in obstetrics mainly as:

  1. Antidote for magnesium sulphate toxicity – 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV slowly over 10 minutes when the woman develops respiratory depression or loss of reflexes; it must be kept at the bedside of every woman on MgSO₄.
  2. Treatment of hypocalcaemia (tetany) after massive blood transfusion in PPH (citrate binds calcium).
  3. Emergency treatment of hyperkalaemia with ECG changes (protects the heart).

Precautions: inject slowly (rapid injection causes bradycardia and arrhythmia); avoid leakage (tissue necrosis); do not mix with sodium bicarbonate.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Drugs used for Pregnant Women during Antenatal Period, Labour and Postnatal Period
question: Why is vitamin K1 given to the newborn? Write its dose.
answer_html:
Newborns have low vitamin K stores (poor placental transfer, sterile gut, low vitamin K in breast milk), so they can develop vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) – bleeding from the umbilicus, gut, skin or, most dangerously, inside the skull (late VKDB at 2–12 weeks in exclusively breastfed babies).

Dose: vitamin K1 (phytomenadione) 1 mg IM (0.5 mg for babies weighing less than 1000 g) soon after birth, in the anterolateral thigh.

Nursing points: give to every newborn after initial breastfeeding/skin-to-skin contact, record in the birth register and MCP card, and give a dose before circumcision or surgery if missed.

question: Write the schedule of tetanus prophylaxis in pregnancy.
answer_html:
Under India's immunisation programme, Td (tetanus–diphtheria) vaccine has replaced TT for pregnant women.

Schedule (0.5 mL deep IM in the upper arm):

  1. Td-1 – as early as possible in pregnancy (at registration).
  2. Td-2 – 4 weeks after Td-1 (preferably at least 2 weeks before delivery).
  3. Td booster – one dose if the woman received two doses in a previous pregnancy within the last 3 years.

Purpose: protects the mother from tetanus after delivery or abortion and passes antibodies to the baby, preventing neonatal tetanus; supported by clean delivery and clean cord-care practices.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Describe the drugs used in de-addiction.
answer_html:
Introduction De-addiction (substance dependence) treatment has two phases: detoxification – safe management of withdrawal – and relapse prevention/maintenance – helping the person stay away from the substance. Drugs are combined with counselling, family support and rehabilitation. India runs de-addiction services through district hospitals, the Drug Treatment Clinics, NACO's opioid substitution centres and the Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan.

1. Drugs used in alcohol dependence A. Detoxification (withdrawal)

  • Benzodiazepines – chlordiazepoxide (e.g. 20–40 mg four times daily, tapered over 7–10 days) or diazepam; lorazepam in liver disease and the elderly – prevent tremors, seizures and delirium tremens.
  • Thiamine 100 mg IV/IM daily (higher doses in Wernicke's encephalopathy), given before glucose, plus multivitamins – prevent Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome.
  • Fluids, electrolytes (magnesium, potassium), nutrition.

B. Relapse prevention | Drug | Action | Points | |---|---|---| | Disulfiram 250 mg/day | Blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase → unpleasant reaction with alcohol (aversion therapy) | Start only after 12–24 hours of abstinence, with consent; avoid in heart disease, psychosis | | Naltrexone 50 mg/day | Opioid antagonist – reduces craving and the "high" | Avoid in liver failure and in patients on opioids | | Acamprosate 666 mg three times daily | Restores glutamate–GABA balance – reduces craving | Safe in liver disease; avoid in kidney failure | | Baclofen, topiramate | Reduce craving | Used by specialists |

2. Drugs used in opioid dependence

  • Detoxification: clonidine (reduces sweating, anxiety, restlessness), buprenorphine in tapering doses; symptomatic drugs – NSAIDs for aches, loperamide for diarrhoea, antiemetics, sleep aids.
  • Opioid substitution (maintenance) therapy (OST): buprenorphine (sublingual; often with naloxone to prevent injection misuse) or methadone (oral liquid) – reduce craving, injection drug use and HIV/hepatitis C spread.
  • Relapse prevention: naltrexone after complete detoxification.
  • Overdose: naloxone.

3. Drugs used in nicotine (tobacco) dependence

  • Nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) – gum (2 mg/4 mg), lozenges, patches – relieve withdrawal.
  • Varenicline – partial agonist at nicotinic receptors (0.5 mg once daily, increased to 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks); nausea, vivid dreams.
  • Bupropion SR – 150 mg daily, then twice daily; avoid in seizure disorders.
  • National Tobacco Quitline support.

4. Other substances

  • No specific approved drugs for cannabis, cocaine or inhalant dependence – treatment is symptomatic (sedatives, antipsychotics for psychosis) with psychosocial therapy.

5. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Assess the substance, quantity, last use and withdrawal signs (e.g. CIWA-Ar scale for alcohol, COWS for opioids); monitor vitals and seizures.
  2. Give thiamine before IV dextrose in alcohol-dependent patients.
  3. Supervise disulfiram with the patient's informed consent; warn about hidden alcohol (cough syrups, tonics, mouthwashes, aftershave) and the reaction lasting up to 2 weeks after stopping.
  4. Ensure safe storage and witnessed dosing of buprenorphine/methadone; watch for sedation and respiratory depression.
  5. Use a non-judgemental, motivational approach; involve the family; link to self-help groups (Alcoholics Anonymous, Narcotics Anonymous) and rehabilitation; screen for depression and suicidal risk.

Conclusion De-addiction drugs manage withdrawal (benzodiazepines, thiamine, clonidine), reduce craving (naltrexone, acamprosate), cause aversion (disulfiram) or replace the drug safely (buprenorphine, methadone, NRT). Combined with counselling and family support, they help people recover and stay abstinent.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Briefly describe disulfiram aversion therapy.
answer_html:
Disulfiram is used to help a motivated, consenting person stay abstinent from alcohol.

  • Mechanism: it blocks the enzyme aldehyde dehydrogenase, so if the person drinks, acetaldehyde accumulates in the blood.
  • Disulfiram–ethanol reaction (within 10–30 minutes of drinking): flushing, throbbing headache, nausea, vomiting, sweating, palpitations, breathlessness, chest pain, hypotension; rarely collapse.
  • The fear of this unpleasant reaction creates a conditioned aversion to alcohol.
  • Dose: 250 mg daily (125–500 mg), started at least 12–24 hours after the last drink, preferably supervised by a family member.
  • Precautions: avoid hidden alcohol (cough syrups, tonics, mouthwashes, sauces, aftershave); the reaction can occur up to 2 weeks after stopping; contraindicated in heart disease, psychosis and pregnancy.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Describe the drugs used in cardiopulmonary resuscitation and other medical emergencies, with their actions, doses and nursing responsibilities.

diagram.caption: Drug timing in adult cardiac arrest
labels: adrenaline 1 mg after second shock then every 3–5 minutes
amiodarone 300 mg after third shock and 150 mg after fifth; non-shockable (asystole/PEA): adrenaline 1 mg as soon as possible then every 3–5 minutes

answer_html:
Introduction Emergency drugs are medicines needed within minutes to save life in cardiac arrest, anaphylaxis, shock, arrhythmias, severe asthma, hypoglycaemia, seizures and poisoning. They are kept ready on the crash cart (emergency trolley) in every ward, ICU, OT and casualty. Knowing their actions, doses and dangers allows the nurse to prepare and give them quickly and safely.

1. Adrenaline (epinephrine)

  • Action: stimulates α receptors (vasoconstriction → ↑ BP and coronary perfusion during CPR) and β receptors (↑ heart rate and force, bronchodilation, stabilises mast cells).
  • Strengths: 1:1000 (1 mg/mL) for IM use; 1:10,000 (1 mg in 10 mL) for IV use.
  • Cardiac arrest: 1 mg IV/IO every 3–5 minutes (as soon as possible in asystole/PEA; after the second shock in VF/pulseless VT).
  • Anaphylaxis: 0.5 mg IM (0.5 mL of 1:1000) in the anterolateral thigh, repeated after 5 minutes if needed; children 0.01 mg/kg (maximum 0.5 mg).
  • Infusion in shock and severe bradycardia (titrated); nebulised in croup.
  • Adverse effects: tachycardia, arrhythmias, hypertension, tissue necrosis if leaked.

2. Amiodarone

  • Action: class III antiarrhythmic – prolongs repolarisation.
  • Dose: VF/pulseless VT – 300 mg IV bolus after the third shock, a further 150 mg after the fifth shock; for stable VT/AF – 150 mg over 10 minutes, then infusion.
  • Points: dilute in 5% dextrose; causes hypotension, bradycardia and phlebitis – use a large vein or central line.
  • Lignocaine 1–1.5 mg/kg IV is an alternative when amiodarone is not available.

3. Atropine

  • Action: blocks vagal (muscarinic) action → ↑ heart rate.
  • Dose: symptomatic bradycardia – 1 mg IV, repeated every 3–5 minutes (maximum 3 mg); organophosphate poisoning – 2–4 mg IV, doubled every 5 minutes until atropinisation (dry chest, heart rate above 80, systolic BP above 80 mmHg).
  • Adverse effects: dry mouth, tachycardia, urinary retention, confusion; not used routinely in asystole now.

4. Adenosine

  • Action: briefly blocks AV-node conduction – terminates supraventricular tachycardia (SVT).
  • Dose: 6 mg rapid IV push followed immediately by a 20 mL saline flush; if no effect, 12 mg.
  • Points: warn the patient of chest tightness, flushing and a brief pause of the heart; use an antecubital vein; record the ECG strip; caution in asthma.

5. Drugs for anaphylaxis (after adrenaline)

  • Chlorpheniramine 10 mg IM/slow IV – relieves itching and urticaria (adjunct, not life-saving).
  • Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV – may prevent late reactions (adjunct).
  • IV fluids – 500–1000 mL rapid normal saline for hypotension; oxygen; nebulised salbutamol for wheeze.

6. Corticosteroids

  • Hydrocortisone 100–200 mg IV – acute severe asthma, adrenal crisis (100 mg IV then 50 mg 6-hourly), refractory septic shock.
  • Dexamethasone – cerebral oedema due to brain tumour (8–10 mg IV, then 4 mg 6-hourly), laryngeal oedema and croup, severe COVID-19 pneumonia, antenatal lung maturation, antiemetic in chemotherapy.
  • Adverse effects: hyperglycaemia, fluid retention, mood changes.

7. Sodium bicarbonate (8.4% = 1 mEq/mL)

  • Uses: severe metabolic acidosis, hyperkalaemia, tricyclic antidepressant overdose, prolonged cardiac arrest (not routine).
  • Dangers: metabolic alkalosis, hypernatraemia, fluid overload, tissue necrosis on leakage; inactivates adrenaline and precipitates with calcium – flush the line between drugs.

8. Calcium (calcium gluconate 10% / calcium chloride 10%)

  • Uses: hyperkalaemia with ECG changes (protects the heart), hypocalcaemia, calcium channel blocker overdose, magnesium sulphate toxicity.
  • Dose: calcium gluconate 10% 10–30 mL slow IV; inject slowly (bradycardia); avoid leakage.

9. Dextrose

  • Hypoglycaemia: 25–50 mL of 50% dextrose IV (or 100 mL of 25%) in adults; 2–5 mL/kg of 10% dextrose in children; follow with food or dextrose infusion.
  • With insulin in hyperkalaemia; give thiamine first in alcoholics.

10. Other emergency drugs | Drug | Emergency use | |---|---| | Naloxone 0.4–2 mg IV/IM | Opioid overdose | | Diazepam/lorazepam/midazolam | Status epilepticus | | Magnesium sulphate 2 g IV | Torsades de pointes, eclampsia, severe asthma | | Nitroglycerin (sublingual/IV) | Angina, acute pulmonary oedema, hypertensive emergency (avoid if SBP below 90 mmHg) | | Furosemide 40–80 mg IV | Acute pulmonary oedema | | Noradrenaline, dopamine, dobutamine infusions | Shock and low cardiac output | | Salbutamol nebulisation | Acute asthma, hyperkalaemia | | Tranexamic acid 1 g IV | Trauma and postpartum haemorrhage | | Oxygen | All life-threatening emergencies |

11. Nurse's responsibilities

  1. Check the crash cart every shift – drugs, strengths, quantities, expiry dates, seals; restock immediately after use; keep a checklist.
  2. Know the location and doses of key drugs; keep pre-filled or clearly labelled syringes (drug, dose, time) during a code.
  3. Use closed-loop communication – repeat the order aloud ("adrenaline 1 mg IV given at 10:05").
  4. Give drugs through a large vein or intraosseous route, followed by a 20 mL saline flush and elevation of the limb; never mix incompatible drugs.
  5. Time drug doses (every 3–5 minutes for adrenaline) and record every drug, dose, route and time on the code sheet.
  6. Monitor ECG, BP, SpO₂, blood glucose and the IV site; observe for adverse effects after the emergency.
  7. Keep emergency drugs out of reach of unauthorised persons; store refrigerated items (e.g. succinylcholine) correctly.

Nursing importance

  • In cardiac arrest and anaphylaxis, every minute of delay reduces survival; the nurse is often the first responder who must give adrenaline promptly.
  • Medication errors in emergencies (wrong strength of adrenaline, wrong route) are common and dangerous – training and standard protocols prevent them.

Conclusion Adrenaline, amiodarone, atropine, adenosine, corticosteroids, antihistamines, bicarbonate, calcium, dextrose and naloxone are the core emergency drugs. A well-maintained crash cart, sound knowledge of doses and calm, accurate administration by the nurse save lives.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Classify intravenous fluids. Describe their composition, indications, complications and the nurse's responsibilities, including electrolyte replacement with potassium chloride.

diagram.caption: Effect of isotonic, hypotonic and hypertonic fluids on red cells and body compartments
labels: isotonic – no change in cell size (normal saline
Ringer's lactate); hypotonic – water moves into cells
free water from 5% dextrose); hypertonic – water moves out of cells

answer_html:
Introduction Intravenous (IV) fluids are sterile solutions given into a vein to replace water and electrolytes, maintain daily requirements, correct electrolyte and acid–base disorders, supply glucose and carry drugs. They are drugs: the wrong fluid, the wrong amount or the wrong rate can kill. The choice depends on what the patient has lost and the tonicity of the fluid.

1. Classification A. According to type

  • Crystalloids – solutions of electrolytes and/or glucose that pass freely through capillary walls (normal saline, Ringer's lactate, dextrose solutions).
  • Colloids – contain large molecules that stay in the blood vessels (albumin, gelatin, starch) – used as plasma expanders.
  • Blood and blood products.

B. According to tonicity (compared with plasma, about 285–295 mOsm/L)

  • Isotonic – normal saline (0.9% NaCl), Ringer's lactate, 5% dextrose (in the bag).
  • Hypotonic – 0.45% NaCl (half normal saline); 5% dextrose acts as hypotonic after its glucose is used up (it gives free water).
  • Hypertonic – 3% NaCl, 10%, 25% and 50% dextrose, DNS (5% dextrose in 0.9% NaCl).

C. According to purpose

  • Replacement fluids (NS, RL), maintenance fluids (DNS, Isolyte-type multiple electrolyte solutions, 5% dextrose with saline and potassium), special-purpose fluids (3% saline, sodium bicarbonate, mannitol, dextrose 25–50%).

2. Composition and uses of common crystalloids | Fluid | Composition (per litre) | Main uses | Cautions | |---|---|---|---| | 0.9% NaCl (normal saline) | Na⁺ 154, Cl⁻ 154 mEq; 308 mOsm | Shock, dehydration, vomiting, hyponatraemia, diabetic ketoacidosis (initial), with blood transfusion, drug dilution | Hyperchloraemic acidosis, fluid overload | | Ringer's lactate (Hartmann's) | Na⁺ 130, K⁺ 4, Ca²⁺ 3, Cl⁻ 109, lactate 28 mEq; 273 mOsm | Surgery, trauma, burns (Parkland formula), diarrhoea, intra-operative replacement | Avoid with blood transfusion line (calcium clots blood); caution in severe liver failure and hyperkalaemia | | 5% dextrose (D5W) | Glucose 50 g (170 kcal); no electrolytes | Water deficit, hypernatraemia, keeping the vein open, diluting drugs (e.g. amiodarone) | Never for resuscitation; causes hyponatraemia and cerebral oedema if overused (especially children, head injury) | | DNS (5% dextrose in 0.9% NaCl) | Glucose 50 g + Na⁺ 154, Cl⁻ 154 | Maintenance with calories, post-operative patients, vomiting | Fluid and sodium overload | | 0.45% NaCl | Na⁺ 77, Cl⁻ 77 | Hypernatraemia, maintenance in selected adults | Hypotonic – avoid in head injury | | 3% NaCl (hypertonic saline) | Na⁺ 513 mEq | Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia, raised ICP | Correct Na⁺ by not more than 8–10 mEq/L in 24 hours (osmotic demyelination); central line preferred | | 10% dextrose | Glucose 100 g | Hypoglycaemia, neonatal maintenance, with insulin in hyperkalaemia | Phlebitis, hyperglycaemia | | 25%/50% dextrose | 250/500 g | Emergency treatment of hypoglycaemia | Very irritant – large vein, slow IV | | Multiple electrolyte solutions (e.g. Isolyte-P for children, Isolyte-G for gastric losses, Plasma-Lyte) | Balanced Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, acetate/lactate | Maintenance; replacement of specific losses | Check composition before use |

3. Electrolyte replacement A. Potassium chloride (KCl)

  • 15% KCl ampoule = 2 mEq/mL (10 mL = 20 mEq) – a high-alert concentrated electrolyte.
  • Rules for IV potassium:
    1. Never give as IV push or bolus – can cause cardiac arrest.
    2. Always dilute – usually not more than 40 mEq per litre through a peripheral vein; mix thoroughly (invert the bag several times).
    3. Rate not more than 10 mEq/hour peripherally (up to 20 mEq/hour only through a central line with ECG monitoring in ICU).
    4. Check urine output ("no urine, no potassium") – at least 0.5 mL/kg/hour.
    5. Monitor serum K⁺ and ECG; watch the IV site (KCl is painful and irritant).
    6. Store KCl ampoules separately from other ampoules, with warning labels; prefer premixed bags.
  • Oral KCl syrup/tablets for mild hypokalaemia – dilute and give after food.

B. Other electrolyte preparations

  • Sodium bicarbonate 7.5–8.4% – metabolic acidosis (as ordered after ABG).
  • Calcium gluconate 10% – hypocalcaemia, hyperkalaemia.
  • Magnesium sulphate – hypomagnesaemia (e.g. 1–2 g IV diluted over 1 hour).
  • ORS – preferred whenever the patient can drink (mild–moderate dehydration).

4. Complications of IV fluid therapy

  • Fluid overload – raised JVP, breathlessness, basal crepitations, pulmonary oedema, oedema, weight gain (elderly, heart and kidney disease, children).
  • Electrolyte imbalance – hyponatraemia (excess D5W), hypernatraemia, hyperchloraemic acidosis, hypo/hyperkalaemia; hyperglycaemia with dextrose.
  • Local – phlebitis, infiltration and extravasation (dextrose 25–50%, KCl, bicarbonate, calcium), haematoma, infection.
  • Systemic – catheter-related bloodstream infection, air embolism, pyrogenic reactions from contaminated fluids, speed shock (drugs given too fast).

5. Nurse's responsibilities

  1. Check the doctor's order – type, volume, additives, rate and duration; verify the bag (name, concentration, expiry date, clarity, no leaks or particles).
  2. Label bags with additives (drug, dose, date, time, signature); never add drugs to blood or to running bags without mixing.
  3. Calculate the drip rate correctly: drops/min = volume (mL) × drop factor ÷ time (min) (macro-drip 15–20 drops/mL, micro-drip 60 drops/mL); use infusion pumps for high-risk fluids, children and the elderly.
  4. Maintain an intake–output chart, daily weight, and record vital signs, breath sounds, oedema and level of consciousness.
  5. Monitor serum electrolytes, blood sugar, urea and creatinine as ordered.
  6. Inspect the cannula site every shift using a phlebitis (VIP) score; change sites and sets as per policy; maintain asepsis.
  7. Prefer isotonic fluids in children and in head injury; avoid excessive 5% dextrose.
  8. Stop the infusion and inform the doctor at signs of overload, reaction or infiltration.

Nursing importance

  • IV fluids are given to almost every hospitalised patient; fluid overload and electrolyte errors (especially potassium) are common, serious and preventable.
  • Accurate drip calculation, careful observation and the intake–output chart are the nurse's most powerful safety tools.

Conclusion Crystalloids such as normal saline and Ringer's lactate replace ECF losses, dextrose solutions supply water and calories, and hypertonic and special fluids correct specific disorders. Choosing the right fluid, giving potassium by strict rules and closely monitoring the patient make IV therapy safe.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Explain the general principles of management of poisoning and the drugs used in its treatment – decontaminating agents, drugs enhancing elimination and specific antidotes.

diagram.caption: Steps in management of an acutely poisoned patient

answer_html:
Introduction Poisoning is the harmful effect of a substance taken accidentally or deliberately. In India, common poisons include organophosphate and other pesticides, aluminium phosphide, rat poisons, kerosene, drug overdoses (paracetamol, benzodiazepines), corrosives, alcohol (methanol), snake bites and scorpion stings. Most patients recover with good supportive care; specific antidotes are available for only a few poisons.

1. General principles of management

  1. Resuscitation (ABC) – secure airway, oxygen, ventilation if needed; treat shock, arrhythmias and seizures; check blood glucose.
  2. History and examination – what, how much, when, route, intent; empty containers; recognise toxidromes (e.g. pinpoint pupils + respiratory depression = opioid; salivation, sweating, small pupils, fasciculations = organophosphate; hot, dry, flushed, dilated pupils = anticholinergic).
  3. Decontamination – prevent further absorption.
  4. Enhanced elimination – remove absorbed poison.
  5. Specific antidote where available.
  6. Supportive care and monitoring.
  7. Psychiatric assessment (self-harm) and medico-legal formalities.

2. Decontamination

  • Skin and eyes: remove contaminated clothes (wear gloves for pesticides), wash skin with soap and water; irrigate eyes with saline for 15–20 minutes.
  • Activated charcoal: 1 g/kg (adults about 50 g) as a slurry, orally or by nasogastric tube, preferably within 1 hour; adsorbs most drugs. Multiple doses (every 4 hours) for carbamazepine, phenobarbitone, theophylline, dapsone.
    • Not effective for alcohols, iron, lithium, heavy metals, acids, alkalis.
    • Contraindicated in unprotected airway, corrosives, hydrocarbons (kerosene), bowel obstruction.
  • Gastric lavage: only within about 1 hour of a life-threatening ingestion, with the airway protected (left lateral, head low); never in corrosive or kerosene poisoning.
  • Induced vomiting (syrup of ipecac): no longer recommended.
  • Whole bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol solution – iron, lithium, sustained-release tablets, drug packets.

3. Enhanced elimination

  • Urinary alkalinisation with IV sodium bicarbonate – salicylates, phenobarbitone.
  • Haemodialysis – methanol, ethylene glycol, lithium, salicylates, some others with kidney failure.
  • Multiple-dose activated charcoal ("gut dialysis").

4. Specific antidotes | Poison | Antidote | |---|---| | Paracetamol | N-acetylcysteine (IV or oral) | | Opioids | Naloxone | | Benzodiazepines | Flumazenil (selected cases) | | Organophosphates, carbamates | Atropine + pralidoxime (oxime for organophosphates) | | Anticholinergics (datura, atropine) | Physostigmine (rarely) | | Iron | Desferrioxamine | | Lead, arsenic, mercury | Dimercaprol (BAL), calcium disodium EDTA, succimer (DMSA) | | Copper, Wilson's disease | Penicillamine | | Methanol, ethylene glycol | Fomepizole or ethanol, folinic acid | | Cyanide | Hydroxocobalamin, or sodium nitrite + sodium thiosulphate | | Carbon monoxide | 100% oxygen (hyperbaric if available) | | Heparin | Protamine sulphate | | Warfarin, rat poisons (superwarfarins) | Vitamin K1, fresh frozen plasma/prothrombin complex | | Digoxin | Digoxin-specific antibody fragments; correct potassium | | β-blockers | Glucagon; calcium channel blockers – calcium, high-dose insulin | | Tricyclic antidepressants | Sodium bicarbonate | | Methaemoglobinaemia (nitrites, dapsone) | Methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV | | Isoniazid | Pyridoxine | | Sulfonylureas, insulin | Dextrose, octreotide | | Local anaesthetic toxicity | 20% lipid emulsion | | Snake bite | Polyvalent anti-snake venom | | Scorpion sting (Indian red scorpion) | Prazosin (pioneered in Maharashtra), scorpion antivenom | | Aluminium phosphide, paraquat, organochlorines | No specific antidote – supportive care |

5. Supportive care

  • Oxygen and ventilation, IV fluids, vasopressors, anticonvulsants (benzodiazepines), correction of glucose, electrolytes and acidosis, cooling or warming, prevention of aspiration, dialysis for kidney failure.

6. Nurse's responsibilities

  1. Immediate care: ABC, lateral position, suction, oxygen, IV access, monitor vital signs, GCS, pupils, SpO₂ and blood glucose.
  2. Give activated charcoal and antidotes exactly as ordered; note times; watch for antidote reactions (anaphylactoid reaction with IV NAC, withdrawal with naloxone, seizures with flumazenil).
  3. Collect and preserve samples – vomitus, gastric aspirate, blood and urine – sealed and labelled; keep containers and tablets for identification.
  4. Medico-legal case (MLC): inform the duty doctor and police as per hospital policy; document accurately and objectively.
  5. Suicide precautions – one-to-one observation, remove harmful objects, early psychiatric referral; support the family.
  6. Educate the community – safe storage of pesticides and medicines away from children, use of child-resistant containers, avoiding illicit liquor; poison information helplines.

7. Drug points in common Indian poisonings

  • Organophosphate (pesticide) poisoning – atropine in doubling doses until atropinisation, pralidoxime infusion as per protocol, decontamination of skin; watch for intermediate syndrome (neck and respiratory muscle weakness after 24–96 hours).
  • Aluminium phosphide (celphos) tablets – no antidote; manage shock with fluids and vasopressors, correct acidosis and magnesium as ordered; avoid water lavage that releases more phosphine gas unless advised.
  • Kerosene and other hydrocarbons – no vomiting, no lavage, no charcoal; watch for chemical pneumonitis and give oxygen.
  • Corrosives (acids, toilet cleaners) – no lavage, no neutralising agents; keep nil by mouth, give analgesics and PPIs, plan endoscopy.
  • Rat poison (superwarfarins, zinc phosphide) – check INR and give vitamin K1 for prolonged periods if INR rises; phosphides are treated supportively.

Nursing importance

  • Survival in poisoning depends mostly on prompt resuscitation and good supportive nursing; early recognition of deterioration (respiratory failure in organophosphate, delayed liver failure in paracetamol) saves lives.
  • Accurate documentation and sample handling are essential because poisoning cases are medico-legal.

Conclusion Management of poisoning rests on resuscitation, decontamination, enhanced elimination, specific antidotes and supportive care. Activated charcoal and a small set of antidotes – N-acetylcysteine, naloxone, atropine with pralidoxime, desferrioxamine, chelators, fomepizole, vitamin K and ASV – are life-saving when used correctly.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Explain anti-snake venom (ASV) – indications, dose, administration, adverse reactions and nursing responsibilities.
answer_html:
Introduction Snakebite is a major but neglected public health problem in rural India – especially among farmers in Maharashtra and Vidarbha during the monsoon – causing tens of thousands of deaths every year. Anti-snake venom (ASV) is the only specific antidote. India's polyvalent ASV is prepared from horse serum and neutralises the venom of the "Big Four": Indian cobra, common krait, Russell's viper and saw-scaled viper. India launched a National Action Plan for Prevention and Control of Snakebite Envenoming (2024) aiming to halve snakebite deaths by 2030.

1. Types of envenomation

  • Neurotoxic (cobra, krait) – ptosis, double vision, difficulty swallowing and speaking, neck muscle weakness, respiratory paralysis; krait bites are often painless, at night, during sleep on the floor.
  • Haemotoxic/vasculotoxic (Russell's viper, saw-scaled viper) – local swelling, blistering, bleeding from gums and bite site, blood in urine, incoagulable blood, shock, acute kidney injury (Russell's viper).

2. Indications for ASV (only if signs of envenomation are present)

  1. Incoagulable blood – positive 20-minute whole blood clotting test (20WBCT) or spontaneous bleeding.
  2. Neurotoxic signs – ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, bulbar or respiratory weakness.
  3. Shock, arrhythmia, acute kidney injury, dark urine.
  4. Local swelling involving more than half of the bitten limb, rapidly progressing swelling, or swelling of a bitten finger/toe. - ASV is not given for a bite without envenomation (dry bite) – such patients are observed for 24 hours.

3. Dose and administration

  • Initial dose: 8–10 vials (80–100 mL) IV – the same dose for children and adults (snakes inject the same amount of venom).
  • Given as an IV infusion in 5–10 mL/kg normal saline over about 1 hour, or slow IV injection (about 2 mL/min) after reconstitution.
  • No skin test dose – it does not predict reactions and wastes time.
  • Repeat doses: in haemotoxic bites, the 20WBCT is repeated every 6 hours and further ASV given until blood clots; in neurotoxic bites, a repeat dose may be given if no improvement after 1–2 hours, with neostigmine–atropine trial and ventilatory support.
  • ASV can be given at any time while signs of envenomation persist, even days after the bite.

4. Adverse reactions

  • Early anaphylactic reactions (within minutes to 3 hours) – itching, urticaria, fever, vomiting, bronchospasm, hypotension → stop ASV, give adrenaline 0.5 mg IM (1:1000), antihistamine and hydrocortisone; restart slowly once the reaction settles.
  • Pyrogenic reactions – fever, chills.
  • Late serum sickness (5–24 days) – fever, urticaria, joint pains, lymph node swelling → antihistamines, prednisolone.

5. Nursing responsibilities

  1. First aid – reassure, immobilise the limb like a fracture, keep it at heart level, remove rings and tight clothes, transport quickly; avoid tourniquets, cutting, sucking, ice and herbal remedies.
  2. Perform 20WBCT: 2 mL of fresh venous blood in a new, clean, dry glass test tube, left undisturbed for 20 minutes, then tilted – if the blood is still liquid, it is incoagulable.
  3. Keep adrenaline, oxygen, suction, Ambu bag and intubation equipment ready before starting ASV; monitor every 15 minutes during infusion.
  4. Monitor neurological signs (ptosis, single breath count, neck flexion), bleeding, urine output and colour, BP and SpO₂.
  5. Give tetanus prophylaxis and wound care; do not open blisters; watch for compartment syndrome.
  6. Store ASV correctly (lyophilised below 25°C; liquid ASV 2–8°C), record batch numbers, and report cases as per state notification rules.
  7. Educate communities – wearing footwear, using a torch at night, sleeping on cots under mosquito nets, keeping surroundings clear.

Conclusion Polyvalent ASV neutralises the venom of India's Big Four snakes and must be given promptly when signs of envenomation appear. Correct dosing guided by the 20WBCT, readiness to treat reactions, close monitoring and supportive care by nurses save many rural lives.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Explain the vitamins and minerals given by injection in hospitals, with their indications and nursing precautions.
answer_html:
Introduction Most vitamin and mineral needs are met by diet or oral supplements. Injections are used when there is severe deficiency, malabsorption, inability to take orally, an emergency, or a need for rapid correction. Nurses must know their uses and the special precautions for each.

1. Vitamins given by injection | Vitamin | Preparation and dose | Main indications | Precautions | |---|---|---|---| | Thiamine (B1) | 100 mg IM/IV; 200–500 mg IV three times daily in Wernicke's | Alcohol dependence, Wernicke's encephalopathy, hyperemesis gravidarum, malnutrition, refeeding | Give before IV glucose in at-risk patients; dilute and infuse slowly – rare anaphylaxis | | Vitamin K1 (phytomenadione) | 1–10 mg slow IV/IM; 1 mg IM for newborns | Warfarin over-anticoagulation and bleeding, obstructive jaundice before surgery, rat-poison ingestion, newborn prophylaxis | Slow IV (not faster than 1 mg/min) – anaphylactoid reactions; protect from light | | Vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin, hydroxocobalamin, methylcobalamin) | 1000 µg IM, repeated as per schedule | Pernicious anaemia (life-long), after gastrectomy or ileal resection, B12-deficiency neuropathy | Check folate too; watch potassium in severe anaemia when treatment starts | | Folinic acid (calcium leucovorin) | As ordered | Methotrexate rescue, with 5-fluorouracil in chemotherapy, methanol poisoning | Timing is critical in methotrexate rescue | | Vitamin C | IV | Scurvy, adjunct in methaemoglobinaemia | High doses – kidney stones | | Multivitamin infusion (MVI) and trace elements | Added to IV fluids or total parenteral nutrition (TPN) | Patients on TPN, critically ill, burns | Add just before use; protect from light |

2. Minerals given by injection | Mineral | Indication | Precautions | |---|---|---| | Iron – iron sucrose (100–200 mg slow IV) and ferric carboxymaltose (up to 1000 mg over about 15 minutes) | Moderate to severe iron-deficiency anaemia in pregnancy (Anaemia Mukt Bharat), CKD, intolerance or failure of oral iron | Observe for 30 minutes for hypersensitivity; avoid in the first trimester; extravasation causes skin staining; resuscitation drugs at hand | | Potassium chloride | Hypokalaemia | Never IV push; dilute; maximum rate rules | | Magnesium sulphate | Hypomagnesaemia, eclampsia, torsades | Monitor reflexes and respiration | | Calcium gluconate | Hypocalcaemia, hyperkalaemia | Slow IV; avoid leakage | | Zinc, selenium, copper (trace elements) | TPN, severe burns, chronic diarrhoea | As per TPN protocol | | Sodium bicarbonate, phosphate | Acidosis, hypophosphataemia (refeeding) | Guided by blood tests |

3. Nursing precautions

  1. Verify the exact drug, strength, dose and route; many vitamin ampoules look alike.
  2. Follow the dilution and rate instructions; use infusion pumps for iron and electrolytes.
  3. Keep adrenaline and resuscitation equipment ready for IV iron, thiamine and vitamin K.
  4. Protect light-sensitive preparations (vitamin K, MVI, B12) and give freshly prepared admixtures.
  5. Monitor blood tests – Hb, ferritin, electrolytes, INR – to judge response.
  6. Educate patients about diet and oral supplements to prevent recurrence.

Conclusion Parenteral vitamins and minerals such as thiamine, vitamin K1, vitamin B12, IV iron and electrolytes correct serious deficiencies quickly. Correct dilution, slow administration and readiness for reactions ensure their safe use.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Explain the sera and immunoglobulins used for passive immunisation, with their indications and nursing precautions.
answer_html:
Introduction Passive immunisation means giving ready-made antibodies to provide immediate but short-lived protection (weeks to months). It is used when there is no time for a vaccine to act, after high-risk exposure, or to neutralise toxins. These products are called sera (antisera) when obtained from animals and immunoglobulins when obtained from humans.

1. Types A. Heterologous sera (from horses – equine)

  • Anti-snake venom (ASV) – Big Four snake envenomation.
  • Anti-diphtheritic serum (ADS) – diphtheria (with antibiotics).
  • Equine rabies immunoglobulin (ERIG) – 40 IU/kg in category III rabies exposure.
  • Anti-tetanus serum (ATS) – largely replaced by human tetanus immunoglobulin.
  • Antiscorpion venom.
  • Risk of anaphylaxis and serum sickness is higher than with human products.

B. Homologous immunoglobulins (from humans) | Product | Main indication | |---|---| | Normal human immunoglobulin (IVIG/IM) | Primary immunodeficiency, Guillain–Barré syndrome, ITP, Kawasaki disease, prevention of hepatitis A and measles in contacts | | Human rabies immunoglobulin (HRIG) 20 IU/kg | Category III rabies exposure – infiltrated into the wound | | Rabies monoclonal antibody (developed in India) | Alternative to RIG in category III exposures | | Human tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG) 250–500 IU IM | Tetanus-prone wounds in non-immunised persons; higher doses in tetanus treatment | | Hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) | Newborns of HBsAg-positive mothers (within 12 hours, with hepatitis B vaccine), needle-stick injury in non-immune persons | | Varicella-zoster immunoglobulin (VZIG) | Exposed pregnant women, newborns and immunocompromised persons | | Anti-D (Rh) immunoglobulin | Rh-negative mother after delivery of an Rh-positive baby (within 72 hours), abortion, antepartum bleeding, at 28 weeks | | Monoclonal antibodies such as palivizumab | RSV prevention in high-risk infants |

2. Advantages and disadvantages

  • Advantages: immediate protection; life-saving when exposure has already occurred.
  • Disadvantages: short protection, no memory, expensive, hypersensitivity reactions, and they interfere with live vaccines given soon after (measles/MR vaccine should usually be delayed for about 3 months after immunoglobulin).

3. Nursing precautions

  1. Take an allergy history; keep adrenaline 1:1000, antihistamine, hydrocortisone and resuscitation equipment ready; observe for at least 30 minutes (longer for equine sera).
  2. Infiltrate RIG into and around all wounds as much as anatomically possible; never give RIG in the same syringe or at the same site as the vaccine.
  3. Give large IM volumes into big muscles (anterolateral thigh/gluteal as appropriate); IVIG by slow infusion with pump, monitoring pulse, BP and temperature.
  4. Maintain the cold chain (2–8°C); do not freeze; check expiry.
  5. Record product name, batch number, dose and site; explain to the patient about delayed serum sickness (fever, rash, joint pains after 1–2 weeks).
  6. Ensure the active vaccine course (rabies, tetanus, hepatitis B) is also completed.

Conclusion Sera and immunoglobulins give instant, temporary protection by supplying antibodies. Correct selection, careful administration, observation for allergy and completion of active immunisation make them effective and safe.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: What is an adverse event following immunisation (AEFI)? Explain its classification, common reactions and the nurse's role in safe immunisation.
answer_html:
Definition An adverse event following immunisation (AEFI) is any untoward medical occurrence that follows immunisation and does not necessarily have a causal relationship with the vaccine. It may be a mild local reaction or a serious event requiring hospitalisation. Prompt reporting and investigation of AEFIs maintain public trust in vaccination.

1. Classification (WHO, cause-specific)

  1. Vaccine product-related reaction – due to the inherent properties of the vaccine (e.g. fever after pentavalent, BCG lymphadenitis).
  2. Vaccine quality defect-related reaction – manufacturing defect.
  3. Immunisation error-related reaction (programme error) – wrong diluent, wrong dose or route, reuse of syringes, contaminated reconstituted vaccine (e.g. toxic shock syndrome from measles vaccine kept for many hours).
  4. Immunisation anxiety-related reaction – fainting, hyperventilation, especially in adolescents.
  5. Coincidental event – illness that would have occurred anyway. - Serious AEFI: death, hospitalisation, disability, life-threatening events (anaphylaxis, seizures), and clusters of events.

2. Common vaccine reactions | Vaccine | Common/expected reactions | Rare serious reactions | |---|---|---| | BCG | Papule → small ulcer → scar in 6–12 weeks | Abscess, suppurative lymphadenitis, disseminated BCG (immunodeficiency) | | Pentavalent/DPT | Fever, pain, swelling, irritability, persistent crying | Febrile seizures, hypotonic–hyporesponsive episode, anaphylaxis | | OPV | Usually none | Vaccine-associated paralytic polio (very rare) | | Measles–rubella (MR) | Fever and rash after 5–12 days | Febrile seizures, low platelets | | Hepatitis B, PCV, fIPV, JE | Local pain, mild fever | Anaphylaxis (about 1 per million doses) | | Rotavirus | Mild diarrhoea, vomiting | Intussusception (very rare) |

3. Nurse's role in safe immunisation and AEFI management

  1. Screen before vaccinating – previous severe allergy to the same vaccine (contraindication), immunodeficiency and pregnancy for live vaccines; minor illness and low-grade fever are not contraindications.
  2. Follow safe injection practices – auto-disable syringes, correct site and route, no recapping, hub cutter and proper waste disposal.
  3. Use the correct diluent supplied with the vaccine; follow the open vial policy – some opened vials (OPV, pentavalent, Td, hepatitis B, PCV, fIPV) may be reused in later sessions within 28 days under conditions, while reconstituted vaccines (BCG, MR, JE) are discarded after 4–6 hours or at the end of the session; check the VVM and expiry.
  4. Keep an AEFI kit (adrenaline 1:1000, syringes, IV cannula and fluids) at every session; know the adrenaline dose for anaphylaxis (0.01 mL/kg of 1:1000 IM, maximum 0.5 mL).
  5. Observe every beneficiary for 30 minutes after vaccination.
  6. Counsel parents – fever and pain are common; give paracetamol as advised; do not apply anything on the BCG ulcer; return if high fever, persistent crying, seizures or breathing difficulty.
  7. Report serious AEFIs immediately (within 24 hours) to the medical officer/district immunisation officer using the prescribed forms, and help in investigation and causality assessment; preserve the vial and syringe.
  8. Address rumours and vaccine hesitancy with facts and empathy.

Conclusion Most AEFIs are mild and self-limiting, but serious events and programme errors must be prevented, recognised and reported. Careful screening, safe vaccine handling, observation and clear counselling by nurses keep immunisation safe and trusted.
