question: Classify anticancer (antineoplastic) drugs. Explain their mechanism of action, common adverse effects and the nurse's responsibilities in safe administration of chemotherapy.

diagram.caption: Cell cycle and phase-specific anticancer drugs
labels: G0 resting cells; cell-cycle non-specific drugs (alkylating agents

answer_html:
Introduction Anticancer (antineoplastic) drugs are used to kill or stop the growth of cancer cells. Classical cytotoxic drugs act on rapidly dividing cells – so they also damage normal fast-dividing tissues (bone marrow, gut lining, hair follicles, gonads). Newer targeted drugs and immunotherapies act on specific features of cancer cells or on the immune system. Cancer is now a leading cause of death in India, and chemotherapy day-care units are found in most district cancer centres.

1. Classification | Group | Examples | Main mechanism | |---|---|---| | A. Alkylating agents | Cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, chlorambucil, melphalan, busulfan, dacarbazine, temozolomide; platinum compounds – cisplatin, carboplatin, oxaliplatin | Cross-link DNA strands → cell cannot divide (cell-cycle non-specific) | | B. Antimetabolites | Methotrexate (folate antagonist); 5-fluorouracil, capecitabine, cytarabine, gemcitabine (pyrimidine antagonists); 6-mercaptopurine, fludarabine (purine antagonists) | Block DNA synthesis in S phase | | C. Plant products | Vincristine, vinblastine (vinca alkaloids); paclitaxel, docetaxel (taxanes); etoposide; irinotecan | Disrupt microtubules (M phase) or block topoisomerase | | D. Antitumour antibiotics | Doxorubicin, daunorubicin, bleomycin, actinomycin D, mitomycin C | Intercalate DNA, free radicals, topoisomerase II inhibition | | E. Hormones and antagonists | Prednisolone; tamoxifen; letrozole, anastrozole; bicalutamide, enzalutamide; leuprolide, goserelin | Block hormone-dependent growth (breast, prostate cancers, lymphomas) | | F. Targeted therapy | Imatinib (CML), gefitinib, erlotinib (lung), rituximab (lymphoma), trastuzumab (HER2 breast cancer), bevacizumab, bortezomib | Block specific growth signals or surface molecules | | G. Immunotherapy | Checkpoint inhibitors (pembrolizumab, nivolumab), interferon-α, BCG (bladder), CAR-T cell therapy (India's own CAR-T therapy approved in 2023) | Strengthen the body's immune attack on cancer | | H. Miscellaneous | Hydroxyurea, L-asparaginase, all-trans retinoic acid and arsenic trioxide (acute promyelocytic leukaemia), thalidomide/lenalidomide | Various |

2. Principles of cancer chemotherapy

  • Combination chemotherapy – drugs with different actions and toxicities (e.g. CHOP for lymphoma, ABVD for Hodgkin's, FOLFOX for colon cancer) → better effect, less resistance.
  • Given in cycles (e.g. every 3 weeks) to allow normal cells to recover.
  • Doses calculated by body surface area (mg/m²); adjusted to blood counts and kidney/liver function.
  • Neoadjuvant (before surgery), adjuvant (after surgery), curative (leukaemia, lymphoma, testicular cancer) or palliative.

3. Common adverse effects

  1. Bone-marrow suppression – lowest counts (nadir) about 7–14 days after a dose: neutropenia (infection, febrile neutropenia), thrombocytopenia (bleeding), anaemia (fatigue).
  2. Gastrointestinal – nausea and vomiting (severe with cisplatin), mucositis/stomatitis, diarrhoea, loss of appetite and taste changes.
  3. Alopecia – usually temporary.
  4. Gonadal toxicity – infertility, amenorrhoea; drugs are teratogenic.
  5. Tumour lysis syndrome – hyperuricaemia, hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, kidney failure (prevented by hydration and allopurinol).
  6. Extravasation injury – vesicants (doxorubicin, vincristine, vinblastine, dacarbazine, mitomycin) cause severe tissue necrosis if they leak.
  7. Drug-specific toxicities:
    • Cyclophosphamide – haemorrhagic cystitis (prevented by hydration and mesna).
    • Cisplatin – nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neuropathy, severe vomiting, low magnesium.
    • Doxorubicin – cardiotoxicity (cumulative dose limit), red urine.
    • Bleomycin – pulmonary fibrosis, fever.
    • Vincristine – peripheral neuropathy, constipation; fatal if given intrathecally.
    • Methotrexate – mucositis, liver damage, myelosuppression (folinic acid rescue).
    • 5-FU/capecitabine – mucositis, diarrhoea, hand–foot syndrome.
    • Paclitaxel – hypersensitivity (premedication needed), neuropathy.
    • Tamoxifen – hot flushes, DVT, endometrial cancer.
    • Targeted/immunotherapy – infusion reactions, skin rash, immune-related inflammation of organs (colitis, pneumonitis, thyroiditis).
  8. Long-term – second cancers, organ damage.

4. Nurse's responsibilities in safe administration A. Before administration

  1. Verify the order with two trained nurses independently – patient, regimen, cycle and day, dose calculated from height and weight (BSA), route, rate, diluent.
  2. Check blood counts (e.g. neutrophils, platelets), kidney and liver function as per protocol; report abnormal values before starting.
  3. Obtain informed consent; explain the plan and side effects; assess baseline weight, vital signs, mouth and skin.
  4. Give premedication – antiemetics (ondansetron, dexamethasone, aprepitant), antihistamines and steroids for paclitaxel, hydration and mesna as ordered.

B. Safe handling (protecting staff and environment)

  1. Prepare drugs in a biological safety cabinet by trained staff using chemotherapy-tested double gloves, impermeable gown, mask and eye protection; use closed-system transfer devices where available.
  2. Pregnant and breastfeeding staff should not prepare or give cytotoxic drugs.
  3. Keep a spill kit; dispose of cytotoxic waste in labelled yellow "cytotoxic" bags/containers for incineration as per the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016.
  4. Handle the patient's urine, vomit and linen with gloves for 48 hours after chemotherapy.

C. During administration

  1. Use a free-flowing IV line in a large vein, preferably a central line, PICC or port for vesicants; check blood return before and during infusion.
  2. Watch for extravasation – pain, burning, swelling, redness, slow flow: stop the infusion immediately, leave the cannula, aspirate the drug, inform the doctor, elevate the limb, apply cold (anthracyclines) or warm (vinca alkaloids) compresses and antidotes as per protocol, and document.
  3. Monitor for hypersensitivity/infusion reactions – stop, give emergency drugs, inform.
  4. Label vincristine syringes "For intravenous use only – fatal if given by other routes".

D. After administration

  1. Neutropenic precautions – hand hygiene, avoid crowds and sick visitors, safe food, check temperature; treat fever of 38°C or more as an emergency (febrile neutropenia).
  2. Bleeding precautions – soft toothbrush, no IM injections, avoid aspirin.
  3. Mouth care – soft brush, saline/soda mouthwashes, avoid spicy food; adequate nutrition and fluids (2–3 litres/day unless restricted).
  4. Counsel on alopecia (scarf, wig), contraception during therapy, fertility preservation (sperm/oocyte banking) before therapy, and psychosocial support.

Nursing importance

  • Chemotherapy is high-risk for patients and staff; double-checks, safe handling and early detection of complications are central nursing duties.
  • Nurses spend the most time with patients during treatment and are key to symptom control, adherence and emotional support.

Conclusion Anticancer drugs – alkylating agents, antimetabolites, plant products, antibiotics, hormones, targeted drugs and immunotherapy – attack cancer cells through different mechanisms but share toxic effects on normal tissues. Safe preparation, careful administration, monitoring and supportive care by trained nurses make chemotherapy effective and safe.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Explain the immunosuppressants and immunostimulants with their uses, adverse effects and nursing implications.
answer_html:
Introduction Immunosuppressants are drugs that reduce the immune response; they are used to prevent rejection of transplanted organs and to treat autoimmune diseases. Immunostimulants (immunomodulators) enhance immune function in infections, immunodeficiency and cancer.

1. Immunosuppressants | Group | Examples | Key adverse effects | |---|---|---| | Calcineurin inhibitors | Cyclosporine, tacrolimus | Nephrotoxicity, hypertension, tremor, hyperglycaemia (tacrolimus), gum hypertrophy and hirsutism (cyclosporine) | | Antiproliferative agents | Azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, low-dose methotrexate | Bone-marrow suppression, GI upset, liver toxicity; mycophenolate is teratogenic | | mTOR inhibitors | Sirolimus, everolimus | Poor wound healing, high lipids, mouth ulcers | | Glucocorticoids | Prednisolone, methylprednisolone (pulse) | Infection, diabetes, osteoporosis, cushingoid features, peptic ulcer | | Biological agents | Antithymocyte globulin, basiliximab, rituximab, TNF-α inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept), tocilizumab | Infusion reactions, serious infections, reactivation of tuberculosis and hepatitis B | | Cytotoxic drugs | Cyclophosphamide | Myelosuppression, haemorrhagic cystitis |

Uses

  • Organ transplantation (kidney, liver, heart) – induction, lifelong maintenance (commonly tacrolimus + mycophenolate + prednisolone), treatment of rejection; bone-marrow transplant (graft-versus-host disease).
  • Autoimmune and inflammatory diseases – rheumatoid arthritis, SLE and lupus nephritis, inflammatory bowel disease, psoriasis, nephrotic syndrome, myasthenia gravis, autoimmune hepatitis.

Common risks: opportunistic infections (CMV, TB, fungal, Pneumocystis), cancers (skin cancer, lymphoma) with long-term use.

2. Immunostimulants | Drug | Use | |---|---| | Interferon-α | Hepatitis B, some leukaemias and melanoma | | Interferon-β | Multiple sclerosis | | Interleukin-2 | Renal cell carcinoma, melanoma | | Colony-stimulating factors – filgrastim (G-CSF), GM-CSF | Chemotherapy-induced neutropenia, stem cell mobilisation | | BCG (intravesical) | Superficial bladder cancer | | Levamisole | Steroid-sparing agent in childhood nephrotic syndrome; anthelmintic | | Imiquimod (topical) | Genital warts, superficial skin cancers | | Vaccines and checkpoint inhibitors | Prevention of infection; cancer immunotherapy | Adverse effects: flu-like symptoms (fever, chills, myalgia) with interferons, bone pain with filgrastim, depression (interferon), injection-site reactions.

3. Nursing implications

  1. Give immunosuppressants at the same time every day; never miss or stop doses – missed doses lead to rejection.
  2. Collect trough blood levels (before the morning dose) of tacrolimus/cyclosporine as ordered; report interacting drugs (rifampicin lowers, azoles and macrolides raise levels).
  3. Infection prevention – hand hygiene, masks in crowds, safe food and water, oral care; no live vaccines; report fever early.
  4. Screen for TB and hepatitis B before biologics (important in India's high-TB setting).
  5. Monitor BP, blood sugar, kidney and liver function, blood counts and lipids.
  6. Teach transplant recipients the signs of rejection – fever, pain over the graft, reduced urine output, weight gain.
  7. Advise sun protection and regular skin checks; contraception with teratogenic drugs.
  8. For immunostimulants – give paracetamol for flu-like symptoms, rotate injection sites, monitor blood counts.

Conclusion Immunosuppressants protect transplanted organs and control autoimmune diseases but increase infection and cancer risk, while immunostimulants boost defence in neutropenia, infections and cancer. Strict adherence, drug-level monitoring and infection prevention are essential nursing roles.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Write the dose, uses and contraindications of activated charcoal.
answer_html:
Activated charcoal is a fine black powder with a huge surface area that adsorbs (binds) many drugs and poisons in the gut, preventing their absorption.

  • Dose: 1 g/kg (adults about 50 g) as a slurry in water, orally or by nasogastric tube, ideally within 1 hour of ingestion; multiple doses (every 4 hours) for carbamazepine, phenobarbitone, theophylline, dapsone.
  • Uses: most drug overdoses and many poisons.
  • Not effective for: alcohols (methanol, ethanol), iron, lithium, heavy metals, acids and alkalis.
  • Contraindications: unprotected airway (drowsy patient without intubation), corrosive ingestion, hydrocarbons (kerosene), bowel obstruction or perforation.
  • Side effects: vomiting, aspiration, constipation, black stools.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Write the uses of N-acetylcysteine.
answer_html:
N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is a precursor of glutathione and a mucolytic.

Uses

  1. Antidote in paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning – replenishes glutathione, which detoxifies the toxic metabolite NAPQI; given IV (about 20–21 hour regimen) or orally, best within 8–10 hours, but useful even later.
  2. Mucolytic – oral or nebulised; breaks disulfide bonds in thick mucus (COPD, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis).
  3. Used in paracetamol-related acute liver failure and in some other liver failures as advised.

Adverse effects: anaphylactoid reaction with IV infusion (rash, wheeze, hypotension – slow or stop the infusion), nausea and vomiting with oral use, bronchospasm with nebulisation in asthmatics.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Write the post-exposure prophylaxis schedule of anti-rabies vaccine.
answer_html:
Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) after an animal bite (as per India's National Rabies Control Programme guidelines):

  1. Wound washing – immediately with soap and running water for 15 minutes, then an antiseptic (povidone-iodine); do not suture immediately.
  2. Category of exposure: I (touching, licks on intact skin) – no PEP; II (minor scratches without bleeding) – vaccine; III (bites/scratches with bleeding, licks on broken skin or mucosa) – vaccine + rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) or rabies monoclonal antibody infiltrated into the wound.
  3. Vaccine schedules:
    • Intramuscular (Essen): days 0, 3, 7, 14 and 28 – one dose in the deltoid (never gluteal).
    • Intradermal: 0.1 mL at two sites on days 0, 3, 7 and 28.
  4. Previously vaccinated persons: two doses on days 0 and 3; RIG not needed.

Rabies is almost 100% fatal once symptoms appear, so PEP must be started without delay and completed.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Introduction to Drugs used in Alternative Systems of Medicine
question: Explain the alternative (AYUSH) systems of medicine – Ayurveda, Unani and Siddha – with their basic principles, drugs used for common ailments, safety issues and the role of the nurse.

diagram.caption: Panchamahabhuta and Tridosha in Ayurveda
labels: earth) combining to form Vata (space + air)
Pitta (fire + water) and Kapha (water + earth); health as balance of the three doshas

answer_html:
Introduction India has a rich heritage of traditional medicine. The Ministry of AYUSH (created in 2014) promotes Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy. AYUSH medicines are used by a large proportion of Indian families, often alongside modern (allopathic) drugs. AYUSH drugs are regulated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 (special chapter for Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani drugs), and AYUSH services are integrated into many government hospitals and Ayushman Arogya Mandirs through the National AYUSH Mission. Nurses must understand these systems to give safe, respectful, integrated care.

1. Ayurveda ("science of life") a) Origin: classical texts – Charaka Samhita (medicine), Sushruta Samhita (surgery) and Ashtanga Hridaya.

b) Basic principles

  • Panchamahabhuta – the body and all matter are made of five elements: space (akasha), air (vayu), fire (agni), water (jala) and earth (prithvi).
  • Tridosha – three functional energies: Vata (movement, nervous activity), Pitta (digestion, metabolism, heat) and Kapha (structure, lubrication, immunity). Health is the balance of the three doshas; disease is their imbalance.
  • Saptadhatu – seven body tissues (rasa, rakta, mamsa, meda, asthi, majja, shukra) and malas (wastes – urine, faeces, sweat).
  • Agni (digestive fire) and ama (undigested toxic material); prakriti – individual constitution.

c) Approach to treatment

  • Shodhana (purification – Panchakarma), Shamana (pacification with herbs), Rasayana (rejuvenation), Ahara (diet) and Vihara (lifestyle), along with Yoga.
  • Dosage forms: churna (powder), kwatha (decoction), asava/arishta (fermented liquids), ghrita (medicated ghee), taila (oil), vati (tablets), avaleha (semi-solid, e.g. Chyawanprash), bhasma (calcined metal/mineral preparations).

d) Common Ayurvedic drugs for common ailments | Ailment | Commonly used preparations | |---|---| | Constipation | Triphala churna, Isabgol | | Indigestion, flatulence, acidity | Hingvashtak churna, Avipattikar churna | | Cough and cold | Sitopaladi churna, Talisadi churna, Tulsi, Yashtimadhu (liquorice) | | Fever, low immunity | Guduchi (giloy), Tulsi | | Stress, fatigue | Ashwagandha | | Joint pain | Mahanarayan taila (massage), Shallaki, Guggulu preparations | | Skin problems | Neem, Haridra (turmeric), Aloe vera (kumari) | | Memory, anxiety | Brahmi | | General tonic | Chyawanprash, Amla |

2. Unani system a) Origin: Greco-Arabic medicine based on Hippocrates and Galen, developed by Arab and Persian physicians such as Ibn Sina (Avicenna); well established in India.

b) Basic principles

  • Four humours (akhlat): dam (blood), balgham (phlegm), safra (yellow bile) and sauda (black bile); health depends on their balance.
  • Temperament (mizaj): hot, cold, moist, dry – individual constitution.
  • Quwwat-e-mudabbira-e-badan – the body's own healing power, which treatment supports.

c) Modes of treatment

  • Ilaj-bil-tadbeer (regimental therapy) – cupping (hijama), massage, exercise, Turkish bath, leech therapy.
  • Ilaj-bil-ghiza (diet therapy), ilaj-bil-dawa (drug therapy), ilaj-bil-yad (surgery).
  • Common dosage forms: joshanda (herbal decoction for cold and cough), khamira (semi-solid), majoon, itrifal, sharbat (syrups), arq (distillates), habb (pills), safoof (powders).

3. Siddha system a) Origin: ancient Tamil system attributed to the Siddhars (Agathiyar and others), practised mainly in Tamil Nadu.

b) Basic principles

  • Five elements and three humours – vatham, pitham and kabam (similar to the Tridosha).
  • 96 thathuvas – basic principles making up the human being.
  • Envagai thervu – eight-fold examination: tongue, colour, voice, eyes, touch, stools, urine and pulse (naadi).

c) Treatment

  • Herbal, mineral and metal preparations (parpam, chenduram), Kaya Kalpa (rejuvenation), Varmam (pressure-point therapy), diet and yoga.
  • Well-known preparations: Nilavembu kudineer (fever, used widely during dengue and chikungunya outbreaks), Kabasura kudineer (fever, respiratory symptoms).

4. Safety issues with AYUSH drugs

  1. "Natural" does not always mean safe – herbs contain active chemicals.
  2. Heavy metals – some herbo-mineral preparations (bhasmas, rasa preparations) may contain lead, mercury or arsenic; cases of lead poisoning have been reported.
  3. Adulteration – some unlicensed products are mixed with steroids, NSAIDs or antidiabetic drugs.
  4. Herb–drug interactions – e.g. turmeric, garlic, ginkgo with warfarin (bleeding); liquorice with diuretics (low potassium, high BP); karela, methi and gurmar with antidiabetic drugs (hypoglycaemia).
  5. Organ toxicity – liver injury reported with some herbal products when overused.
  6. Delay in effective treatment of serious diseases (TB, cancer, diabetes) when patients rely only on alternative remedies.
  7. Lack of standardised doses and quality in some products – buy only licensed products with a manufacturing licence number and AYUSH quality marks.

5. Role of the nurse

  1. Ask every patient about AYUSH, herbal and home remedies during the drug history and record them.
  2. Respect patients' beliefs; do not ridicule traditional practices; discuss them with the treating doctor.
  3. Watch for interactions and adverse effects (bleeding, hypoglycaemia, liver injury) and report suspected reactions through the pharmacovigilance programme for AYUSH drugs.
  4. Advise patients not to stop prescribed drugs (insulin, antiepileptics, ART, anti-TB drugs) in favour of alternative remedies.
  5. Promote evidence-based, safe practices – yoga, healthy diet and lifestyle – which are common to all systems.
  6. Work in integrated AYUSH wings, wellness centres and Ayushman Arogya Mandirs as part of the team.

Nursing importance

  • Many patients in Vidarbha villages and towns use Ayurvedic, Unani or home remedies along with hospital drugs; the nurse's careful history prevents dangerous interactions and missed treatment.
  • An open, respectful attitude builds trust and allows honest disclosure.

Conclusion Ayurveda (Tridosha), Unani (four humours) and Siddha (three humours and eight-fold examination) are holistic systems that use herbs, minerals, diet and lifestyle to restore balance. Nurses should respect these systems, know their common remedies and safety issues, and integrate them safely with modern treatment.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Introduction to Drugs used in Alternative Systems of Medicine
question: Explain the principles of homoeopathy and list the commonly used homoeopathic medicines with their uses.
answer_html:
Introduction Homoeopathy was developed by the German physician Dr Samuel Hahnemann (1755–1843) at the end of the 18th century. It is widely used in India, which has one of the largest numbers of homoeopathic practitioners and colleges in the world, regulated under the National Commission for Homoeopathy.

1. Principles of homoeopathy Four cardinal principles

  1. Law of similars ("similia similibus curentur" – like cures like): a substance that produces certain symptoms in a healthy person can cure similar symptoms in a sick person (e.g. onion causes watery eyes and nose – Allium cepa is used for colds with such symptoms).
  2. Single remedy (simplex): only one medicine at a time, chosen to match all the patient's symptoms.
  3. Minimum dose: the smallest possible dose that can stimulate healing.
  4. Potentisation (dynamisation): medicines are prepared by serial dilution with vigorous shaking (succussion), written as potencies – 6C, 30C, 200C, or decimal (X) potencies; mother tinctures (Q) are undiluted extracts.

Other principles

  • Individualisation – treatment based on the totality of symptoms of the individual, not just the disease name.
  • Drug proving – effects of medicines are studied on healthy volunteers.
  • Vital force – disease is a disturbance of the body's vital force; the remedy stimulates self-healing.
  • Theory of chronic diseases (miasms) – psora, sycosis and syphilis.

2. Commonly used homoeopathic medicines | Medicine | Common uses | |---|---| | Arnica montana | Bruises, injuries, muscle soreness, after tooth extraction | | Belladonna | Sudden high fever with flushed hot face, throbbing headache, sore throat | | Nux vomica | Indigestion, acidity, constipation, effects of over-eating or alcohol | | Pulsatilla | Cold with thick yellow discharge, ear ache, menstrual complaints | | Rhus toxicodendron | Joint and back stiffness better with movement, sprains | | Bryonia alba | Dry painful cough, pains worse on movement | | Aconitum napellus | Sudden onset of cold or fever after exposure, fright | | Chamomilla | Teething troubles, colic in children | | Calendula (topical) | Cuts, wounds, burns | | Arsenicum album | Diarrhoea, food poisoning, anxiety, restlessness | | Gelsemium | Flu-like illness, anticipatory anxiety |

3. Dosage forms

  • Medicated sugar globules (pills), liquid dilutions in alcohol, tablets, mother tinctures and ointments.

4. Safety and nursing points

  1. Highly diluted remedies are generally non-toxic, but mother tinctures contain active plant material and alcohol.
  2. The main danger is delay or refusal of effective treatment for serious conditions (e.g. infections, diabetes, cancer).
  3. Sugar globules should be considered in diabetic patients; alcohol-based drops in children and alcohol-dependent persons.
  4. Instruct patients to take globules on a clean tongue, away from strong-smelling substances, as advised by the practitioner; keep away from children.
  5. Record homoeopathic medicines in the drug history and encourage patients to continue essential prescribed drugs.

Conclusion Homoeopathy is based on the law of similars, single remedy, minimum dose and potentisation, with emphasis on individualisation. It is popular in India for many common ailments; nurses should respect patient choice while ensuring that essential modern treatment is not missed.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Introduction to Drugs used in Alternative Systems of Medicine
question: Explain the safety concerns of herbal and Ayurvedic drugs, including important herb–drug interactions, and the nurse's role.
answer_html:
Introduction Herbal and Ayurvedic medicines are widely used for chronic diseases, immunity and general health, often without a prescription. Many people believe they are completely safe because they are "natural". However, herbs contain pharmacologically active substances and can cause adverse effects, toxicity and interactions with modern drugs.

1. Types of safety problems

  1. Intrinsic toxicity – e.g. liver injury from excessive use of some herbs (cases have been reported with overuse of giloy and certain weight-loss products), kidney damage from aristolochic acid-containing plants, bleeding with high-dose turmeric or garlic.
  2. Heavy-metal contamination – some herbo-mineral (rasa/bhasma) preparations contain lead, mercury or arsenic, causing abdominal pain, anaemia and neuropathy.
  3. Adulteration – unlicensed "herbal" products may contain hidden steroids (dexamethasone in joint-pain powders), NSAIDs, sildenafil or antidiabetic drugs.
  4. Contamination with pesticides, microbes or toxic plants; misidentification of plants.
  5. Allergic reactions and skin rashes.
  6. Unsafe use in pregnancy, breastfeeding and children.
  7. Delay in diagnosis and treatment of serious illness.

2. Important herb–drug interactions | Herb/product | Interacting drugs | Effect | |---|---|---| | Turmeric (high dose), garlic, ginger, ginkgo | Warfarin, aspirin, clopidogrel | Increased bleeding | | Liquorice (yashtimadhu) | Diuretics, digoxin, antihypertensives | Hypokalaemia, raised BP, digoxin toxicity | | Karela (bitter gourd), methi, gurmar, jamun | Insulin, sulfonylureas | Hypoglycaemia | | Ashwagandha | Sedatives, thyroid hormones | Excess sedation; altered thyroid levels | | St John's wort (enzyme inducer) | Oral contraceptives, cyclosporine, warfarin, antiretrovirals | Treatment failure | | Guggulu | Propranolol, diltiazem | Reduced drug effect | | Isabgol and other fibres | Many oral drugs | Reduced absorption – give 2 hours apart |

3. Nurse's role

  1. Take a complete drug history, specifically asking about herbal, Ayurvedic, Unani, Siddha and homoeopathic remedies, home remedies and supplements.
  2. Check for interactions – especially in patients on anticoagulants, antidiabetic drugs, antiepileptics, immunosuppressants, ART and anti-TB drugs; inform the doctor.
  3. Advise stopping herbal products 1–2 weeks before surgery if they increase bleeding, as per the surgeon's advice.
  4. Encourage patients to use only licensed products from reliable sources and to avoid products promising "miracle cures".
  5. Report suspected adverse reactions to the pharmacovigilance programme for AYUSH drugs.
  6. Respect cultural beliefs while giving clear, evidence-based information.

Conclusion Herbal and Ayurvedic medicines can be beneficial but are not free of risk. Toxicity, contamination, adulteration and herb–drug interactions must be anticipated, and the nurse's careful questioning, monitoring and education keep integrated care safe.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Introduction to Drugs used in Alternative Systems of Medicine
question: List four homoeopathic medicines with their uses.
answer_html:
Four commonly used homoeopathic medicines

  1. Arnica montana – bruises, sprains, muscle soreness and injuries (also after tooth extraction).
  2. Belladonna – sudden high fever with red flushed face, throbbing headache, sore throat.
  3. Nux vomica – indigestion, acidity, constipation, effects of over-eating or alcohol.
  4. Rhus toxicodendron – joint pain and stiffness that improve with movement, sprains.

Others: Pulsatilla (cold with thick discharge), Bryonia (dry painful cough), Aconite (sudden cold/fever), Calendula (wounds), Chamomilla (teething).

They are given as sugar globules, liquid dilutions or mother tinctures according to the potency prescribed by the homoeopath.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
unit_title: Introduction to Drugs used in Alternative Systems of Medicine
question: What is Panchakarma? Name its five procedures.
answer_html:
Panchakarma ("five actions") is the purification (shodhana) therapy of Ayurveda used to remove vitiated doshas and toxins (ama) from the body.

Five procedures

  1. Vamana – therapeutic emesis (mainly for Kapha disorders – e.g. asthma, skin diseases).
  2. Virechana – therapeutic purgation (mainly for Pitta disorders).
  3. Basti – medicated enema with oils or decoctions (mainly for Vata disorders – e.g. joint and nerve problems).
  4. Nasya – administration of medicated oils or powders through the nose (head and neck disorders).
  5. Raktamokshana – bloodletting, including leech therapy (skin diseases, abscesses).

It is preceded by oleation (snehana) and sudation (swedana) and followed by a graded diet; it should be done only under qualified supervision.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Describe the prescriptive role of a nurse and nurse practitioner.

diagram.caption: Models of nurse prescribing
labels: supplementary/collaborative prescribing under a clinical management plan
continuation/repeat prescribing; arrows showing increasing autonomy and training

answer_html:
Introduction Prescribing is the process of assessing a patient, deciding that a medicine is needed, choosing the right drug, dose and duration, issuing a prescription and monitoring its effect. Traditionally, prescribing in India has been done by doctors, while nurses administer and monitor drugs. Worldwide, nurses and nurse practitioners (NPs) have been given prescriptive authority to improve access to care. The INC introduced the Fundamentals of Prescribing module in the 2021 B.Sc. Nursing curriculum to prepare nurses for such expanded roles.

1. Definitions

  • Nurse prescriber: a registered nurse who has completed recognised training and is legally authorised to prescribe medicines within a defined scope.
  • Nurse practitioner (NP): an advanced practice registered nurse with postgraduate education and clinical training who can assess, diagnose, order investigations, prescribe and manage selected conditions independently or in collaboration.

2. Models of nurse prescribing

  1. Independent (autonomous) prescribing – the nurse is fully responsible for assessment, diagnosis and prescribing from a broad formulary (e.g. nurse independent prescribers in the UK, NPs in many US states).
  2. Supplementary (dependent/collaborative) prescribing – after a doctor has made the diagnosis, the nurse prescribes and adjusts drugs according to an agreed clinical management plan.
  3. Protocol-based prescribing / standing orders / group protocols – the nurse gives specific drugs in defined situations as per a written, approved protocol (most common in India).
  4. Limited formulary prescribing – community nurses prescribe from a restricted list (dressings, simple analgesics, antiseptics).
  5. Continuation or repeat prescribing – the nurse continues or refills medicines started by a doctor for stable chronic disease.

3. Global scenario (brief)

  • USA – NPs prescribe, including controlled drugs in most states; many states allow full practice authority.
  • UK – nurse independent and supplementary prescribers since the early 2000s.
  • Australia, Canada, New Zealand – endorsed NPs prescribe.
  • Africa and Asia – task-sharing: nurses initiate antiretroviral therapy, TB treatment and family-planning methods, recommended by WHO to expand access.

4. Indian scenario

  • Prescription-only medicines are legally to be sold on the prescription of a registered medical practitioner; nurses do not yet have general independent prescriptive authority.
  • Nurses already perform protocol-based prescribing in many programmes:
    • Community Health Officers (CHOs) – B.Sc. Nursing/GNM graduates with bridge training – at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (health and wellness centres) dispense medicines from the essential list and continue treatment for hypertension, diabetes, TB and other conditions as per standard treatment protocols and teleconsultation.
    • ANMs and staff nurses under standing orders – oxytocin/misoprostol for PPH prevention, loading dose of magnesium sulphate in eclampsia, antenatal corticosteroids, IFA and calcium, ORS–zinc, first-dose antibiotics in sick newborns, contraceptives (pills, DMPA injection).
    • Nurse Practitioners in Critical Care (NPCC) and Nurse Practitioners in Midwifery (NPM) – advanced practice programmes recognised by INC; midwifery-led care units under the MoHFW midwifery initiative.
  • The National Nursing and Midwifery Commission Act, 2023 provides the regulatory framework for nursing education and practice, including advanced practice roles; full prescriptive authority would need specific rules and training standards.

5. Responsibilities in the prescriptive role

  1. Assessment – detailed history (including allergies, current medicines, AYUSH use), examination, interpretation of investigations.
  2. Diagnosis – within the nurse's scope; recognising when to refer.
  3. Shared decision-making – discussing options, benefits, risks and costs with the patient.
  4. Selection of the drug – evidence-based, essential and generic medicines; correct dose, route, frequency and duration.
  5. Writing a clear, legal prescription or following the protocol exactly.
  6. Patient education – how and when to take, side effects, warning signs, follow-up.
  7. Monitoring and review – response, adverse effects, adherence; stopping drugs that are not needed.
  8. Documentation and reporting – records, ADR reporting to the Pharmacovigilance Programme of India, error reporting.
  9. Collaboration – with doctors, pharmacists and the team.
  10. Continuing professional development and working within legal and ethical limits.

6. Benefits of nurse prescribing

  • Better access to medicines in rural and underserved areas where doctors are few.
  • Timely treatment and reduced waiting time; continuity of care in chronic illness.
  • Cost-effective use of the health workforce (task-sharing).
  • Improved adherence and patient satisfaction due to the nurse's close relationship with patients.
  • Professional growth and recognition of nursing.

7. Challenges

  • Lack of a clear legal framework and prescribing formulary for nurses in India.
  • Need for standardised education, competency assessment and credentialing.
  • Resistance from other professions; unclear liability and indemnity.
  • Workload, limited diagnostic facilities, pressure from patients for injections and antibiotics, and influence of pharmaceutical promotion.

Nursing importance

  • Nurses already make many prescribing-type decisions under protocols; understanding prescribing principles makes these decisions safer.
  • Expanded nurse prescribing can help India achieve Universal Health Coverage by bringing essential medicines closer to people.

Conclusion The prescriptive role of nurses and nurse practitioners ranges from protocol-based and supplementary prescribing to independent prescribing. In India, CHOs, midwives and nurses already prescribe within protocols; with proper legal backing, training and accountability, nurse prescribing can greatly improve access to safe medicines.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Explain the principles of prescribing and the ethical issues related to prescribing.
answer_html:
Introduction Good prescribing means giving the right drug to the right patient, in the right dose, by the right route, at the right time and for the right duration, at the lowest cost, with the patient understanding and agreeing to it. Poor prescribing – unnecessary antibiotics, injections and irrational combinations – causes harm, waste and antimicrobial resistance. Principles and ethics guide the prescriber to act safely and fairly.

A. Principles of prescribing

  1. Be clear about the reason for prescribing – establish a diagnosis (at least provisional); do not prescribe "just in case" or to satisfy demand.
  2. Take a full medication history – current drugs (including OTC, AYUSH and supplements), previous responses, allergies and adherence.
  3. Consider patient factors that alter benefit and risk – age, weight, pregnancy, breastfeeding, kidney and liver function, other diseases, genetic factors.
  4. Consider the patient's ideas, concerns and expectations – involve the patient in shared decision-making; respect cultural beliefs.
  5. Choose effective, safe, suitable and affordable medicines – prefer drugs from the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM), use the "P-drug" approach, and prefer non-drug measures where suitable.
  6. Follow national guidelines and local formularies – ICMR and national programme protocols (NTEP, NACO, IHCI, NVBDCP), antibiotic policies.
  7. Prescribe by generic name, legibly (preferably in capital letters), with complete details; support Jan Aushadhi generic medicines to reduce cost.
  8. Avoid irrational fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) – India has banned hundreds of irrational FDCs; use combinations only when proven useful (e.g. anti-TB, antiretroviral, antihypertensive fixed combinations).
  9. Use the simplest regimen – fewest drugs, oral route when possible, once or twice daily dosing to improve adherence; avoid unnecessary injections.
  10. Write an unambiguous, legal prescription – correct format, units, duration and quantity.
  11. Inform and educate the patient – purpose, dose, timing, side effects, what to do if a dose is missed, warning signs and follow-up.
  12. Monitor benefit and harm – review response, adverse effects and interactions; stop drugs that are no longer needed.
  13. Communicate and document decisions and reasons; inform other members of the team.
  14. Prescribe within your competence and legal authority – refer when in doubt.

B. Ethical issues related to prescribing

  1. Autonomy and informed consent
    • Patients have the right to know about their treatment, alternatives, risks and costs, and to accept or refuse it.
    • Special care with children, the elderly, mentally ill and unconscious patients (surrogate decision-makers).
  2. Beneficence and non-maleficence
    • Prescribe only when benefits outweigh risks; avoid polypharmacy and unnecessary drugs.
    • Use high-risk drugs (opioids, anticoagulants, chemotherapy) with careful monitoring.
  3. Justice
    • Equitable access – consider affordability; prefer generics and free government supplies; do not discriminate by caste, gender, religion or ability to pay.
  4. Veracity (truthfulness) – honest information about side effects and uncertainty; no false promises.
  5. Confidentiality – protect information about HIV, mental illness, contraception, MTP and substance use.
  6. Conflict of interest
    • Gifts, sponsored travel or incentives from pharmaceutical companies can bias prescribing; the Uniform Code for Pharmaceutical Marketing Practices (UCPMP), 2024 restricts such practices.
    • Prescribing must be based on evidence and patient need, not personal gain.
  7. Patient pressure and "defensive" prescribing – demands for antibiotics, injections or tonics; prescribing to avoid complaints rather than for benefit.
  8. Off-label and unlicensed use – may be justified when evidence supports it, but needs explanation, consent and documentation.
  9. Prescribing for oneself, family or friends – generally avoided because objectivity is lost.
  10. Placebos – deception conflicts with honesty; use only within ethical guidelines.
  11. End-of-life prescribing – adequate pain relief with opioids is ethical even if it may shorten life slightly (principle of double effect); respect for advance directives.
  12. Professional boundaries – prescribing beyond one's authority or competence is both unethical and illegal.
  13. Antimicrobial resistance – a responsibility to society to avoid unnecessary antibiotics.
  14. Accountability – owning and reporting errors, ADR reporting, honest documentation.

C. Role of the nurse

  • Apply these principles while working under standing orders and when continuing treatment (CHOs).
  • Question unclear or unsafe orders; act as the patient's advocate.
  • Educate patients and families about rational drug use and self-medication risks.

Nursing importance

  • Rational, ethical prescribing improves outcomes, reduces costs and prevents drug resistance – all major public health priorities in India.
  • Nurses with prescribing responsibilities must be as accountable as any prescriber.

Conclusion The principles of prescribing – clear indication, full history, patient-centred choice, essential and generic medicines, simple regimens, clear prescriptions, education and monitoring – ensure rational drug use. Ethical prescribing respects autonomy, does good, avoids harm, is fair and honest, and is free from conflicts of interest.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Explain the steps of prescribing (WHO Guide to Good Prescribing) with a suitable example.

diagram.caption: WHO six steps of rational prescribing
labels: 3 verify the suitability of your P-drug
6 monitor (and stop) the treatment; feedback arrow from monitoring to step 1

answer_html:
Introduction The WHO Guide to Good Prescribing (1994) describes a logical, step-by-step method that helps prescribers choose and use medicines rationally. It is based on the idea of a "P-drug" (personal drug) – the drug the prescriber has already chosen, after careful comparison, as the first choice for a common condition. The same steps apply to nurses who prescribe under protocols or continue treatment.

Preliminary stage – choosing P-drugs (building a personal formulary)

  1. Define the diagnosis (e.g. essential hypertension).
  2. Specify the therapeutic objective (lower BP to target, prevent stroke).
  3. Make an inventory of effective drug groups (diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, calcium channel blockers, β-blockers).
  4. Choose an effective group using criteria – efficacy, safety, suitability and cost.
  5. Choose a P-drug from that group (e.g. amlodipine) with its usual dosage form, dose schedule and duration.

The six steps of rational treatment of an individual patient Step 1: Define the patient's problem

  • Take history, examine, investigate; identify the diagnosis and any other problems (e.g. pregnancy, kidney disease, poor adherence, cost concerns).
  • Remember that the patient's complaint may have several causes, or may not need drugs at all.

Step 2: Specify the therapeutic objective

  • State clearly what you want to achieve – cure, symptom relief, prevention or control, with a measurable target (e.g. BP below 140/90 mmHg; afebrile in 48 hours).
  • This prevents unnecessary drugs and helps monitoring.

Step 3: Verify the suitability of your P-drug for this patient

  • Is it effective for this patient's condition?
  • Is it safe – allergies, contraindications (pregnancy, asthma, kidney/liver disease), interactions with current medicines?
  • Is the dosage form, dose schedule and duration suitable – can the patient swallow tablets, take it twice daily, afford it, store it?
  • If unsuitable, choose an alternative; consider non-drug treatment (diet, exercise, ORS, rest).

Step 4: Write a prescription

  • Include prescriber details, date, patient name, age, weight (children), diagnosis, drug in generic name, strength, dosage form, dose, route, frequency, duration, total quantity, instructions and signature.
  • Write legibly, avoid dangerous abbreviations, and use the local language for instructions where possible.

Step 5: Give information, instructions and warnings

  • Effects – what the drug will do and when (e.g. "BP will come down slowly over 2–4 weeks").
  • Side effects – common ones and what to do (e.g. ankle swelling with amlodipine).
  • Instructions – how, when and how long to take; what to do if a dose is missed; storage.
  • Warnings – serious adverse effects that require stopping the drug and seeking help.
  • Next appointment and when to return earlier; check understanding by asking the patient to repeat ("teach-back").

Step 6: Monitor (and stop) the treatment

  • Passive monitoring – patient returns if there is a problem.
  • Active monitoring – scheduled follow-up to check response, side effects and adherence.
  • If the treatment is effective and the disease cured – stop the drug; if effective but chronic – continue and review periodically; if ineffective or harmful – re-check all steps (diagnosis, objective, drug choice, adherence, dose).

Example: Mr. R, 52 years, newly diagnosed uncomplicated hypertension (BP 160/96 mmHg) at an Ayushman Arogya Mandir | Step | Application | |---|---| | 1. Problem | Stage 2 essential hypertension; non-smoker; no diabetes or kidney disease; farmer who cannot visit often | | 2. Objective | BP below 140/90 mmHg within 1–3 months; prevent stroke and heart attack | | 3. P-drug suitability | Amlodipine 5 mg (calcium channel blocker) – effective, once daily, cheap, free in government supply; no contraindication; first step of the state hypertension protocol under the India Hypertension Control Initiative | | 4. Prescription | AMLODIPINE 5 mg tablet – one tablet orally once daily in the morning × 30 days (30 tablets) | | 5. Information | Take daily even when feeling well; may cause ankle swelling or headache; reduce salt (below 5 g/day), walk 30 minutes daily, avoid tobacco and alcohol; return if chest pain, breathlessness or severe headache | | 6. Monitoring | BP check after 2–4 weeks; if not controlled, step up as per protocol (increase dose or add telmisartan); monthly refill and BP record in the NCD card; yearly kidney function and sugar |

Nursing importance

  • Following these steps makes nurse-led protocol prescribing and chronic-disease follow-up systematic and safe.
  • Steps 5 and 6 – information and monitoring – are where nurses contribute most to treatment success.

Conclusion The WHO six-step method – define the problem, set the objective, check the P-drug, write the prescription, inform the patient and monitor – turns prescribing into a rational, patient-centred process. Using it consistently reduces errors, improves adherence and achieves better outcomes.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Explain the competencies required for safe prescribing.

diagram.caption: Competency framework for prescribers
labels: Domain 1 – the consultation: assess the patient
present options and reach a shared decision
monitor and review; Domain 2 – prescribing governance: prescribe safely
prescribe as part of a team

answer_html:
Introduction Prescribing competency is the combination of knowledge, skills, attitudes and behaviours that a prescriber needs to prescribe safely and effectively. Internationally used frameworks (such as the Competency Framework for All Prescribers) describe ten competencies in two domains – the consultation and prescribing governance. These apply to all prescribers – doctors, nurses, pharmacists and others – and form the basis of the prescribing module in nursing education.

DOMAIN 1: THE CONSULTATION 1. Assess the patient

  • Take a relevant history – presenting problem, past illness, current and previous medicines (including OTC, AYUSH, supplements), allergies and previous adverse reactions, social history (alcohol, tobacco, occupation), pregnancy/breastfeeding.
  • Perform appropriate physical examination; request and interpret investigations.
  • Make or understand the working diagnosis; recognise red flags and refer when needed.

2. Identify evidence-based treatment options

  • Know the pharmacology – mechanism, pharmacokinetics, adverse effects, interactions, contraindications.
  • Consider non-drug options, no treatment, or referral.
  • Use national guidelines, essential medicines lists and local formularies.
  • Assess risks and benefits for this particular patient.

3. Present options and reach a shared decision

  • Explain options in simple language, including benefits, risks and costs.
  • Respect the patient's values, beliefs and preferences; check understanding.
  • Agree a plan; obtain consent; respect the right to refuse.

4. Prescribe

  • Select the correct drug, dose, form, route, frequency and duration; calculate doses accurately (weight-based, BSA-based, renal adjustment).
  • Check for interactions and duplication.
  • Write legible, complete, legal prescriptions (paper or electronic).
  • Know when not to prescribe.

5. Provide information

  • Give clear oral and written information – how to take, side effects, warnings, what to do if doses are missed.
  • Make sure the patient knows when and how to seek help and when follow-up is due.

6. Monitor and review

  • Check effectiveness, adverse effects and adherence; arrange laboratory monitoring (e.g. INR, potassium, drug levels).
  • Adjust, continue or stop treatment (deprescribe) as appropriate; report ADRs.

DOMAIN 2: PRESCRIBING GOVERNANCE 7. Prescribe safely

  • Prescribe within one's competence and legal scope; know one's limits.
  • Use systems that reduce errors – double checks for high-alert medicines, avoiding dangerous abbreviations, allergy checks.
  • Report errors and near misses and learn from them.

8. Prescribe professionally

  • Follow laws and regulations (Drugs and Cosmetics Act, NDPS Act, telemedicine guidelines, nursing council regulations).
  • Maintain ethics – honesty, confidentiality, avoiding conflict of interest; take responsibility and accountability for decisions.

9. Improve prescribing practice

  • Reflect on one's own prescribing; take part in audits and feedback.
  • Keep knowledge updated through continuing education.
  • Support antimicrobial stewardship and cost-effective prescribing.

10. Prescribe as part of a team

  • Communicate with doctors, pharmacists and other nurses; share decisions and records.
  • Ensure continuity of care at transfer and discharge (medication reconciliation).
  • Accept and give challenges about unsafe prescriptions in a professional way.

Core knowledge and skills underlying these competencies

  • Applied pharmacology and therapeutics; clinical assessment skills; numeracy (dose calculations and conversions); communication and counselling; knowledge of law and ethics; documentation and digital health (e-prescriptions, ABHA-linked health records); use of drug information sources (national formulary, drug references).

Attitudes

  • Patient-centredness, honesty, humility to seek help, commitment to safety, respect for evidence and teamwork.

Developing competencies in nursing students

  • Classroom pharmacology, case-based learning, simulation of consultations, supervised practice with standing orders, prescription-writing exercises, OSCE assessment and logbooks.

Competencies in action – an example A Community Health Officer reviewing Mrs. S, a 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes on metformin, shows each competency: she assesses symptoms, foot condition, blood sugar and kidney function; identifies options using the state NCD protocol; explains the choice of increasing metformin versus adding a sulfonylurea and agrees a plan with the patient; prescribes/continues the drug exactly as per protocol after teleconsultation; informs her about hypoglycaemia, diet and foot care; monitors sugar at the next visit; works safely and legally within the protocol; records the visit in the NCD register and portal; refers to the medical officer if sugar remains high; and discusses the case at the monthly review meeting to improve practice.

Assessment of prescribing competence

  • Supervised clinical practice with a log of cases, prescription-writing audits, objective structured clinical examinations (OSCEs), case-based discussions and feedback from supervisors and patients.

Nursing importance

  • Competency-based prescribing ensures that expanding nurses' roles also improves patient safety.
  • Even when nurses do not prescribe, these competencies help them check prescriptions, detect errors and educate patients.

Conclusion Safe prescribing requires competencies in assessment, choice of evidence-based treatment, shared decision-making, accurate prescribing, patient information and monitoring, supported by safe, professional, reflective and team-based practice. Nurses who develop these competencies become reliable partners in rational drug therapy.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Explain the legal aspects of prescribing and medication management for nurses in India.
answer_html:
Introduction Prescribing, dispensing and administering medicines are controlled by law to protect the public. Nurses must know these laws because they administer most drugs in hospitals, work under standing orders and increasingly continue treatment in the community. Acting outside legal limits can lead to disciplinary action and civil or criminal liability.

1. Important laws and regulations

  • Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules, 1945 – regulate manufacture, sale and distribution of drugs, including schedules:
    • Schedule H – prescription-only drugs ("Rx" symbol).
    • Schedule H1 – certain newer antibiotics, anti-TB drugs and habit-forming drugs; sold only on prescription, with a register kept by the chemist.
    • Schedule X – certain narcotic and psychotropic drugs; prescription in duplicate, strict storage and records.
    • Schedule G – drugs to be used under medical supervision.
  • Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985 (amended 2014) – controls opioids; the amendment eased access to Essential Narcotic Drugs such as morphine for pain relief and palliative care through recognised institutions.
  • Pharmacy Act, 1948 – dispensing by registered pharmacists.
  • Telemedicine Practice Guidelines, 2020 – define which drugs can be prescribed after teleconsultation (used at health and wellness centres).
  • Nursing council regulations and the National Nursing and Midwifery Commission Act, 2023 – define nursing education and scope of practice.
  • Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (death by negligence) – liability for negligent care.
  • Programme-specific guidelines (NTEP, NACO, RMNCH+A) authorise trained nurses to give certain drugs under protocols.

2. Legal responsibilities of nurses

  1. Administer drugs only on a valid written order or an approved standing order/protocol; verbal or telephone orders only in emergencies, read back, document and get them signed within 24 hours.
  2. Do not prescribe beyond authority – changing drugs or doses without authorisation is illegal.
  3. Follow standing orders exactly – they must be written, signed, dated, specific (condition, drug, dose, route, contraindications) and reviewed regularly.
  4. Controlled drugs – store under double lock, keep the narcotic register, two signatures for each dose, record wastage, return empty ampoules, report discrepancies.
  5. Documentation – accurate, contemporaneous recording of drug, dose, route, time and signature; never pre-chart or alter records.
  6. Informed consent and confidentiality.
  7. Report adverse drug reactions to the Pharmacovigilance Programme of India (PvPI) and medication errors through hospital systems.
  8. Refuse to give a drug if the order is clearly unsafe, and inform the prescriber and supervisor.

3. Consequences of breaching the law

  • Disciplinary action by the nursing council (suspension of registration), civil compensation claims, and criminal prosecution for gross negligence.

Conclusion Drug laws such as the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, NDPS Act and Pharmacy Act, together with nursing regulations, define what nurses can and cannot do with medicines. Working within these limits, following valid orders and protocols, and documenting carefully protect both patients and nurses.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Explain the components of a prescription and the rules of good prescription writing.
answer_html:
Definition A prescription is a written order by an authorised prescriber to a pharmacist to dispense a medicine, with directions to the patient on how to use it. It is a legal document.

1. Components of a prescription

  1. Prescriber's details – name, qualification, registration number, address, contact (letterhead).
  2. Date of prescription.
  3. Patient's details – name, age, sex, address, OPD/IPD number; weight for children; allergies.
  4. Diagnosis (or provisional diagnosis).
  5. Superscription – the symbol "Rx" (Latin recipe, "take thou").
  6. Inscription – the drug name (generic), dosage form and strength (e.g. TAB. PARACETAMOL 500 mg).
  7. Subscription – instructions to the pharmacist: quantity to dispense (e.g. 15 tablets).
  8. Signatura (transcription) – directions to the patient: dose, route, frequency, timing in relation to food and duration (e.g. one tablet orally three times daily after food for 5 days), preferably in the patient's language.
  9. Additional advice – diet, rest, warnings, follow-up date.
  10. Signature and stamp of the prescriber.

2. Rules of good prescription writing

  1. Write legibly, preferably in CAPITAL LETTERS, or use electronic prescriptions.
  2. Use generic names; avoid brand-only prescribing; one drug per line.
  3. Write the strength and units clearly – "mg", "micrograms" (avoid "µg"), "units" (never "U" or "IU" abbreviations that may be misread).
  4. No trailing zero (write 1 mg, not 1.0 mg) and always a leading zero (0.5 mg, not .5 mg).
  5. Avoid dangerous or ambiguous abbreviations (e.g. "OD" can be read as "right eye"; "QD", "SC" may be misread); write "once daily" in full for high-alert drugs.
  6. State the duration and total quantity; for controlled drugs write quantities in words and figures.
  7. Mention route (oral, IV, IM) and special instructions (before food, at bedtime, shake well).
  8. Check for allergies, interactions and duplication before signing.
  9. Cancel unused space and sign every prescription; keep a copy where required.
  10. For children, write the dose per kg and total dose; double-check calculations.

3. Common abbreviations used

  • OD – once daily; BD – twice daily; TDS – three times daily; QID – four times daily; HS – at bedtime; AC – before meals; PC – after meals; SOS – if needed (once); PRN – as needed; STAT – immediately.

Conclusion A complete prescription contains the prescriber's and patient's details, diagnosis, Rx, inscription, subscription, signatura and signature. Clear, legible, generic and unambiguous prescriptions prevent medication errors and help the patient take medicines correctly.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Explain the principles of prescribing in special groups – pregnancy, breastfeeding, children, the elderly and patients with kidney or liver disease.
answer_html:
Introduction Some patients handle drugs differently or are more vulnerable to harm. Prescribing for them needs special care in choice of drug and dose.

1. Pregnancy

  • Avoid drugs unless clearly needed, especially in the first trimester (organogenesis).
  • Known teratogens to avoid: valproate, isotretinoin, warfarin, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, methotrexate, tetracyclines, misoprostol (unless for abortion), statins, lithium, thalidomide.
  • Generally preferred: paracetamol, penicillins and cephalosporins, methyldopa, labetalol, nifedipine, insulin, levothyroxine, folic acid and iron.
  • Remember physiological changes (more blood volume, faster kidney clearance) may need dose changes.

2. Breastfeeding

  • Most drugs are safe; choose drugs with short half-life, low milk transfer and a long safety record; give just after a feed.
  • Avoid: anticancer drugs, radioactive agents, amiodarone, ergot alkaloids, high-dose aspirin; use lithium and benzodiazepines with caution; COCs may reduce milk.
  • Encourage continued breastfeeding where possible.

3. Children

  • Dose by weight (mg/kg) or body surface area; never exceed adult dose; double-check calculations (decimal errors are common).
  • Use suitable formulations – syrups, drops, dispersible tablets.
  • Newborns have immature liver and kidneys – chloramphenicol (grey baby syndrome), sulfonamides (kernicterus).
  • Avoid aspirin (Reye's syndrome), tetracyclines below 8 years (teeth staining), codeine below 12 years, nimesulide below 12 years, sedating antihistamines in infants.

4. The elderly

  • Reduced kidney and liver function, more body fat, less body water, more sensitive brain → drugs accumulate and cause falls, confusion and kidney injury.
  • "Start low, go slow"; review all medicines regularly; avoid polypharmacy.
  • Avoid potentially inappropriate drugs (Beers criteria) – long-acting benzodiazepines, strong anticholinergics (e.g. diphenhydramine, amitriptyline), long-term NSAIDs, sliding-scale insulin.
  • Use simple regimens, large-print labels and pill organisers; involve caregivers.

5. Kidney disease

  • Estimate creatinine clearance (Cockcroft–Gault: [(140 – age) × weight in kg] ÷ [72 × serum creatinine mg/dL], × 0.85 for women) or eGFR.
  • Reduce dose or interval of renally cleared drugs – aminoglycosides, vancomycin, digoxin, LMWH, gabapentin, many antibiotics; avoid metformin in severe kidney failure, NSAIDs and other nephrotoxins.

6. Liver disease

  • Avoid hepatotoxic drugs where possible; reduce doses of drugs metabolised by the liver (opioids, benzodiazepines – prefer lorazepam/oxazepam).
  • Avoid sedatives (may precipitate hepatic encephalopathy), NSAIDs (bleeding, kidney injury) and constipating drugs; monitor INR with anticoagulants.

Nursing implications

  • Ask about pregnancy and breastfeeding in every woman of reproductive age; check weight and kidney/liver function results before giving drugs; question doses that seem unusual; monitor closely for adverse effects.

Conclusion Pregnant and breastfeeding women, children, the elderly and patients with kidney or liver disease need individualised prescribing – safe drug choice, adjusted doses, simple regimens and close monitoring – to prevent avoidable harm.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: What is polypharmacy? Explain deprescribing in older adults and the nurse's role.
answer_html:
Definition Polypharmacy is the regular use of five or more medicines by a patient. It may be appropriate (several chronic diseases each needing treatment) or problematic – when medicines are unnecessary, harmful or more than needed. Deprescribing is the planned and supervised process of reducing the dose or stopping medicines that may be causing harm or are no longer providing benefit.

1. Problems caused by polypharmacy

  • Adverse drug reactions and interactions – falls, confusion, kidney injury, bleeding, hypoglycaemia.
  • Prescribing cascade – a side effect is mistaken for a new disease and treated with another drug (e.g. amlodipine causes ankle swelling → furosemide is added → low potassium and falls).
  • Poor adherence, medication errors, high cost and hospital admissions.

2. Common medicines considered for deprescribing

  • Long-term benzodiazepines and Z-drugs (falls, confusion).
  • Proton pump inhibitors taken for years without a clear indication.
  • Antipsychotics for behaviour problems in dementia.
  • Sulfonylureas and tight glucose targets in frail elderly (hypoglycaemia).
  • Anticholinergic drugs (antihistamines, bladder antispasmodics, amitriptyline).
  • NSAIDs; aspirin for primary prevention in very old people; statins in the last months of life; unnecessary vitamins and tonics.

3. Steps of deprescribing

  1. Ascertain all medicines the patient is taking and the reason for each ("brown-bag" review – patient brings all medicines, including AYUSH and OTC).
  2. Consider the overall risk of drug-induced harm (number of drugs, age, frailty, previous ADRs).
  3. Assess each drug for current indication, benefit and harm (using tools such as Beers criteria and STOPP/START).
  4. Prioritise drugs to stop – most harmful and least beneficial first; involve the patient and family.
  5. Implement and monitor – stop one drug at a time, taper drugs that cause withdrawal (benzodiazepines, β-blockers, antidepressants, steroids), and watch for return of symptoms.

4. Nurse's role

  • Conduct medication reconciliation at admission, transfer and discharge.
  • Observe and report side effects – falls, drowsiness, confusion, low BP, low sugar.
  • Help simplify regimens – pill organisers, dosing charts, once-daily drugs; educate patients and caregivers.
  • Support patients during tapering and reassure them; record changes and communicate with the team.

Conclusion Polypharmacy is common in older adults and increases the risk of harm. Regular medication review and careful, patient-centred deprescribing – with nurses monitoring and educating – improve safety and quality of life.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Explain prescribing (medication) errors – types, causes and measures to prevent them.
answer_html:
Definition A medication error is any preventable event that may cause or lead to inappropriate medication use or patient harm while the medication is in the control of the health professional, patient or consumer. Prescribing errors occur at the stage of deciding on and writing the prescription, and are among the most common and harmful medication errors.

1. Types of prescribing errors

  • Wrong drug – look-alike or sound-alike names, wrong drug for the condition, prescribing a drug to which the patient is allergic.
  • Wrong dose – decimal-point and zero errors (tenfold overdose), mg/microgram confusion, wrong weight-based calculation in children.
  • Wrong frequency, route or duration; omission of a needed drug; duplication (two brands of the same drug).
  • Contraindicated drug or dangerous interaction (e.g. NSAID with warfarin).
  • Incomplete or illegible prescriptions, ambiguous abbreviations.
  • Wrong patient; transcription errors when copying orders; misheard verbal orders.

2. Causes

  • Workload, fatigue, interruptions, inexperience and knowledge gaps.
  • Poor handwriting, abbreviations, lack of standard order forms.
  • Incomplete patient information (weight, allergies, kidney function); poor communication at handover and discharge.
  • Similar drug names and packaging; multiple strengths of the same drug.

3. Prevention measures

  1. Legible, complete prescriptions in capitals with generic names; standard prescription and drug charts.
  2. Computerised prescriber order entry (CPOE) with decision support for allergy, dose and interaction checks.
  3. Avoid dangerous abbreviations; use leading zeros and no trailing zeros; write "units" in full.
  4. Double-check high-alert medicines – insulin, heparin, potassium chloride, opioids, chemotherapy, magnesium sulphate.
  5. Tall-man lettering and separate storage for look-alike drugs.
  6. Medication reconciliation at admission, transfer and discharge.
  7. Read-back of verbal/telephone orders; limit verbal orders to emergencies.
  8. Pharmacist review of prescriptions; nurse checks before administration (the "rights" of medication).
  9. Involve patients – encourage them to ask questions and know their medicines.
  10. Non-punitive reporting of errors and near misses, with learning from analysis; follow WHO's "Medication Without Harm" global patient safety challenge and NABH standards.

4. Nurse's role

  • Act as the last line of defence – check every order for appropriateness before giving; question doubtful orders; report errors honestly; educate patients.

Conclusion Prescribing errors arise from human and system factors and can cause serious harm. Clear prescriptions, electronic systems, double checks, reconciliation, teamwork and a just reporting culture prevent most of them.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Explain antimicrobial stewardship and the role of the prescriber and nurse in preventing antimicrobial resistance.
answer_html:
Definition Antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) is a coordinated set of actions that promotes the responsible use of antimicrobials – the right drug, dose, route and duration only when needed – to improve patient outcomes, reduce adverse effects and slow antimicrobial resistance (AMR). India has one of the highest burdens of AMR, driven by over-the-counter antibiotic sales, self-medication and incomplete courses.

1. National and global efforts

  • National Action Plan on AMR (2017) with a One Health approach (humans, animals, environment).
  • ICMR Treatment Guidelines for Antimicrobial Use in Common Syndromes and hospital antibiotic policies.
  • "Red Line" campaign – prescription-only antibiotic packs carry a red vertical line; do not buy them without a prescription.
  • Kerala's Operation AMRITH – action against sale of antibiotics without prescription.
  • WHO AWaRe classification – Access (first-line, e.g. amoxicillin), Watch (higher resistance potential, e.g. ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin), Reserve (last-resort, e.g. colistin) – with a target that most antibiotic use should be from the Access group.

2. Principles of good antimicrobial prescribing

  1. Prescribe only for bacterial infections – not for colds, most sore throats or acute viral diarrhoea.
  2. Send cultures before starting antibiotics whenever possible.
  3. Choose narrow-spectrum, Access drugs according to guidelines and the local antibiogram.
  4. Correct dose, route and shortest effective duration; document the indication and planned duration.
  5. Review at 48–72 hours ("start smart, then focus") – de-escalate to a narrower drug, switch IV to oral, or stop if infection is unlikely.
  6. Surgical prophylaxis – single dose within 60 minutes before incision, not continued beyond 24 hours in most surgeries.
  7. Prevent infections – hand hygiene, vaccination, infection-control bundles – so fewer antibiotics are needed.

3. Role of the nurse

  • Give the first dose on time (within 1 hour in sepsis) and subsequent doses at correct intervals.
  • Collect samples correctly before the first dose; follow up culture reports and inform the prescriber.
  • Prompt the team about day-3 review, IV-to-oral switch and stop dates.
  • Take an accurate allergy history; avoid unnecessary "allergy labels".
  • Educate patients: complete the course as prescribed, do not save or share leftover antibiotics, do not buy antibiotics without prescription.
  • Practise strict infection prevention and control; take part in AMS committees and audits.

Conclusion Antimicrobial stewardship protects the effectiveness of antibiotics for future generations. Rational prescribing, timely review and de-escalation, infection prevention and patient education – with nurses as active partners – are the keys to controlling AMR.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: What is a P-drug (personal drug)?
answer_html:
A P-drug (personal drug) is the drug that a prescriber has chosen in advance to prescribe regularly as the first choice for a common condition, after comparing alternatives for efficacy, safety, suitability and cost. The concept comes from the WHO Guide to Good Prescribing.

  • A list of P-drugs forms the prescriber's personal formulary.
  • Examples: paracetamol for fever, ORS + zinc for childhood diarrhoea, amlodipine for uncomplicated hypertension, metformin for type 2 diabetes.
  • For each patient, the prescriber checks whether the P-drug is suitable (allergy, pregnancy, kidney disease); if not, an alternative is chosen.
  • Advantages: rational, consistent and quick prescribing; fewer errors; better knowledge of a limited number of drugs.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: What are standing orders? Give examples.
answer_html:
Standing orders are written, signed and approved instructions or protocols that authorise nurses (and other trained health workers) to give specified drugs or treatments in defined clinical situations without an individual prescription for each patient.

Requirements: clear condition, drug, dose, route, frequency, contraindications, monitoring, documentation, the authorising doctor's/institution's signature and a review date.

Examples

  1. Loading dose of magnesium sulphate in eclampsia by nurses/ANMs before referral.
  2. Oxytocin 10 IU IM (or misoprostol at home births) for prevention of PPH.
  3. Adrenaline IM for anaphylaxis; dextrose IV for hypoglycaemia.
  4. ORS and zinc for diarrhoea; IFA and calcium in pregnancy.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: Write the meaning of the following abbreviations used in prescriptions: OD, BD, TDS, QID, HS, AC, PC, SOS, STAT.
answer_html:
Abbreviation Meaning
OD Once daily
BD (BID) Twice daily
TDS (TID) Three times daily
QID Four times daily
HS At bedtime
AC Before meals
PC After meals
SOS If necessary (one dose)
STAT Immediately

These abbreviations come from Latin terms – for example bis in die (BD, twice a day), ter die sumendum (TDS, three times a day), hora somni (HS, at the hour of sleep), ante cibum and post cibum (AC/PC, before and after food) and si opus sit (SOS, if needed).

Caution: abbreviations can be misread (e.g. "OD" also means "right eye"); for high-alert medicines write instructions in full, and never abbreviate "units" as "U". Also used: PRN – as needed; PO – by mouth.

subject: Pharmacology II (including Fundamentals of Prescribing module)
question: What are Schedule H, Schedule H1 and Schedule X drugs?
answer_html:
These are categories under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 that control the sale of medicines in India.

  1. Schedule H – prescription-only drugs; the label carries the symbol "Rx" and a warning that the drug is to be sold by retail only on the prescription of a registered medical practitioner (e.g. most antibiotics, antihypertensives).
  2. Schedule H1 – introduced to curb misuse of certain newer antibiotics, anti-TB drugs and habit-forming drugs (e.g. third/fourth-generation cephalosporins, carbapenems, alprazolam, codeine, tramadol); Rx in red with a boxed warning; the chemist must keep a register of prescriber, patient, drug and quantity.
  3. Schedule X – certain narcotic and psychotropic drugs (e.g. amphetamines, methylphenidate, some barbiturates); prescription in duplicate, one copy retained by the chemist; stored under lock and key with strict records.
